books.title: A Christmas Carol
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.setting: The City of London and Camden Town, across a single Christmas Eve and Christmas Day
books.lengthNote: Five staves, around 30,000 words — short enough to be read aloud in an evening, which is what Dickens did with it
books.openingLine: Marley was dead, to begin with.
books.summary: A moneylender who has organised his whole life around refusal is visited in one night by his dead partner and three spirits, and shown his own childhood, the households he has never entered and a grave nobody visits. Dickens calls the divisions staves rather than chapters because the book is meant to be performed, and the argument is not that Scrooge feels sorry but that he pays, visits and turns up the next morning.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of A Christmas Carol
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription of Dickens's text. References give the stave, which is the only division the book itself uses.

structure.label: Stave I
structure.title: Marley's Ghost
structure.summary: Scrooge is defined entirely by what he turns away: his nephew's invitation, two charity collectors, his clerk's fire. Then his dead partner arrives dragging the cash-boxes and ledgers he accumulated instead of a life, and promises three more visitors.

scenes.summary: Fred offers dinner and is refused; the charity collectors are told about prisons and the surplus population.
Marley's face appears in the door knocker, and Scrooge explains it away by arguing with his own digestion.
The ghost states the book's thesis — that mankind, not the ledger, was his business — and names the terms of the visitations.

structure.label: Stave II
structure.title: The First of the Three Spirits
structure.summary: The Ghost of Christmas Past shows scenes Scrooge cannot alter and does not dispute: the boy left at school, Fezziwig's ball, and Belle releasing him from an engagement he has already broken in everything but name. The spirit never argues; it simply declines to stop.

scenes.summary: A solitary child left behind at the holidays, and an old man crying at the sight of himself.
An employer who spends a small sum and buys enormous happiness, which Scrooge himself points out.
She names the golden idol that has displaced her, and asks whether he would choose her now.

structure.label: Stave III
structure.title: The Second of the Three Spirits
structure.summary: The present is shown as a series of doors opening: the Cratchits' dinner in Camden Town, Fred's party, miners, lighthouse keepers and sailors all keeping the day. The spirit quotes Scrooge's own words about the surplus population back at him, and then lifts his robe on two starved children.

scenes.summary: A small goose made to go round, and Tiny Tim's blessing, immediately shadowed by the spirit's answer about the empty seat.
Scrooge watches himself become a parlour game and laughs before he can stop himself.
Two children under the robe, named as Man's and not the spirit's, with a warning about which of them is the more dangerous.

structure.label: Stave IV
structure.title: The Last of the Spirits
structure.summary: The final spirit says nothing at all, so Scrooge has to do the interpreting himself: businessmen bargaining over whether to attend a cheap funeral, a laundress selling bed-curtains stripped from a corpse, an unwatched body, and a family relieved by a death. Only at the grave is the name supplied.

scenes.summary: Merchants treat a death as a minor scheduling question, and Scrooge listens without recognising the subject.
The dead man's curtains, shirt and blankets are haggled over by the people who were nearest him at the end.
Scrooge asks whether these are shadows of what will be or only what may be, and reads his own name.

structure.label: Stave V
structure.title: The End of It
structure.summary: The bed-curtains are still hanging, which is the proof Scrooge wants. The last stave is deliberately made of errands — a turkey bought, a donation whispered, a dinner attended, a salary raised — because Dickens will not let the change stand as a private feeling.

scenes.summary: Scrooge laughs, sends the prize turkey to Camden Town anonymously, and pays for the cab.
He finds the charity collector of the day before and names a sum the text never discloses to the reader.
Bob Cratchit arrives eighteen and a half minutes late, is threatened with a raise, and is told to buy more coal.

characters.name: Ebenezer Scrooge
characters.role: Moneylender, surviving partner of Scrooge and Marley
characters.summary: A man whose coldness is described as a climate he carries about with him rather than a mood he is in. Dickens gives him wit, arguing with his own hallucination about undigested beef, which is why his conversion can be believed: the intelligence was never missing, only the use he put it to.
characters.clue: He argues that a ghost may be a crumb of cheese, reads his own name on a headstone, and ends by buying a turkey too big for a boy to carry.

characters.name: Jacob Marley
characters.summary: Seven years dead and still doing the accounts. He is punished not for cruelty but for a narrow definition of business, and his chain is made of the objects of his trade, which makes the moral visible before it is stated.
characters.clue: He wears cash-boxes, ledgers and keys as a chain, and corrects the meaning of one word in a way that sets up the whole book.

characters.name: Bob Cratchit
characters.summary: Fifteen shillings a week, a white comforter instead of a greatcoat, and a coal-box he is not allowed to reach. Dickens is careful to show him sliding on the ice at Cornhill on the way home, so that his goodness is not simply the patience of a man too tired to object.
characters.clue: He tries to warm himself at a candle, drinks a toast to the man who underpays him, and slides down a lane of boys on his way back to Camden Town.

characters.name: Tiny Tim
characters.summary: He has very few lines and one of them has escaped the book entirely. Dickens keeps him from being merely pathetic by giving him a thought of his own about being seen in church, which turns his visible disability into something he has decided how to use.
characters.clue: He is carried on his father's shoulder, hopes the congregation notices his crutch for a reason of his own, and speaks the last four words of the book.

characters.name: Fred
characters.summary: He makes the case for Christmas in one long unbroken sentence and admits within it that the season has never earned him a penny, which is the strongest argument available. He keeps inviting his uncle to dinner every year and is refused every year, and goes on asking.
characters.clue: He comes in glowing from the frost, argues that a season which has never made him any money has still done him good, and never stops inviting his uncle to dinner.

characters.name: Belle
characters.role: The woman Scrooge was engaged to
characters.summary: She releases him in the gentlest possible terms and the terms are devastating: their contract was made when they were both poor, he is a different man, and she asks whether he would choose her today. She is right, and he cannot answer.
characters.clue: She hands back an engagement without raising her voice, naming the golden idol that has taken her place.

characters.name: Mr Fezziwig
characters.role: The master Scrooge was apprenticed to
characters.summary: An employer who spends a few pounds on a party and buys an amount of happiness that Scrooge, watching, can only describe as a fortune. He is in the book to prove that the alternative to Scrooge's conduct exists inside commerce rather than outside it.
characters.clue: He calls a halt to work, has the shutters up in a minute, and turns a warehouse into a ballroom at very small expense.

characters.name: The Ghost of Christmas Past
characters.role: The first of the three spirits
characters.summary: A figure that is old and young at once, with a jet of light from its head that Scrooge keeps trying to cover. It offers no interpretation of anything it shows, which is the method: the scenes are left to do their own arguing.
characters.clue: Its light can be put out with a cap, and it answers every protest by showing one more thing.

characters.name: The Ghost of Christmas Present
characters.role: The second of the three spirits
characters.summary: A giant among heaped food who greets Scrooge as a man to be known better, and then spends the stave withholding comfort. He gives Scrooge's own words about the surplus population back to him unaltered, and finishes by opening his robe on two children he insists belong to mankind.
characters.clue: He sits on a throne of turkeys, geese and chestnuts, ages visibly in a single night, and keeps two starved children under his skirts.

characters.name: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come
characters.role: The third and last of the spirits
characters.summary: A shrouded shape that never speaks and only points. Because it supplies no commentary, every conclusion in the stave has to be reached by Scrooge himself, which is why the stave frightens him more than the chained ghost did.
characters.clue: It is draped, silent, and does nothing throughout but extend one hand.

themes.name: Whether a person can change
themes.summary: The book stakes everything on a claim most Victorian fiction makes slowly: that a settled character can be remade in one night. Dickens protects the claim by making the evidence cumulative rather than sudden, and by ending with actions rather than resolutions.
themes.development: Scrooge argues with the first ghost, watches the second in silence, and by the fourth is on the ground asking whether what he has seen is fixed. The last stave answers in errands.

themes.name: Poverty and responsibility
themes.summary: Dickens attacks a habit of thought rather than wealth as such. Scrooge's objection to charity is not that money is dear but that institutions already exist, and the book's method is to take him to the places where the institutional answer stops being available.
themes.development: The collectors are refused in Stave I; the same language is turned round on Scrooge in Stave III; Ignorance and Want make the argument visible before Stave IV shows what the refusal costs.

themes.name: Memory and time
themes.summary: The three spirits are three tenses, and the book's structure is a grammar lesson. What the past supplies is not nostalgia but evidence: Scrooge weeps at the schoolboy because he has been given the one perspective he has been refusing, his own.
themes.development: Past explains, present indicts, future threatens; Stave V collapses all three into a single morning in which Scrooge says he will live in all of them at once.

themes.name: Business and the meaning of a word
themes.summary: Marley's correction of one noun is the hinge of the whole book. Scrooge and Marley have treated business as a trade; the ghost redefines it as everything a person is answerable for, and the rest of the story tests the new definition against a turkey, a coal-box and a salary.
themes.development: Stated as doctrine by Marley, dramatised by Fezziwig as something an employer may actually do, and settled in Stave V when Scrooge raises a wage.

themes.name: Christmas and community
themes.summary: Christmas in the book is not a feeling but a set of doors: dinners, parties, toasts, games, the ship's crew and the lighthouse keepers. Its power over Scrooge is that it is happening whether or not he attends, and the spirits' argument is largely just to show him the attendance.
themes.development: Fred's speech puts the case; Stave III proves it across an absurd range of places; Stave IV shows the alternative, a death nobody feels obliged to attend.

themes.name: Isolation
themes.summary: Scrooge's loneliness is presented as an achievement rather than an accident — something he has taken trouble over, warning human sympathy to keep its distance. The book's cruellest stroke is that the future it shows him is not damnation but simply more of the same, uninterrupted.
themes.development: The solitary oyster of Stave I becomes the solitary child of Stave II and the unattended body of Stave IV; the pattern is one life shown three times.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator who speaks openly to the reader, arguing, joking and insisting.
techniques.inThisBook: The book opens by haggling with the reader about a simile — what exactly is dead about a doornail — and only then explains that the point must be conceded or nothing wonderful can follow.

techniques.name: Simile
techniques.definition: An explicit comparison using like or as.
techniques.inThisBook: Scrooge is hard as flint, solitary as an oyster and dead as a doornail by proxy; in the last stave the same device returns inverted, as a feather, an angel, a schoolboy and a drunken man in one breath.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: Abstractions given bodies and names so an argument can be seen.
techniques.inThisBook: Ignorance and Want are children with names on them, and Marley's chain is a balance sheet made wearable; the technique lets Dickens put a social argument on stage without stopping the story.

techniques.name: Gothic machinery
techniques.definition: Bells, darkness, apparitions, graves and locked rooms used to produce dread.
techniques.inThisBook: Every Gothic device here is made to do moral work: the knocker, the clanking chain and the shrouded figure all produce evidence rather than atmosphere alone.

techniques.name: Structural repetition
techniques.definition: The same shape repeated with variations so that changes register.
techniques.inThisBook: Three spirits, three visitations, three refusals in Stave I answered by three acts of generosity in Stave V; the book is built so the reader can hear the rhyme.

techniques.name: Cold as character
techniques.definition: Weather and temperature used as a description of a person rather than a setting.
techniques.inThisBook: Scrooge carries his own low temperature about with him, ices his office in the dog-days and cannot be chilled by any wind — the metaphor is established before a single ghost appears.

quotations.text: Marley was dead, to begin with. There is no doubt whatever about that.
quotations.context: The opening sentences of the book.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'to begin with' is doing two jobs: it dates the death and it flags the fact as a premise the reader has to accept before anything else can be built on it. Dickens spends the next paragraph arguing about doornails precisely so that the death itself slips past unexamined.

quotations.text: Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster.
quotations.context: The first full description of Scrooge, before any action.
quotations.analysis: Three of the four terms are about being closed rather than being cruel, and the flint image concedes that the fire is in there and simply has never been struck. An oyster is also something that can be opened, which is a quiet promise the book will keep in eighty pages.

quotations.text: He carried his own low temperature always about with him; he iced his office in the dog-days, and didn’t thaw it one degree at Christmas.
quotations.context: Continuing the opening portrait of Scrooge.
quotations.analysis: The cold is not something he suffers but something he emits, which makes his effect on the people round him a physical fact rather than an opinion about his manners. 'One degree' turns the sentence into a measurement, the language Scrooge himself would use.

quotations.text: a good time; a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time; the only time I know of, in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely
quotations.speaker: Fred
quotations.context: Fred answering his uncle's demand to know what reason he has to be merry.
quotations.analysis: Fred's whole defence arrives as a single unbroken sentence with the clauses piling up, which is the opposite of Scrooge's clipped questions and refusals. He then concedes the accounting point — Christmas has never put gold or silver in his pocket — and argues that it has done him good anyway, meeting his uncle on his own ground and declining to stay there.

quotations.text: “Are there no prisons?” asked Scrooge.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: His first reply to the two gentlemen collecting for the poor.
quotations.analysis: He answers a request for money with a question about institutions, which moves the conversation from particular people to public provision and lets him leave without giving anything. Four words also make him sound reasonable, and the book has to spend three staves undoing that impression.

quotations.text: “If they would rather die,” said Scrooge, “they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population.”
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Told that many would rather die than go to the workhouse.
quotations.analysis: The phrase belongs to political economy rather than to malice: it treats people as a quantity in excess of a total. Dickens stores it carefully, and in Stave III has the Ghost of Christmas Present quote it back word for word while Scrooge is looking at a child who may be the one it applies to.

quotations.text: There’s more of gravy than of grave about you, whatever you are!
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Explaining to Marley's ghost why he will not believe in it.
quotations.analysis: A pun under that much pressure is a sign of nerve, and it tells us the man is not stupid, only committed. Dickens needs this joke: a Scrooge with no wit could be frightened into reform, and reform by fright alone is exactly what the last stave has to disprove.

quotations.text: “I wear the chain I forged in life,” replied the Ghost. “I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it.”
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: Answering Scrooge's question about why he is fettered.
quotations.analysis: Free will is named twice in one sentence, which removes any suggestion that this is a punishment imposed from outside. The chain is made of cash-boxes, ledgers and keys, so what he is wearing is not a penalty for his trade but his trade itself, simply weighed.

quotations.text: “Business!” cried the Ghost, wringing its hands again. “Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence were, all, my business.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: After Scrooge says that Marley was always a good man of business.
quotations.analysis: The argument is won by repeating a single word until its meaning shifts under it: five uses of 'business' in three sentences, each one widening the term. Marley does not tell Scrooge to stop being a man of business; he tells him he has been doing a small part of the job and calling it the whole.

quotations.text: It is required of every man, that the spirit within him should walk abroad among his fellow-men, and travel far and wide; and, if that spirit goes not forth in life, it is condemned to do so after death.
quotations.speaker: Marley's Ghost
quotations.context: Explaining what kind of afterlife he is serving.
quotations.analysis: The punishment is exactly the neglected duty, performed compulsorily and too late — the ghost is not in torment for anything he did but for a journey he declined to make. It also quietly explains the plot: Scrooge is about to be walked round London against his will.

quotations.text: “The school is not quite deserted,” said the Ghost. “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Past
quotations.context: Arriving at the schoolroom of Scrooge's boyhood.
quotations.analysis: The ghost describes the boy in the present tense and in the third person, so that Scrooge hears his own childhood reported as a piece of news about a stranger. 'Solitary' has already been used of the adult oyster, and the repetition makes the loneliness a continuous condition rather than a result.

quotations.text: He has the power to render us happy or unhappy; to make our service light or burdensome; a pleasure or a toil.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Defending Fezziwig after the spirit remarks that the ball cost only a few pounds.
quotations.analysis: Dickens notes that Scrooge says this 'speaking unconsciously like his former, not his latter self' — the argument for decent employment comes out of Scrooge's own mouth before he has agreed to it. It also states the case in the vocabulary of power and service, not charity, which is why it will hold in the final stave.

quotations.text: “It matters little,” she said softly. “To you, very little. Another idol has displaced me; and, if it can cheer and comfort you in time to come as I would have tried to do, I have no just cause to grieve.”
quotations.speaker: Belle
quotations.context: Releasing the young Scrooge from their engagement.
quotations.analysis: She accuses him of idolatry and then immediately withdraws her own standing to complain about it, which leaves him nothing to push against. 'Idol' is the strongest word in the sentence and the only religious one in a scene otherwise conducted entirely in the language of contracts.

quotations.text: “Come in!” exclaimed the Ghost. “Come in! and know me better, man!”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: Scrooge's first sight of the second spirit, among heaped food.
quotations.analysis: An invitation, not a summons — the opposite of Stave I, where Scrooge spent the whole evening refusing to come in or let anyone else. The word 'man' at the end is a greeting between equals, and it is the first time anyone in the book has addressed him with that kind of warmth.

quotations.text: He told me, coming home, that he hoped the people saw him in the church, because he was a cripple, and it might be pleasant to them to remember upon Christmas Day who made lame beggars walk and blind men see.
quotations.speaker: Bob Cratchit
quotations.context: Bob reporting what Tiny Tim said on the way back from church.
quotations.analysis: Tim has thought about how he is looked at and decided what he wants the looking to do, which makes him an agent in the scene rather than an object of pity. The thought reaches the reader at two removes — the child told his father, the father tells his wife — so the boy's dignity is never staged for effect.

quotations.text: “God bless us every one!” said Tiny Tim, the last of all.
quotations.speaker: Tiny Tim
quotations.context: The end of the Cratchits' Christmas toast.
quotations.analysis: 'The last of all' places him at the end of a queue of speakers, the smallest voice in the room, and Dickens gives the line no emphasis whatever. It returns as the last sentence of the book, by which time the reader has been shown a future in which it was not said.

quotations.text: This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want. Beware of them both, and all of their degree, but most of all beware this boy, for on his brow I see that written which is Doom, unless the writing be erased.
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: Revealing the two children clinging beneath his robe.
quotations.analysis: The spirit has just said the children are Man's, not his, which places the responsibility before the allegory arrives. Ignorance is ranked above Want as the greater danger, which is a specific political claim about schooling rather than relief, and 'unless the writing be erased' leaves the sentence open in a book whose whole subject is whether a foreseen end can still be changed.

quotations.text: “Are there no prisons?” said the Spirit, turning on him for the last time with his own words. “Are there no workhouses?”
quotations.speaker: The Ghost of Christmas Present
quotations.context: The spirit's final words, immediately after showing Ignorance and Want.
quotations.analysis: Nothing is added and nothing is explained; the whole rebuke consists of Scrooge's own sentences handed back at the right moment. Dickens has waited two staves to use them, and the delay is what gives the repetition its force — the reader recognises the words before Scrooge does.

quotations.text: Are these the shadows of the things that Will be, or are they shadows of the things that May be only?
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: At the neglected grave, before he is made to read the name on it.
quotations.analysis: The question the whole book turns on, and the silent spirit refuses to answer it. Scrooge is asking about grammar — the difference between a future tense and a conditional — and the novella's position is that the difference is entirely made of what he does on Christmas morning.

quotations.text: I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year. I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future. The Spirits of all Three shall strive within me.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Clutching at the robe of the last spirit, beside his own headstone.
quotations.analysis: He promises to keep all three tenses running at once, which is a precise description of what the book has just done to him. 'Try' is the honest word in the sentence: the vow is made in terror at a graveside, and Dickens leaves a whole stave to test whether it survives daylight.

quotations.text: I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy, I am as giddy as a drunken man.
quotations.speaker: Scrooge
quotations.context: Christmas morning, tangled in his own stockings.
quotations.analysis: The same device that fixed him in Stave I — hard as flint, solitary as an oyster — comes back running in the other direction, four similes where there had been four. Two of them, the schoolboy and the drunken man, restore exactly the parts of a life the earlier staves showed him losing.

quotations.text: Scrooge was better than his word. He did it all, and infinitely more; and to Tiny Tim, who did not die, he was a second father.
quotations.context: The narrator's account of what followed.
quotations.analysis: 'Who did not die' is slipped in as a subordinate clause, as though it were incidental, and it is the single most important fact in the book. Dickens measures the conversion by other people's outcomes rather than by Scrooge's feelings, which is why the sentence is about what he was to somebody rather than what he became.

quotations.text: And so, as Tiny Tim observed, “God Bless Us, Every One!”
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novella.
quotations.analysis: The book closes by handing its last words to its smallest character, and by putting them in the past tense of reported speech — 'observed' — as though the blessing were a settled matter of record. The capitals are new since Stave III: the same four words, now printed as a title.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Chapman and Hall, as A Christmas Carol. In Prose. Being a Ghost Story of Christmas.

atAGlance.label: Illustrator
atAGlance.note: Four hand-coloured plates and four wood engravings for the first edition.

atAGlance.label: Divisions
atAGlance.note: A stave is the ruled set of lines music is written on; the title promises a carol, and the book keeps the promise.

atAGlance.label: Time span
atAGlance.note: Everything between Marley's arrival and the Christmas morning bells happens in a few hours of story time.

criticalViews.position: A social argument in the shape of a fable
criticalViews.summary: Read alongside Dickens's public speaking of 1843 and the reports on child labour he had been reading, the book looks like an intervention in the poor-relief debate that chose allegory because allegory sells at Christmas.
criticalViews.counter: It leaves the remedy with individual generosity: Scrooge raises one salary, and nothing in the system he defended in Stave I has been touched.

criticalViews.position: A conversion narrative
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading treats the book as a religious structure in secular dress — warning, examination of conscience, terror, penitence and works — with the spirits functioning as three stages of self-examination.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away how much of the change is produced by fear of a grave rather than by the memory and pity of the earlier staves.

criticalViews.position: The book that made Christmas
criticalViews.summary: A long-running argument in cultural history holds that the novella did not invent the festival but fixed a particular version of it — domestic, charitable, sentimental — at the moment when Christmas print and gift-giving were expanding fastest.
criticalViews.counter: The claim is easy to overstate: carols, feasting and seasonal charity long predate 1843, and the book's popularity may record a change as much as cause it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens present Scrooge's transformation?
essayQuestions.focus: Character, structure and proof
plan: Start with the Stave I portrait and note that the flint image already concedes the fire is present and unstruck.
Show the ghosts working by different methods: the past supplies evidence, the present indicts, the future threatens and says nothing.
Use the moment in Stave II where Scrooge defends Fezziwig 'unconsciously like his former, not his latter self' as the first sign of movement.
Argue about the mechanism: is he reformed by pity at the schoolroom, or by terror at the grave, and does the book need both?
Close on Stave V, where Dickens measures the change in turkeys, cab fares, coal and a salary rather than in feelings.

essayQuestions.question: What does A Christmas Carol say about poverty and responsibility?
essayQuestions.focus: The Poor Law, charity and the limits of the fable
plan: Open with the charity collectors: Scrooge answers a request for money with a question about institutions.
Track the phrase about the surplus population from Stave I to the moment the Ghost of Christmas Present returns it in Stave III.
Read Ignorance and Want closely, noting that the spirit calls them Man's and ranks Ignorance as the greater danger.
Set the Cratchit scenes against the Stave IV visit to old Joe's shop, where poverty produces theft rather than loyalty.
Weigh the ending: one employer improves, which may be the book's answer or the limit of it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens use the supernatural in the novella?
essayQuestions.focus: Gothic form doing moral work
plan: Establish the ground rules: the narrator insists on Marley's death so that the return can mean something.
Compare the three spirits as three kinds of evidence — shown, opened and withheld.
Examine why the silent spirit frightens Scrooge most, and what work the silence forces him to do.
Look at Marley's chain as an allegory that is also a stage property, visible to an audience at a public reading.
Decide whether the supernatural machinery makes the social argument sharper or lets the reader off it.

essayQuestions.question: 'The book's real subject is time, not money.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Past, present and future as structure
plan: Set out the design: three spirits, three tenses, and a story that takes one night to cover a lifetime.
Use the schoolroom and Belle's release to show the past functioning as evidence rather than nostalgia.
Note how Stave III insists on simultaneity — miners, sailors and a lighthouse all keeping the day at once.
Test the case on Scrooge's question at the grave about shadows of what will be and what may be only.
Answer with Stave IV's vow to live in all three tenses at once, and ask whether money or time is what he has been wasting.

discussionQuestions: The last spirit never speaks. Does that make it more frightening than Marley, and if so why?
Scrooge raises one clerk's wages. Is that a solution to anything the book has described?
Dickens calls the divisions staves and the book a carol. What does the musical framing change about how you read it?
Tiny Tim has very few lines. Is he a character or a device, and does the distinction matter?
Would the conversion be as convincing if Stave V ended in the bedroom rather than in the street?

timeline.label: Dickens born in Portsmouth
timeline.detail: The family's later collapse into debt gave him the clerk's-eye view of London money that runs through the novella.

timeline.label: Poor Law Amendment Act
timeline.detail: The workhouse system Scrooge names so confidently when he is asked for a donation.

timeline.label: Dickens speaks in Manchester
timeline.detail: He addressed the Athenaeum there in October, on education and poverty, weeks before beginning the book.

timeline.label: A Christmas Carol published
timeline.detail: Chapman and Hall issued it on 19 December as a gift book with gilt edges and John Leech's illustrations; the production costs cut deeply into Dickens's profit.

timeline.label: Stage versions within weeks
timeline.detail: Edward Stirling's adaptation opened at the Adelphi Theatre in February, one of several unauthorised dramatisations.

timeline.label: The Chimes

timeline.label: Dickens begins reading the Carol in public
timeline.detail: The first readings were given in Birmingham at the end of the year, and he went on performing an abridged text for the rest of his life.

The last of the Christmas books, and the inverse experiment: a man granted the power to forget.
Dickens twenty years later on the same question of what money does to a person's judgement of the people who raised them.
The domestic side of the Christmas books, and a useful contrast with the Carol's social sharpness.
The customs, food and print culture the novella arrived in and helped to shape.

books.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Athens and a wood outside it, over four days and one very long night
books.lengthNote: Around 2,100 lines, with four separate companies of characters to keep in the air
books.openingLine: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour Draws on apace
books.summary: A father asks the Duke of Athens to have his daughter killed if she will not marry the man he has chosen, and the comedy proceeds from there. Four young people run into a wood where a quarrelling fairy king and queen are already using a drug that makes the sleeper love whatever they see first, and a company of Athenian tradesmen are rehearsing a tragedy they cannot act. The play's interest is that magic does not invent the lovers' cruelty to one another; it only speeds it up.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of A Midsummer Night's Dream
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Modern editions based on the 1600 quarto may differ by a line or two.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A law, a deadline and a cast list
structure.summary: Theseus is four days from marrying a woman he defeated in battle when Egeus arrives demanding the Athenian law that lets a father dispose of a daughter. Hermia is given a month to obey, die or enter a convent; she and Lysander agree to run, tell Helena, and Helena tells Demetrius. In a separate room six tradesmen are allocating parts in a play about a double suicide.

scenes.title: The law
scenes.summary: Egeus demands his right; Theseus upholds it; the lovers plan to escape and Helena betrays the plan.

scenes.title: The casting
scenes.summary: Quince hands out parts and Bottom offers to play all of them.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A quarrel that has spoiled the weather
structure.summary: Oberon and Titania have fallen out over a stolen Indian boy, and the dispute has stopped the seasons behaving. Oberon sends for a flower whose juice makes the sleeper dote on whatever they first see, intending it for his wife, and adds an instruction about the Athenian youth he has just watched treat a woman badly. Puck anoints the wrong Athenian.

scenes.title: The flower
scenes.summary: Oberon and Titania quarrel; Helena pursues Demetrius through the wood; Puck is sent for love-in-idleness.

scenes.title: The mistake
scenes.summary: Titania is drugged asleep; Puck finds Lysander and Hermia lying apart and anoints the wrong man.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Everything wrong at once
structure.summary: Bottom acquires an ass's head, his friends run, and the fairy queen wakes and falls in love with him. In the other half of the wood both men now love Helena, who is certain she is being mocked, and the two women who grew up together insult each other's height until the men go off to fight. Oberon has Puck fog the wood and put them all to sleep.

scenes.title: The ass's head
scenes.summary: The rehearsal is interrupted; Bottom is transformed and Titania wakes to adore him.

scenes.title: The quarrel
scenes.summary: Both men court Helena, the two women fall out, and Puck leads the rivals astray in the dark.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Waking up, and not asking questions
structure.summary: Oberon has what he wanted, releases Titania and says nothing about how he got it. Theseus finds the four lovers asleep in the wood, overrules Egeus and adds them to his own wedding — while Demetrius, alone of the four, is still under the drug. Bottom wakes last, in the middle of the stage, trying to describe something he has no words for.

scenes.title: The waking
scenes.summary: Titania is released; the hunt finds the lovers; Theseus overrules the law; Bottom wakes and gropes for his dream.

scenes.title: Back in Athens
scenes.summary: The players mourn their lost leading man until he walks in with news of a wedding.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The worst play ever performed, and a blessing
structure.summary: Three couples watch Pyramus and Thisbe, a tragedy of forbidden love and mistaken death performed by men who explain the wall and apologise for the lion. The court heckles it; the play they are mocking is the story they have just escaped. The fairies then come indoors to bless the marriages, and Puck asks the audience to call the whole thing a dream.

scenes.title: Pyramus and Thisbe, and the epilogue
scenes.summary: The mechanicals perform; the court comments; Oberon and Titania bless the house; Puck asks for pardon.

characters.name: Theseus
characters.summary: He begins by upholding a law that would kill a girl for choosing the wrong husband and ends by overruling it without explanation, having changed nothing about his beliefs in between. His great speech dismisses lovers, lunatics and poets as the same kind of unreliable witness, which is spoken in a play that has just shown the audience fairies.
characters.clue: He won his bride in battle, tells a girl her father made her as a seal makes an impression in wax, and does not believe a word of what the lovers report.

characters.name: Hippolyta
characters.role: Queen of the Amazons, betrothed to Theseus
characters.summary: She says very little and almost all of it disagrees with her future husband. When he explains away the lovers' night as imagination, she points out that four people telling the same story is evidence of something, which is the only argument in the play for believing the audience's own eyes.

characters.name: Egeus
characters.summary: He appears twice, asks for his daughter's death both times, and is then simply overruled and forgotten. Shakespeare gives the comedy's opening crisis to a man with no interior life at all, so that the law he invokes looks like a piece of machinery rather than a feeling.

characters.name: Hermia
characters.role: Egeus's daughter, in love with Lysander
characters.summary: Threatened with death in the first scene, she argues back in front of a duke and then leaves the city. In the wood she loses her certainty piece by piece — first her lover, then her oldest friend — and the play's harshest comedy is about her height, which is the one thing she cannot answer.
characters.clue: Ordered to marry a man she does not want or die, she runs; by dawn she is being called a bead, an acorn and a painted maypole by her closest friend.

characters.name: Lysander
characters.role: An Athenian in love with Hermia
characters.summary: He is Demetrius's equal in everything except the father's approval, which is the whole plot. Drugged, he turns on Hermia with a viciousness the spell does not really account for, and the play never gives him a line acknowledging what he said.

characters.name: Helena
characters.role: In love with Demetrius, who has abandoned her
characters.summary: She betrays her friend's escape plan in order to be thanked by a man who despises her, and knows exactly how little that is worth while she does it. Her offer to be treated like a dog is the most uncomfortable speech in the comedy, and when both men suddenly want her she assumes it is a joke at her expense.
characters.clue: She hands over her best friend's secret to a man who has just told her he is sick when he looks at her, and asks only to be beaten and followed like a spaniel.

characters.name: Demetrius
characters.summary: He courted Helena, dropped her, and threatens her with violence in the wood when she will not stop following him. He is the only one of the four never released from the drug: the comedy's final pairing rests on an enchantment nobody on stage mentions again.

relationships.label: abandoned, then restored to by magic

characters.name: Oberon
characters.summary: He wants a boy his wife is raising and drugs her into humiliation until she gives him up. The same night he also takes pity on a woman he has never met and tries to fix her love life, and the play makes no attempt to reconcile the two impulses in one character.
characters.clue: He watches everything from the edge of the stage, corrects one couple out of pity and destroys his wife's dignity to win an argument about a child.

characters.name: Titania
characters.summary: Her account of the ruined seasons makes the fairy quarrel a matter of flooded fields and human disease, which is a larger claim than any other character makes for themselves. She keeps the changeling boy out of loyalty to his dead mother, and loses him while drugged into loving a weaver with an ass's head.
characters.clue: She keeps a dead friend's child, blames the rotted corn and the drowned fields on her marriage, and wakes to find herself feeding apricots to a man with an ass's head.

characters.name: Puck
characters.summary: He belongs to English village folklore rather than to Athens, and he is brought into the play as both an employee and a hazard: he does what he is told and enjoys what goes wrong with it. He is given the last word, and uses it to offer the audience a way out of everything they have seen.
characters.clue: He frightens village girls, curdles the milk, mistakes one Athenian for another, and finally asks the audience to pretend they were asleep.

characters.name: Nick Bottom
characters.summary: He wants to play every part in the play and is the only mortal who meets the fairies awake and is not frightened of them. He is also the only one who tries to describe the night afterwards, and the speech in which he fails — senses swapped over, words giving out — is the play's most serious statement about what has happened to everyone.
characters.clue: A weaver who offers to play the lion, the lady and the tyrant, is given an ass's head, and wakes up trying to say what his eye has heard.

themes.name: Love without reason
themes.summary: The play's working definition of love is that it cannot be argued with and cannot be trusted: Helena says it looks with the mind rather than the eyes, Bottom observes that reason and love keep little company, and a flower produces the same effect as a lifetime's devotion. What the drug does is not unnatural; it is only quicker.
themes.development: Stated as theory in 1.1, demonstrated on the lovers in Acts II and III, and left standing at the end with Demetrius still under the influence.

themes.name: Law, fathers and consent
themes.summary: Athens opens with a father asking a duke to enforce his right to kill his daughter, and the duke agreeing that this is the law. Nothing in the last act repeals it — Theseus simply stops applying it, which leaves the comedy's happy ending resting on a ruler's mood.
themes.development: Egeus makes his demand in 1.1 and repeats it in 4.1; Theseus overrules him without argument, and Egeus is given nothing further to say.

themes.name: Transformation
themes.summary: Everyone in the wood is altered and almost nobody notices at the time. The one visible change, Bottom's head, is the least distressing of them: it is the invisible changes — a man waking to loathe the woman he loved — that the play treats as frightening.
themes.development: Titania is drugged in 2.2, Lysander in the same scene, Bottom transformed in 3.1; three of the four are undone by 4.1 and the fourth is not.

themes.name: Night, sleep and the morning story
themes.summary: The play's settlement depends on everybody agreeing to call the night a dream. Theseus produces the sceptical account, Hippolyta doubts it, Bottom cannot fit his experience into words, and Puck finally offers the whole audience the same bargain.
themes.development: The lovers wake half-remembering in 4.1; Theseus explains it away in 5.1; the epilogue makes the explanation the audience's responsibility.

themes.name: Theatre about theatre
themes.summary: The mechanicals worry about the things real companies worry about — casting, props, whether the audience will be frightened, whether a boy can play a woman — and solve them by explaining everything aloud. Their failure demonstrates the conventions the surrounding play is relying on at that exact moment.
themes.development: Rehearsal in 1.2 and 3.1, performance in 5.1, and an epilogue that asks the same indulgence the mechanicals begged for in their prologue.

themes.name: Who is allowed to decide
themes.summary: Fathers, dukes and fairy kings all get what they want, and each of them frames it as correction rather than force. The play lets that pattern show by repeating it at three social levels within an hour of stage time.
themes.development: Egeus invokes the law, Theseus invokes his sword and his wedding, Oberon invokes a flower; the changeling boy changes hands offstage and is never mentioned again.

techniques.name: Verse registers
techniques.definition: Giving different groups of characters distinct metres and forms.
techniques.inThisBook: The court speaks blank verse, the lovers slide into rhymed couplets as they become more ridiculous, the fairies use a short trochaic line, and the mechanicals speak prose except when performing, where they are given deliberately terrible verse.

techniques.name: Play within a play
techniques.definition: A staged performance watched by characters who are themselves being watched.
techniques.inThisBook: Pyramus and Thisbe is a tragedy of parental prohibition and mistaken death, performed for four people who have just escaped one. The court's mockery is aimed at conventions the audience has been accepting all evening.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: One actor taking two parts, so that the audience sees a resemblance the text does not state.
techniques.inThisBook: Theseus and Oberon, Hippolyta and Titania, and Philostrate and Puck have often been doubled since Peter Brook's 1970 production, which turns the fairy quarrel into the same marriage seen at night.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A sudden drop from the elevated to the ridiculous.
techniques.inThisBook: It is the engine of the whole last act — 'the wall is down that parted their fathers' — and also of the wood, where a fairy queen's love speech is answered by a weaver talking about the difficulty of getting out of a wood.

techniques.name: The catalogue
techniques.definition: A list used to build a world faster than description can.
techniques.inThisBook: Oberon's bank of wild thyme, oxlips, violets, woodbine, musk-roses and eglantine gives the wood a physical existence on a bare stage in six lines, and Titania's list of rotted corn and drowned fields does the same for the damage.

techniques.name: Epilogue
techniques.definition: A direct address to the audience after the story has closed.
techniques.inThisBook: Puck offers the audience the same excuse the characters have used on themselves — that they were asleep and this was a dream — which makes accepting the comedy an act the spectators have to perform.

quotations.text: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour Draws on apace; four happy days bring in Another moon: but, O, methinks, how slow This old moon wanes!
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The opening lines, four days before the wedding.
quotations.analysis: The play starts a clock and immediately complains about it, which is how the whole comedy will run: everything is dated to the moon. The image Theseus reaches for — an old woman withering away a young man's inheritance — puts impatience and money in the first speech of a play about who may marry whom.

quotations.text: Hippolyta, I woo'd thee with my sword, And won thy love, doing thee injuries; But I will wed thee in another key,
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: To his bride, in the same opening speech.
quotations.analysis: He describes a conquest as a courtship without appearing to notice the difference, and 'doing thee injuries' is left in the sentence as a plain fact. 'In another key' is a musical term, so the change he promises is one of tone rather than of relation — which is precisely the question Oberon and Titania will act out in the wood.

quotations.text: I beg the ancient privilege of Athens, As she is mine, I may dispose of her: Which shall be either to this gentleman Or to her death, according to our law
quotations.speaker: Egeus
quotations.context: Asking the duke to enforce his right over his daughter.
quotations.analysis: 'Dispose of' is a term for property, and the alternatives offered are a husband or an execution, in that order and in the same sentence. Egeus is not presented as a monster: he is invoking something he calls ancient and the duke agrees it exists, which is what makes the first scene of a comedy cold.

quotations.text: To you your father should be as a god; One that composed your beauties, yea, and one To whom you are but as a form in wax By him imprinted and within his power To leave the figure or disfigure it.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Advising Hermia to obey, before setting out her choices.
quotations.analysis: The image makes a daughter a seal impression rather than a person, and the pun on figure and disfigure lets destruction sound like a matter of craft. It is offered as kindly counsel, which is the point: the play's cruelty is spoken in the register of good sense.

quotations.text: The course of true love never did run smooth;
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: Comforting Hermia after the duke's judgement.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted line in the play is a young man consoling his girlfriend by telling her that their situation is an old story, and he is about to list the ways love goes wrong as if reciting from a book. What follows is not comfort but a catalogue of obstacles, ending in the image of darkness swallowing light.

quotations.text: And ere a man hath power to say 'Behold!' The jaws of darkness do devour it up: So quick bright things come to confusion.
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: The end of his list of the ways love is thwarted.
quotations.analysis: Three heavy monosyllables — jaws, darkness, devour — arrive in a comedy fifteen minutes old. 'Quick' means living as well as fast, so the line describes both a flash of lightning and a short life, and it is the closest this play comes to the tragedy the mechanicals will perform badly in the last act.

quotations.text: Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind:
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Alone, deciding to betray Hermia's escape plan to Demetrius.
quotations.analysis: She works out the play's theory of love before any magic has appeared, and then acts on it in the worst available way. The rhymed couplets she has slipped into mark the moment a character stops talking to other people and starts constructing an argument for herself.

quotations.text: Let me play the lion too: I will roar, that I will do any man's heart good to hear me;
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: At the casting, having already asked to play Pyramus and Thisbe.
quotations.analysis: 'Too' is the joke: he has accepted the lead and wants the other parts as well, including the one with no words. Quince talks him out of it by explaining that a convincing lion would get the company hanged, which is the first of the play's several reminders that theatre in 1595 was a licensed activity.

quotations.text: Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: The first meeting of the fairy king and queen in the play.
quotations.analysis: Six words establish that this marriage is in the middle of a long argument, and the greeting inverts a courtesy — well met — into its opposite. Everything the fairies do for the rest of the night is a move in a quarrel that began before the audience arrived.

quotations.text: And thorough this distemperature we see The seasons alter: hoary-headed frosts Far in the fresh lap of the crimson rose,
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: In the middle of her account of the damage the quarrel has done.
quotations.analysis: The speech puts flooded fields, rotted corn and human disease on the domestic argument's account, which is a far larger claim than any mortal in the play makes. It also dates the comedy for the first audience: the mid-1590s were years of ruined harvests and abnormal weather, and this is the play noticing.

quotations.text: Set your heart at rest: The fairy land buys not the child of me. His mother was a votaress of my order:
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Refusing to hand over the changeling boy.
quotations.analysis: Her reason for keeping the child is not possessiveness but a promise to a dead friend, and the speech that follows is the warmest thing in the play — two women laughing on a beach at the shape of the sails. The boy himself never appears, and after Act IV nobody mentions him again.

quotations.text: It fell upon a little western flower, Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound, And maidens call it love-in-idleness.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: Describing how Cupid's arrow missed an imperial votaress and struck a flower.
quotations.analysis: The drug that drives the rest of the plot is given an origin story in three lines, and its colour is a wound. 'Love-in-idleness' is a real country name for the wild pansy, so the enchantment arrives dressed as folklore rather than as sorcery — which is how the play prefers its magic.

quotations.text: I'll put a girdle round about the earth In forty minutes.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Sent to fetch the flower from wherever it grows.
quotations.analysis: The boast fixes the scale of the wood: the errand crosses the world and takes less time than an act. It also quietly sets the play's clock against the audience's, since forty minutes is roughly how long the fairies are then offstage.

quotations.text: I am your spaniel; and, Demetrius, The more you beat me, I will fawn on you: Use me but as your spaniel, spurn me, strike me, Neglect me, lose me; only give me leave, Unworthy as I am, to follow you.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Pursuing Demetrius into the wood after he has told her to go away.
quotations.analysis: Four imperatives in a row, all of them asking to be hurt, and the one thing she requests is permission rather than affection. Oberon overhears this, which is why he intervenes — the play's only act of supernatural kindness is provoked by a woman debasing herself in front of a stranger.

quotations.text: Your wrongs do set a scandal on my sex: We cannot fight for love, as men may do; We should be wood and were not made to woo.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: After Demetrius threatens to do her mischief in the wood.
quotations.analysis: She identifies the rule she is breaking and states the cost of breaking it in one couplet. 'Wood' puns on wooed and on the old word for mad, and also names the place she is standing in — three meanings in a monosyllable, all of them about a woman who has come to the wrong place to do the wrong thing.

quotations.text: reason and love keep little company together now-a-days; the more the pity that some honest neighbours will not make them friends.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Replying to the fairy queen's declaration of love, while wearing an ass's head.
quotations.analysis: The play's thesis is delivered in prose by the only character who has not been given the drug, and he treats the failure of reason and love as a neighbourly dispute that a bit of mediation might settle. It is also a polite way of telling a queen that she is not making sense.

quotations.text: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Watching the four lovers converge, having caused the confusion himself.
quotations.analysis: The line is usually quoted as detached wisdom; on stage it is an author admiring his own mistake. Puck has just proposed that they stay and watch, which makes the lovers' worst hour into an entertainment with two spectators — the same arrangement the audience is in.

quotations.text: So we grow together, Like to a double cherry, seeming parted, But yet an union in partition; Two lovely berries moulded on one stem;
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Accusing Hermia of joining the men in mocking her.
quotations.analysis: The most tender description of friendship in the play is made in the course of ending one, and every image in it is of two things that cannot be separated. 'Union in partition' is a paradox held together only by the grammar, which is what the friendship has become by this point in the night.

quotations.text: O, when she's angry, she is keen and shrewd! She was a vixen when she went to school; And though she be but little, she is fierce.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Hiding behind the men as Hermia loses her temper.
quotations.analysis: The line most often printed on posters is an insult delivered while retreating, and the evidence for it is what Hermia was like at school — the two women have known each other since childhood and are now using that knowledge as ammunition. Hermia's reply picks out the only word that matters to her: 'Little' again.

quotations.text: My Oberon! what visions have I seen! Methought I was enamour'd of an ass.
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Waking after Oberon has taken the changeling boy and released her.
quotations.analysis: She calls it a vision, he says nothing about what he did, and the boy is never mentioned again by either of them. Her next line — that her eyes now loathe his visage — is aimed at a man asleep three feet away, and the comedy depends on the audience finding that funny rather than looking at it too closely.

quotations.text: The eye of man hath not heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man's hand is not able to taste, his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream was.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Alone on stage, waking after the others have gone.
quotations.analysis: The senses have been shuffled, which is exactly right for someone describing an experience the available vocabulary does not cover; the pattern is a garbled echo of St Paul on what the eye has not seen. The mangling is the meaning — this is the only character who admits that something happened which cannot be tidied into a morning story.

quotations.text: The lunatic, the lover and the poet Are of imagination all compact:
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Dismissing the lovers' account of the night before the entertainment begins.
quotations.analysis: 'All compact' means made entirely of, so the three are not compared but identified. The speech is the rational case against everything the audience has just watched, delivered by a character out of Greek myth in a play with fairies in it, and Hippolyta's reply — that all four tell the same story — is the only answer it gets.

quotations.text: And as imagination bodies forth The forms of things unknown, the poet's pen Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: He intends this as evidence that poets are unreliable, and produces the best description of writing in Shakespeare while doing it. 'A local habitation and a name' is what a stage gives a story — an address and a cast list — so the sceptic accidentally states the terms on which the theatre he is standing in operates.

quotations.text: The best in this kind are but shadows; and the worst are no worse, if imagination amend them.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Answering Hippolyta's complaint that the mechanicals' play is the silliest stuff she ever heard.
quotations.analysis: The defence of bad acting is also a defence of all acting, and it is made by the man who has just explained that imagination is not to be trusted. Hippolyta's answer is the sharper one: then it must be your imagination and not theirs, which puts the work of the theatre squarely on the people watching.

quotations.text: If we shadows have offended, Think but this, and all is mended, That you have but slumber'd here While these visions did appear.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: The epilogue, spoken after the fairies have blessed the house.
quotations.analysis: 'Shadows' is Theseus's word for actors four hundred lines earlier, so the epilogue picks up the court's own dismissal and turns it into an apology. The offer is the one the characters have already accepted about themselves — call it a dream — and the rhymed tetrameter is the fairies' metre, which means the excuse is being made by the people who caused the trouble.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Usually placed close to Romeo and Juliet, whose plot the mechanicals accidentally perform as farce.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed for Thomas Fisher, whose title page says the play had been publicly acted by the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Ovid, Chaucer, English fairy lore and Shakespeare's own theatre, combined rather than adapted.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Court, lovers, fairies and players, each with a different kind of verse.

criticalViews.position: A wedding play
criticalViews.summary: The oldest account reads the comedy as an entertainment for an aristocratic marriage, pointing to the three weddings, the blessing of the house and the compliment to a virgin queen in Oberon's speech about the imperial votaress.
criticalViews.counter: No record connects it to any particular wedding, and the 1600 title page advertises public performance; the theory explains the ending but not the cruelty of Act III.

criticalViews.position: A darker wood
criticalViews.summary: Criticism and production since the middle of the twentieth century have emphasised the coercion in the play: a father demanding a death sentence, a husband drugging his wife, a woman asking to be beaten, and an ending that leaves one man enchanted.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far enough it makes the last act unplayable, and has to treat the mechanicals' comedy as an interruption rather than as the answer the play gives.

criticalViews.position: A play about theatre
criticalViews.summary: A third reading takes Pyramus and Thisbe as the centre: the comedy examines what an audience agrees to do, and the epilogue makes that agreement explicit.
criticalViews.counter: It can turn the lovers into a device and leave the fairy marriage — the one quarrel with consequences for crops and weather — as decoration.

essayQuestions.question: How does the wood change the people who enter it?
essayQuestions.focus: Transformation, law and the limits of magic
plan: Establish what Athens is: a city with a law that can kill a daughter, and a duke who enforces it in the first scene.
Show that the lovers' behaviour in the wood exaggerates what they already do — Helena betrays Hermia before any magic is used.
Read Bottom's transformation against Titania's: one is visible and harmless, the other invisible and humiliating.
Use 4.1 to ask what actually gets undone, and note that Demetrius is never released from the flower.
Conclude on the return to Athens: the law is not repealed, only set aside by a ruler in a good mood.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of women in the play.
essayQuestions.focus: Consent, friendship and the cost of the happy ending
plan: Begin with Hippolyta, won by the sword, and Hermia, offered a husband or a death, both in the first two hundred lines.
Trace Helena's self-abasement in 2.1 and ask what the play does with it: Oberon's pity, and no other consequence.
Use the double-cherry speech in 3.2 to show a friendship of years destroyed in a single scene, and by whom.
Examine Titania's account of the votaress: the one female relationship in the play that is not a rivalry, and the one that is broken offstage.
Weigh the three marriages of Act V against the means by which each was arranged.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of the mechanicals and their play?
essayQuestions.focus: Comedy, craft and theatrical convention
plan: Describe the rehearsal problems of 1.2 and 3.1 as real problems for a real company: casting, fright, the boy playing a woman.
Note that Pyramus and Thisbe is the plot of Romeo and Juliet and very nearly the plot of the lovers' night.
Show how their over-explaining — a man playing Wall, a man apologising for the lion — exposes the conventions the surrounding play relies on.
Read the court's heckling in 5.1 and Theseus's 'the best in this kind are but shadows' as a statement about all acting.
Close with Hippolyta's correction: the imagination that mends a bad play belongs to the audience, not the actors.

essayQuestions.question: 'The comedy ends by asking everyone to call the night a dream.' How satisfying is that ending?
essayQuestions.focus: Sleep, explanation and the epilogue
plan: Collect the waking scenes of 4.1 and note how little the lovers can retrieve and how readily they let it go.
Set Theseus's explanation of lunatic, lover and poet against Hippolyta's objection that four people agree.
Use Bottom's speech as the one refusal to tidy the experience into an account.
Consider what is left unresolved: the changeling boy, Egeus, Demetrius's enchantment.
Finish with Puck's epilogue, which offers the audience the same bargain the characters accepted, and decide whether taking it is a comfort or an evasion.

discussionQuestions: Demetrius is still under the spell at the end. Does that spoil the comedy, or is it the point of it?
Oberon drugs his wife into loving a man with an ass's head in order to win a custody dispute. Can the play be staged without that being cruel?
Helena asks to be treated like a dog. What is an audience supposed to feel during that speech?
The mechanicals perform the tragedy the lovers only just avoided. Why does Shakespeare put it at the end rather than the beginning?
Theseus says imagination cannot be trusted, in a play with fairies in it. Who wins that argument?

timeline.label: The play probably written
timeline.detail: Usually placed in the mid-1590s on stylistic grounds, close to Romeo and Juliet; no document fixes the year.

timeline.label: Francis Meres lists the play in Palladis Tamia
timeline.detail: The earliest external record that it existed, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto, printed for Thomas Fisher
timeline.detail: The title page says the play had been publicly acted by the Lord Chamberlain's Men. Most modern editions descend from this text.

timeline.label: Second Quarto, falsely dated 1600
timeline.detail: Set from Q1 and belonging to the group of reprints associated with Thomas Pavier.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, from the second quarto, with small changes including the substitution of Egeus for Philostrate in the last act.

timeline.label: Samuel Pepys sees the play and detests it
timeline.detail: His diary records one of the bluntest hostile verdicts in the play's reception history.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn composes the overture
timeline.detail: Written when he was seventeen, and still the music most audiences hear in their heads.

timeline.label: Madame Vestris stages the play at Covent Garden
timeline.detail: A production that helped establish the Victorian fairy-spectacle tradition.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn's incidental music
timeline.detail: Added sixteen years after the overture, and the source of the wedding march.

timeline.label: Reinhardt and Dieterle's Hollywood film
timeline.detail: With James Cagney as Bottom and Mickey Rooney as Puck: the play as a studio fantasy.

timeline.label: Britten's opera premieres at Aldeburgh
timeline.detail: The libretto begins in the wood rather than in Athens, shifting the balance from law to enchantment.

timeline.label: Peter Brook's white box production for the RSC
timeline.detail: Sally Jacobs's bare white set, trapezes and circus skills replaced painted foliage and changed how the play could look.

places.name: Athens
places.note: Theseus's city, where the law gives a father the right to dispose of his daughter.

places.name: Sparta
places.note: Named by Theseus and Hippolyta when they compare hunting dogs on the morning after.

places.name: Crete
places.note: Where Hippolyta once heard hounds bay a bear, in the same exchange.

places.name: Thessaly
places.note: The third of the hunting regions Theseus lists when boasting about his pack.

places.name: India
places.note: The changeling boy's country, and the spiced Indian air where Titania's votaress laughed at the sails.

places.name: Fleet Street, London
places.note: Thomas Fisher's shop at the sign of the White Hart, where the 1600 quarto was sold.

related.why: Written at about the same time, with the same plot of parental prohibition and mistaken death — played straight instead of as farce.
The other play of spirits, spells and interrupted entertainments, with the magic put to the business of government.
The other comedy in which leaving the city for a wood rearranges everybody's affections.
Desire misdirected without any magic at all, which makes a useful control on this play's flower.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller textual, critical and performance material.

books.title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
books.author: Mary Shelley
books.setting: Geneva, Ingolstadt, the Alps, the Orkneys and the Arctic ice, in the previous century
books.lengthNote: Four letters and twenty-four chapters, told by three narrators nested inside one another
books.openingLine: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.
books.summary: A student in Ingolstadt works out how to animate dead matter, succeeds, looks at what he has made and runs out of the room. The being he abandons teaches itself to speak and read, is driven off by everyone who sees it, and comes back to demand a companion. Shelley builds the whole argument as a set of nested testimonies, so that neither maker nor made ever gets to tell the story alone.
books.referenceStyle: chapter, with the outer frame given as Letter I to Letter IV

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Frankenstein — Mary Shelley's revised 1831 edition
sourceText.note: The text checked here is the one-volume 1831 revision, not the anonymous 1818 first edition. It can be identified from the inside: it carries Shelley's 1831 introduction about the summer at Geneva, it runs as twenty-four continuous chapters rather than three volumes, and Elizabeth Lavenza arrives as an orphan taken in by the Frankensteins rather than as Victor's cousin.

structure.label: Letters I-IV
structure.title: An explorer writes home and finds a better story than his own
structure.summary: Robert Walton, sailing north in search of a passage and a friend, writes to a sister who never answers. Ice closes around the ship, a huge figure crosses it on a sledge, and the next day the crew pulls aboard a starving European who has been chasing him. Everything that follows is inside a letter.

scenes.summary: Walton, at St Petersburgh, describes an expedition he expects to make him famous.
At Archangel he complains that he has no friend, and no one to correct him.
A short, confident note sent from open sea.
The ship is frozen in; the sledge is sighted; Victor Frankenstein comes aboard and begins to talk.

structure.label: Chapters I-V
structure.title: A Geneva childhood, a university, and one night in November
structure.summary: Victor describes an upbringing so protected that his own account can find nothing in it to blame. At Ingolstadt he moves from discredited alchemists to modern chemistry, works alone for two years, and animates the thing he has assembled. The success lasts one sentence; the horror begins in the next.

scenes.summary: The Frankenstein household, Elizabeth's arrival, and a boy's reading in Agrippa and Paracelsus.
His mother dies; at Ingolstadt, Waldman's lecture redirects him towards modern chemistry.
Two years in charnel houses and dissecting rooms; he breaks off his account to warn Walton.
The creature opens its eye; Victor flees, falls ill, and is nursed by Clerval.

structure.label: Chapters VI-X
structure.title: A child is killed and a servant is hanged for it
structure.summary: News from Geneva: William is dead. Victor sees the creature by lightning on the way home and says nothing while Justine Moritz is tried, persuaded to confess and executed. This is the section that makes the novel a moral problem rather than a horror story, because Victor's silence costs a life and he presents it as suffering.

scenes.summary: Clerval's friendship, then the letter announcing William's murder; a figure seen in a storm near Plainpalais.
Justine's trial and execution; Victor keeps what he knows to himself.
Grief-stricken travel in the Alps; on the Mer de Glace the creature approaches and asks to be heard.

structure.label: Chapters XI-XVI
structure.title: The being's own account of learning to be a person
structure.summary: For six chapters the novel hands its voice to the thing it has been calling a wretch. It describes sensation before language, a year of watching the De Lacey family through a chink, an education gathered from Volney, Milton and Goethe, and the moment Felix beats it out of the cottage. It has been benevolent and is becoming something else.

scenes.summary: First sensations, fire, hunger, flight from villages, and the hovel beside the De Lacey cottage.
Safie's arrival gives the creature language lessons by proxy, and the De Laceys' own history.
Three books, and Victor's laboratory journal; the blind old man listens until his family returns.
The cottage is abandoned; the creature saves a girl and is shot for it, then meets William.

structure.label: Chapters XVII-XXIII
structure.title: A promise made in Chamounix and broken in the Orkneys
structure.summary: The creature asks for one thing: a female of its own kind, and exile. Victor agrees, travels to England and Scotland, and tears the half-made companion apart with the creature watching at the window. The threat that follows is answered by a wedding, which is exactly what the threat was designed to produce.

scenes.summary: The bargain is struck; Victor delays for months, then leaves for England with Clerval.
London, Oxford, Scotland, and a hut on a remote Orkney island.
The second creature is destroyed; the creature promises to be with him on his wedding night.
Clerval is found strangled and Victor is charged; acquitted, he marries Elizabeth, who dies that night.

structure.label: Chapter XXIV and Walton's close
structure.title: Two ruined men and an argument that will not close
structure.summary: Victor chases the creature north until the ice stops both of them, and dies on Walton's ship still recommending ambition in the same breath as warning against it. The creature comes aboard to grieve over him, tells Walton what the pursuit cost on its side, and leaves. Nobody is left to settle who was right.

scenes.summary: The pursuit across Russia and the ice; Victor's last speech to Walton's mutinous crew.
Victor dies; the creature is found weeping over the body and speaks for itself one last time.

characters.name: Victor Frankenstein
characters.summary: He gives two years to the problem of animating dead matter and about ten seconds to the question of what he will do afterwards. His narration is the novel's central difficulty: it is fluent, self-accusing and consistently arranged so that the things he chose look like things that happened to him.
characters.clue: He works alone for two years to make something live, then runs out of the room when it opens its eye, and spends the rest of his life calling that moment his misfortune.
traits: never quite culpable in his own account

characters.name: The creature
characters.role: The being Victor assembles and abandons
characters.summary: Nameless on purpose, and called daemon, wretch and fiend by everyone who describes him, including himself. He is the best reader in the book and the best speaker in it, and he makes his case for a companion in the formal language of rights before he makes his case for revenge.
characters.clue: Eight feet tall, articulate, self-taught from three stolen books, and asking only for one other creature in the world who will not scream at the sight of him.

characters.name: Robert Walton
characters.summary: An amateur with money, no formal education and a plan to reach the pole, who writes home that he wants a friend more than he wants the passage. He is offered the story as a warning and never quite says whether he has taken it; his crew, not his conscience, turns the ship around.
characters.clue: He is frozen into the ice north of Archangel, writing letters to a sister who cannot reply, when a sledge crosses his bow carrying the man whose story fills this book.

characters.name: Elizabeth Lavenza
characters.role: Taken into the Frankenstein household as a child; Victor's betrothed
characters.summary: Presented to Victor as a gift when they are children, and described by him for the rest of his life as a possession he was given. Her longest piece of writing offers to release him from the engagement; he marries her anyway, knowing what has been promised for the wedding night.
characters.clue: Brought home from Italy as a child and handed to a boy who was told she was his present, she dies on her wedding night because her husband assumed a threat was aimed at him.

characters.name: Henry Clerval
characters.summary: The alternative Victor might have been: a student of languages and poetry who nurses his friend through a breakdown without ever asking what caused it.
