He is strangled on a beach in Ireland because he is travelling with the wrong man, and his death produces the book's second wrongful arrest.
characters.clue: A merchant's son who wanted Persian and Sanskrit rather than chemistry, and who nursed his friend for months without asking a single question about the illness.

characters.name: Justine Moritz
characters.summary: Tried for William's murder on the evidence of a miniature planted in her pocket, and convicted after a confessor persuades her that a lie will save her soul. Victor sits in the courtroom knowing who did it. The novel's clearest statement about what respectable silence costs is made by a hanging.
characters.clue: A servant loved by the family she serves, condemned on a planted locket and a confession extracted by a priest, while the one man who could clear her says nothing.

characters.name: The De Lacey family
characters.summary: A blind father, a son and a daughter living in poverty after a political disgrace, watched for months through a chink by a being who chops their firewood at night. They teach it language, history and sympathy without knowing it exists, and then Felix beats it with a stick.
characters.clue: A blind man, his son and his daughter, poor and exiled, who are taught kindness to a stranger by everything except the moment the stranger appears.

characters.name: Margaret Saville
characters.role: Walton's sister in England, the reader of every word
characters.summary: She never speaks, never writes back and never appears, and the entire novel is addressed to her. Her initials are Mary Shelley's reversed, and her silence is structural: every narrator in the book is finally talking to a woman at home who cannot interrupt them.
characters.clue: She is in England, she is the person the whole book is addressed to, and she does not get a single line.

themes.name: Creation and responsibility
themes.summary: The novel is not much interested in whether Victor should have made the creature, and enormously interested in what he owed it afterwards. The abandonment takes one sentence and is never revisited as a decision; every later disaster is traceable to it, and the creature argues the point better than anyone else in the book.
themes.development: A boast in Chapter IV, a flight in Chapter V, an unanswerable case on the Mer de Glace, and a demand for a companion that Victor grants and then breaks in the Orkneys.

themes.name: Loneliness
themes.summary: Everyone in this book is alone in a slightly different way. Walton has no friend, Victor works two years in a room nobody enters, the creature watches a family through a hole in a wall, and Margaret Saville receives every word and answers none. The plot turns on a request for company being refused.
themes.development: Walton states the want in Letter II; the creature makes it a formal demand in Chapter XVII; Victor destroys the answer in Chapter XX and is hunted for it.

themes.name: Knowledge and ambition
themes.summary: Shelley separates the pursuit of knowledge from its use with unusual care. Victor's science works; that is the problem. The novel's warnings are all about appetite rather than method, and its most quoted caution — learn from my example — comes from a man who cannot resist telling the story that will teach it.
themes.development: Alchemy in Chapter II, Waldman's lecture in Chapter III, a two-year secret in Chapter IV, and a deathbed in which the warning is immediately half-withdrawn.

themes.name: Nature and the sublime
themes.summary: Mountains, storms and ice do real work here rather than decorating the scenery. Victor goes to the Alps to be soothed and meets the creature there; the glacier that is supposed to console him produces his accuser. The one landscape that answers him properly is the Arctic, which stops him.
themes.development: A blasted oak in Chapter II, the Mer de Glace in Chapter X, the Orkneys in Chapter XIX, and an ice field that finally holds both pursuer and pursued.

themes.name: Education and what makes a monster
themes.summary: The creature's own narrative is a short course in eighteenth-century theories of mind: sensation first, then language, then books, then a sense of injustice. He tells us plainly that he was benevolent and good and that misery altered him. The novel gives him the evidence to prove it before it lets him kill anyone.
themes.development: Six chapters of self-education end with Felix's stick; the first murder follows the discovery that a child of seven has already learned to scream at him.

themes.name: Justice and testimony
themes.summary: Two innocent people are arrested in this novel and one is hanged, both times on circumstantial evidence and both times because the man who knows the truth decides that telling it would sound mad. Shelley makes the courts reasonable and wrong, which is more disturbing than making them corrupt.
themes.development: Justine's trial in Chapter VIII, Victor's arrest for Clerval's murder in Chapter XXI, and a frame narrative that finally leaves the whole case in an explorer's private letters.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story enclosed within another story, often several layers deep.
techniques.inThisBook: Walton encloses Victor, Victor encloses the creature, and the creature encloses the De Laceys' history. Every claim reaches the reader through at least one person with a reason to shape it.

techniques.name: Epistolary form
techniques.definition: A narrative built out of letters and documents rather than told by an outside narrator.
techniques.inThisBook: Walton's letters, Elizabeth's and Alphonse's letters, and Victor's own laboratory journal read by the creature: the book is a bundle of papers addressed to people who mostly cannot reply.

techniques.name: The Romantic sublime
techniques.definition: The effect of vastness — mountains, storms, ice — that overwhelms and enlarges the observer at once.
techniques.inThisBook: Victor uses Alpine scenery as medication and it fails every time; the sublime in this novel keeps producing the creature rather than consolation.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: A deliberate reference to another text, used to borrow its argument.
techniques.inThisBook: The epigraph is Adam's complaint to God from Paradise Lost, and the creature reads Milton as true history. Volney supplies him with politics and Goethe with grief.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: Two figures constructed so that each one completes or exposes the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Victor and the creature share a vocabulary, a solitude and a pursuit, and by the last chapter it is genuinely hard to say which of them is hunting the other.

techniques.name: Retrospective narration
techniques.definition: An account given after the event by a narrator who already knows how it ends.
techniques.inThisBook: Victor tells the story dying, which lets him load ordinary evenings with foreboding and convert decisions into destiny before the reader can examine them.

quotations.text: I shall satiate my ardent curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never before visited, and may tread a land never before imprinted by the foot of man.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: Walton writes to his sister from St Petersburgh before the expedition sails.
quotations.analysis: The verbs give the game away: satiate belongs to appetite, not to science, and tread is about leaving a mark rather than finding anything. Walton wants the place to be untouched so that he can be the one who touches it, which is precisely the wish Victor will spend the rest of the book regretting.

quotations.text: I have no friend, Margaret: when I am glowing with the enthusiasm of success, there will be none to participate my joy; if I am assailed by disappointment, no one will endeavour to sustain me in dejection.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: From Archangel, waiting for the ice to open.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is addressed to his sister, which means he is telling the one person who loves him that he has nobody. That blindness is the point: Walton defines friendship as an audience for his moods, and within two letters he has found one in a man who will talk for three hundred pages.

quotations.text: One man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the acquirement of the knowledge which I sought; for the dominion I should acquire and transmit over the elemental foes of our race.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: Walton reports what he said to Victor, his rescued passenger, over the first days aboard.
quotations.analysis: He says this to a man who has already paid that price several times over, which is why Victor begins to weep rather than to argue. Note the slide from knowledge to dominion inside one sentence: the enquiry is barely stated before it becomes a claim to rule, and the price is always one man's and never the speaker's.

quotations.text: The world was to me a secret which I desired to divine.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Victor contrasts his own childhood curiosity with Clerval's taste for poetry and adventure.
quotations.analysis: Divine is doing two jobs: to work out, and to do the work of a god. Shelley lets the pun sit there unremarked in a sentence about a small boy, ten chapters before anyone has assembled anything. The world is cast as something withholding information from him, which makes discovery feel like the recovery of a right.

quotations.text: So much has been done, exclaimed the soul of Frankenstein⁠—more, far more, will I achieve: treading in the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and unfold to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Immediately after Waldman's lecture on the achievements of modern chemistry.
quotations.analysis: He quotes himself in the third person and hands the speech to his soul rather than his mouth, which keeps the boast at arm's length while still making it. The one moment of real modesty — treading in the steps already marked — is buried between two promises to go further than anyone has gone.

quotations.text: Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge, and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Victor breaks off his narrative to refuse Walton the secret of animation.
quotations.analysis: The moral is offered as the reason for telling a story that is also, unmistakably, a performance of how far he got. He withholds the method and keeps the glamour, and the alternative he proposes — believing your home town to be the world — is not a life he would accept for himself for an afternoon.

quotations.text: A new species would bless me as its creator and source; many happy and excellent natures would owe their being to me. No father could claim the gratitude of his child so completely as I should deserve theirs.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Working alone through two seasons, imagining what success will mean.
quotations.analysis: Every clause is about what he will receive: blessing, gratitude, a debt so complete that no ordinary father could match it. He imagines fatherhood entirely as a creditor relationship, and the novel then tests the arrangement by giving him exactly one child, who asks him for something.

quotations.text: It was on a dreary night of November, that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the creation scene.
quotations.analysis: Shelley said this was the first sentence she wrote, and the whole chapter is built backwards from it. Beheld makes Victor a spectator at his own experiment, and accomplishment of my toils names the labour rather than the thing produced — the grammar is already looking away from the body on the table.

quotations.text: I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: The moment of animation itself.
quotations.analysis: The most famous event in the novel is reported without a single active verb for Victor: he saw, and then things happened by themselves. There is no lightning, no machinery and no instant of triumph in the text at all, only an eye opening and a man watching. Every screen version has had to invent the scene that Shelley refused to write.

quotations.text: I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Moments after the animation, before he runs from the room.
quotations.analysis: Nothing about the creature has changed between the sentence before and the sentence after; what has changed is that Victor has stopped wanting. The horror is described as arriving in him rather than coming from anything, and the novel will hold him to that all the way to the Arctic: the being is made monstrous by a reaction, not by a defect.

quotations.text: Remember, that I am thy creature; I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: On the Mer de Glace, the first words the creature addresses to Victor at length.
quotations.analysis: He argues in the second person singular that scripture and Milton use for God, and he has picked his precedent with care: Satan fell for a misdeed, and his claim is that he has not committed one. The sentence is a legal submission dressed as a lament, and Victor never answers the argument, only the tone.

quotations.text: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend. Make me happy, and I shall again be virtuous.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: The end of the creature's opening appeal on the glacier.
quotations.analysis: Two short clauses containing the novel's whole theory of character: virtue is a condition, not a substance, and it can be restored by changing the conditions. It is also a threat with the grammar of an offer. The reader has not yet heard the six chapters of evidence that will be produced to support the first half of it.

quotations.text: Of what a strange nature is knowledge! It clings to the mind, when it has once seized on it, like a lichen on the rock.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: After the lessons given to Safie have taught him human history and property.
quotations.analysis: The creature reaches Victor's subject from the opposite direction and comes to the opposite conclusion: knowledge is not something you go and get, it is something that will not let go of you. He chooses an image from the landscape he actually lives in, which is one of the quiet signs that his education has become his own rather than the De Laceys'.

quotations.text: Accursed creator! Why did you form a monster so hideous that even you turned from me in disgust?
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Reading Victor's own laboratory journal, found in the pocket of the clothes he took from the flat.
quotations.analysis: He has learned about his own making from the notes of the man who made him, which is the cruellest use of a document in a novel full of documents. The accusation is not that he was made, but that he was made and then looked at. Even you concedes that everyone else's disgust was to be expected.

quotations.text: Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I live? Why, in that instant, did I not extinguish the spark of existence which you had so wantonly bestowed?
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: After the De Laceys abandon the cottage and he burns it down.
quotations.analysis: Spark of existence is Victor's own phrase for what he infused, handed back with wantonly attached to it. This is the hinge of the creature's narrative: the sentence before it he is grieving, and a few pages later he has met a child in the woods. Shelley puts the turn into a rhetorical question rather than a decision.

quotations.text: You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being. This you alone can do; and I demand it of you as a right which you must not refuse to concede.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: The demand that follows the whole of the creature's narrative.
quotations.analysis: Six chapters of evidence have been building to the word right, and he uses the vocabulary of contract rather than mercy: demand, concede, must not refuse. Shelley's father argued in Political Justice that obligations follow from what a being is capable of feeling, and the creature has just spent his narrative proving his capability.

quotations.text: I am malicious because I am miserable. Am I not shunned and hated by all mankind?
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Replying to Victor's refusal and threats on the Mer de Glace.
quotations.analysis: The causal because is the most contested word in the novel, and the creature puts it in the present tense rather than the past: not misery made me, but misery is making me, now, and can stop. The question that follows shifts the burden of proof onto everyone who has met him.

quotations.text: You are my creator, but I am your master;⁠—obey!
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: After Victor tears the half-finished female apart in the Orkney hut.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning stops here and does not resume. Six words reverse the relation the whole book has been built on, and the dash before obey marks the exact point at which the creature stops asking. Everything he does afterwards is designed to leave Victor alive and alone, which is the punishment he was given first.

quotations.text: Beware; for I am fearless, and therefore powerful.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: The creature's last speech before he leaves the island.
quotations.analysis: He has worked out that he cannot be threatened with anything he has not already lost, and states it as a syllogism. Compare Victor, whose power rests entirely on secrets he is afraid to reveal: the two of them are being measured against each other by what they still have to protect.

quotations.text: It is well. I go; but remember, I shall be with you on your wedding night.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Leaving the Orkneys after the destruction of his companion.
quotations.analysis: Victor reads this as a death sentence on himself and spends three chapters arranging his affairs accordingly. The creature has in fact announced with complete precision what he intends: to take from Victor exactly what Victor took from him, on the night it would be taken. The misreading is entirely Victor's, and it is made of self-importance.

quotations.text: William, Justine, and Henry⁠—they all died by my hands.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: To his father, refusing the comfort offered after his acquittal in Ireland.
quotations.analysis: It is the one moment in Victor's narrative where the grammar puts him in the accusative position he has been avoiding for twenty chapters. His father hears it as the raving of a sick man, which lets Victor keep the confession and lose nothing by it — and Elizabeth's name is not yet on the list only because the wedding has not happened.

quotations.text: I, the miserable and the abandoned, am an abortion, to be spurned at, and kicked, and trampled on.
quotations.speaker: The creature
quotations.context: Speaking to Walton over Victor's body in the cabin.
quotations.analysis: He has adopted the vocabulary of the people who drove him off, and the three passive verbs pile up in the order a body would meet them. Shelley gives the creature the last full speech in the novel and lets him convict himself in language he did not invent, which leaves the reader to decide who taught it to him.

quotations.text: Farewell, Walton! Seek happiness in tranquillity, and avoid ambition, even if it be only the apparently innocent one of distinguishing yourself in science and discoveries.
quotations.speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quotations.context: Victor's last words, on Walton's ship.
quotations.analysis: This is as close as the novel comes to a moral, and Shelley immediately undercuts it: the next sentence has Victor asking why he should say such a thing, since another man might yet succeed. The warning and its withdrawal are in the same breath, and Walton is left holding both.

quotations.text: He was soon borne away by the waves, and lost in darkness and distance.
quotations.speaker: Robert Walton
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel, as the creature leaves the ship on an ice raft.
quotations.analysis: No body, no pyre and no confirmation: the creature announces his own death and the novel declines to show it. The final verb is passive and the last two nouns are abstractions, so the book closes on a failure of evidence — which is consistent, since every fact in it has reached us through someone else's letter.

atAGlance.label: Begun
atAGlance.note: At the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva, after Byron proposed that the party each write a ghost story.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Anonymously, in three volumes, by Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor & Jones.

atAGlance.label: Text used here
atAGlance.note: Shelley's revised single-volume text for Bentley's Standard Novels, with a new introduction.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Walton writes to his sister; Victor speaks inside Walton's letters; the creature speaks inside Victor's account.

criticalViews.position: A myth about science without conscience
criticalViews.summary: The oldest popular reading, and the one the title invites: a man reaches beyond the permitted limits of knowledge and is destroyed by what he makes. It has given the novel a second life in debates about genetics, artificial intelligence and research ethics.
criticalViews.counter: The novel spends almost no time on whether the creation was wrong and a great deal on what happened next. Read closely, the disaster begins not in the laboratory but at the door Victor runs out of.

criticalViews.position: A book about parents, birth and abandonment
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1970s has read the novel through Shelley's own losses — a mother who died giving birth to her, and children of her own who did not survive — and through a creation scene in which a maker recoils from what he has brought into the world.
criticalViews.counter: The biographical fit can flatten the creature's case, which is argued in the public language of rights and obligation rather than the private language of family feeling.

criticalViews.position: A political argument inherited from Godwin and Wollstonecraft
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the novel is a test of the claim that character is formed by circumstance. The creature's six chapters of self-education are the evidence, and Justine's trial is the counter-example in which reasonable institutions kill an innocent woman.
criticalViews.counter: The creature does eventually murder a child and a bride, and the novel never lets the reader treat those acts as merely the output of his conditions.

criticalViews.position: A question about who is allowed to speak
criticalViews.summary: The structure puts the creature at the centre of three frames, so that his account reaches us only through a man who hates him and a man writing home. Adaptations that make him silent are not misreading the book so much as completing a process it describes.
criticalViews.counter: He is also the novel's most persuasive rhetorician, and a reader can reasonably suspect that the eloquence is doing the same work Victor's does — arranging the facts.

essayQuestions.question: Who is responsible for the deaths in Frankenstein?
essayQuestions.focus: Creation, abandonment and the limits of Victor's account
plan: Separate the making from the abandoning: the novel treats them as two decisions and only dwells on one.
Use Chapter V to show how the grammar of Victor's narration removes him from his own actions.
Turn to Chapter VIII, where a silence that costs nothing to break costs Justine her life.
Weigh the creature's case in Chapters X and XVII, in which he argues from what he was made capable of feeling.
Close on the wedding night: Victor's misreading of the threat is the last and most expensive act of self-importance in the book.

essayQuestions.question: How does the frame narrative shape what a reader is able to believe?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, testimony and unreliable narration
plan: Set out the three layers and note that the innermost voice is the one with the fewest witnesses.
Show Walton establishing himself in Letters I-IV as a man predisposed to admire an ambitious stranger.
Examine Victor's retrospective habits: foreboding, destiny and the passive voice.
Read the creature's narrative for its own rhetorical shaping, including his choice of Milton as precedent.
Conclude with the last page: no body, no proof, and a story that reaches us only as a bundle of private letters.

essayQuestions.question: 'The creature is made monstrous by the way he is treated, not by the way he is made.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Nurture, education and the evidence of Chapters XI-XVI
plan: Begin with the creation scene, where nothing about the body changes between wonder and disgust.
Trace the creature's education through sensation, language, books and a sense of injustice.
Use Felix's stick and the shooting in the woods as the two points where kindness is met with violence.
Test the claim against William's murder, which follows the discovery that even a child recoils.
Decide whether the novel endorses his argument, or merely gives him the strongest possible version of it.

essayQuestions.question: What use does Shelley make of landscape?
essayQuestions.focus: The sublime, the Alps and the Arctic
plan: Establish the Romantic convention Victor is relying on: mountains as a cure for the mind.
Show it failing on the Mer de Glace, where the sublime prospect delivers his accuser.
Contrast the Orkney island, where desolation enables the worst thing he does rather than consoling him.
Read the Arctic as the only landscape in the novel that can hold both pursuer and pursued.
Conclude with the blasted oak of Chapter II: the novel's first image of power is destructive and impersonal.

discussionQuestions: Victor never gives the creature a name. What does the novel gain by refusing him one?
Walton is offered the story as a warning. By the last page, has he taken it?
The creature asks for a companion and promises exile. Should Victor have agreed?
Every narrator in the novel is finally addressing Margaret Saville, who never replies. What difference does that make to how the book reads?
Would you rather read the 1818 text or the 1831 revision, and on what grounds would you choose?

timeline.label: Mary Wollstonecraft publishes A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
timeline.detail: The author's mother, whose arguments about education and sympathy run through the creature's narrative.

timeline.label: William Godwin publishes Political Justice
timeline.detail: The author's father, and the source of the novel's habit of testing obligation by argument rather than by feeling.

timeline.label: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin is born in London
timeline.detail: Her mother died within days, of complications following the birth.

timeline.label: Giovanni Aldini's galvanic demonstrations in London
timeline.detail: Electrical experiments on the body of a hanged man at the Royal College of Surgeons, widely reported.

timeline.label: The summer at the Villa Diodati
timeline.detail: Byron proposes a ghost-story competition beside Lake Geneva; Shelley, then eighteen, begins the tale.

timeline.label: Frankenstein published anonymously in three volumes
timeline.detail: Dedicated to Godwin, with a preface written by Percy Bysshe Shelley, which led several reviewers to assume he was the author.

timeline.label: Presumption; or, The Fate of Frankenstein opens in London
timeline.detail: Richard Brinsley Peake's version gives the creature no speech at all — the first of many adaptations to take his argument away.

timeline.label: A second edition names Mary Shelley as the author
timeline.detail: Published in two volumes while she was abroad, and seen through the press by her father.

timeline.label: The revised one-volume edition for Bentley's Standard Novels
timeline.detail: Shelley adds the introduction about the Diodati summer and alters the novel's account of Elizabeth, chance and fate. This is the text used here.

timeline.label: Mary Shelley dies in London
timeline.detail: She had outlived Percy Shelley by nearly thirty years and all but one of her children.

timeline.label: Edison Studios releases the first screen Frankenstein
timeline.detail: A single reel, long thought lost, in which the creature is produced in a vat rather than on a table.

timeline.label: James Whale's Frankenstein for Universal
timeline.detail: Boris Karloff's flat-headed, inarticulate creature becomes the popular image of a character who, in the novel, argues fluently for his rights.

places.name: Geneva
places.note: The Frankenstein household, and the city whose courts hang Justine.

places.name: Cologny, Lake Geneva
places.note: The Villa Diodati, where the ghost-story competition of 1816 produced the novel.

places.name: Ingolstadt
places.note: The university where Victor works alone for two years and animates the creature.

places.name: Chamonix and the Mer de Glace
places.note: The glacier where the creature finally makes his case, in the novel's spelling Chamounix.

places.name: Orkney
places.note: The remote island hut where Victor begins and then destroys the female companion.

places.name: Archangel
places.note: Walton's last port before the ice, and the place from which he writes that he has no friend.

related.why: The other great novel assembled out of letters and journals, where documents are again the only evidence anyone has.
A second experiment carried out in private by a respectable man who cannot afterwards control what he has released.
The creature's own reading, and the source of the epigraph: Adam's complaint that he did not ask to be made.
Shelley quotes it directly, and it supplies the model of a haunted man compelled to tell his story to a stranger.
Another novel that puts a violent story inside a mild narrator's account and lets the frame do the moral work.

books.title: Great Expectations
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.setting: The Kent marshes near the Thames estuary, and London, in the first half of the nineteenth century
books.lengthNote: Fifty-nine chapters in three stages of Pip's expectations, written to fit thirty-five weekly instalments
books.openingLine: My father’s family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip.
books.summary: A blacksmith's boy who once fed a starving convict on the marshes is given a fortune by an anonymous benefactor and sent to London to be made into a gentleman. He assumes the money comes from the woman in the decayed wedding dress, and it does not. The book is narrated by the older Pip, who knows from the first page exactly how badly the younger one behaved to the people who loved him, and declines to spare either of them.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Great Expectations
sourceText.note: References give the chapter, which the text numbers in roman. The text is the revised ending as published in 1861, not the ending Dickens first wrote.

structure.label: Chapters 1–7
structure.title: The churchyard and the file
structure.summary: Pip is turned upside down among the graves of his parents and told to bring food and a file to a man with an iron on his leg. He steals from his own kitchen, is not found out, and the convict protects him by confessing to the theft — a debt the book will take fifty chapters to call in.

scenes.summary: The convict rises from among the graves; Pip learns the identity of things by being held over them.
The pork pie, the brandy and the file, taken from a house where everything is counted.
The soldiers retake both convicts on the marsh; Magwitch takes the blame for the stolen food.
Joe tells Pip about his own father, and about why he lets Mrs Joe rule the forge.

structure.label: Chapters 8–19
structure.title: Satis House, and the end of the first stage
structure.summary: Pip is sent to play at a house where the clocks stopped at twenty to nine and the wedding breakfast is still on the table. Estella calls his hands coarse and his boots thick, and he comes home ashamed of a life he had been perfectly happy in. Then Jaggers arrives with money from a source Pip is forbidden to ask about.

scenes.summary: Cards with Estella; Pip looks at his own hands afterwards and does not like them.
He lies about the visit to his sister and Pumblechook, and Joe tells him plainly that lies are lies.
Miss Havisham pays for the apprenticeship, and Pip is bound to the forge he now despises.
Jaggers announces the great expectations, the condition of secrecy and the removal to London.
Pip leaves for London; the mists rise, and the first stage of his expectations ends.

structure.label: Chapters 20–28
structure.title: Little Britain, Barnard's Inn and the Castle
structure.summary: London turns out to be smaller and dirtier than expected. Pip meets Herbert Pocket, who renames him Handel and teaches him how to hold a fork; Wemmick, who keeps a drawbridge between his office and his feelings; and Jaggers, who washes his hands of his clients with scented soap. Joe visits and is made miserable by good manners.

scenes.summary: Smithfield, Newgate and the crowd of people waiting outside Jaggers's office.
Herbert gives Pip the history of Miss Havisham and the bridegroom who did not come.
Walworth, the Aged P, the drawbridge and the gun: Wemmick's second life.
Joe comes to London, calls him sir, and leaves rather than go on being out of place.

structure.label: Chapters 29–39
structure.title: Debts, Estella, and the end of the second stage
structure.summary: Pip believes Miss Havisham has designed Estella for him; Miss Havisham lets him. He runs up debts, half-ruins Herbert and secretly rescues him, buries his sister and neglects Joe. On a wild night in his rooms above the river, a man climbs the stairs and holds out both hands.

scenes.summary: Estella returns as a woman, and Miss Havisham tells Pip to love her whatever it costs him.
Mrs Joe's funeral, larks over the grave, and Pip's promise to visit that he does not keep.
Estella warns him that she has no heart and must be taken as she has been made.
Magwitch returns, names himself the source of the money, and the second stage ends.

structure.label: Chapters 40–52
structure.title: Convict money
structure.summary: Everything Pip has built rests on a man who will be hanged if he is found in England. Herbert learns Magwitch's history; Compeyson turns out to be Miss Havisham's bridegroom; Estella marries Drummle; and Miss Havisham, asking what she has done, catches fire in her own wedding dress.

scenes.summary: Magwitch's account of his own childhood, and of the gentleman who took the lighter sentence.
Pip tells Estella she is part of his existence; she tells him she is to marry Bentley Drummle.
Miss Havisham asks Pip's forgiveness, repeats one question until the dress catches.
Pip works out Estella's parentage and makes Jaggers admit it without admitting anything.

structure.label: Chapters 53–59
structure.title: The river, the fever and the garden
structure.summary: Orlick nearly kills Pip in the sluice-house on the marshes; the escape down the Thames fails within sight of the steamer; Magwitch dies in the prison infirmary believing his daughter is alive and a lady. Pip falls ill, is nursed by Joe, works eleven years in the East, and comes back to a demolished house.

scenes.summary: Orlick, the lime-kiln, and an accounting of every injury Pip never noticed he was causing.
The rowing boat, the customs galley and Compeyson under the paddle-wheel.
Magwitch's death, and the only lie in the book that is entirely kind.
The ruined garden at Satis House eleven years later, and the evening mists rising.

characters.name: Pip
characters.role: Philip Pirrip; narrator, blacksmith's apprentice, then a gentleman on someone else's money
characters.summary: Two people at once: the boy who behaves badly and the man telling you about it, who supplies the judgements the boy could not. The book's great difficulty is that his snobbery is presented from inside, so the reader is made to feel the shame of the thick boots before being invited to despise him for feeling it.
characters.clue: He gives himself his own name as an infant because he cannot manage the real one, and spends the novel being ashamed of the man who taught him to read.
traits: harder on himself than on anyone

relationships.label: brother-in-law and, in effect, son of

characters.name: Joe Gargery
characters.summary: He cannot spell, will not raise his hand in his own house, and is the moral centre of the novel without ever being told so. His explanation of why he allows his wife to rule — that his own father beat his mother, and he would rather be hit himself — is the best piece of reasoning anyone in the book manages.
characters.clue: He calls a court card a Jack, stands at the forge in an apron, and comes to London to be called sir by a boy he taught to read.

characters.name: Mrs Joe Gargery
characters.summary: She has brought Pip up by hand and never stops saying so; the phrase covers both the rearing and the beating. Dickens complicates the caricature by having her, after Orlick's attack, become mild and anxious to be forgiven by the man who hurt her, which is harder to read than the tyranny was.
characters.clue: She keeps the pantry locked, wears a bib full of pins, and after an assault she never describes spends her last months trying to placate her attacker.

characters.name: Biddy
characters.summary: She teaches Pip everything he learns before Jaggers arrives and is the only person who tells him the truth about his conduct to his face. The novel gives her the sharpest line in it — that Pip need not be ashamed of Joe, and is — and then rewards her with the life Pip threw away.
characters.clue: She learns everything Pip learns at the same speed and with none of the help, and marries the blacksmith on the day Pip comes home to propose to her.

characters.name: Estella
characters.summary: Trained from childhood to break hearts, and honest about it to the one person who will not listen. Her warnings to Pip are not coquetry — she tells him repeatedly and in plain terms that she has no heart and will do him harm — and the plot's cruellest turn is that her real parents are a convict and a murderess.
characters.clue: She is raised to wound, says so out loud, and marries the worst man available partly because he is the only one she cannot damage.

characters.name: Miss Havisham
characters.role: Of Satis House, jilted on her wedding morning
characters.summary: She has stopped the clocks, kept on one shoe and left the cake to the mice, and she is aware the whole arrangement is theatre. What she has done to Estella is worse than what was done to her, and the novel makes her say so herself before the fire — she wanted to save a child from misery and made one instead.
characters.clue: One shoe on, one stocking, a yellowed veil, and clocks that all read twenty minutes to nine.

relationships.label: lets him believe she is his benefactor

characters.name: Abel Magwitch
characters.role: Transported convict; Pip's benefactor, under the name Provis
characters.summary: He begins as a threat in a graveyard and ends as the one character who has given everything he had for another person. His speech about making a gentleman is the book's hinge: he has bought Pip the way a man buys a racehorse, out of love, and Pip's revulsion at being owned is inseparable from his revulsion at the ownership being working-class.
characters.clue: He limps out of the marsh mist with an iron on his leg, eats like a dog, and comes back from Australia to look at what his money made.

relationships.label: secretly funds and claims as a son

characters.name: Mr Jaggers
characters.summary: He bites his forefinger, never admits a fact and washes his hands after every client. The routine is not cynicism but the only defence available to a man who knows exactly where the money in London comes from, and who has quietly saved one woman from the gallows and placed one child in a rich house.
characters.clue: He smells of scented soap, will accept no statement that is not evidence, and keeps a towel behind a closet door for use after every client.

characters.name: Wemmick
characters.role: Jaggers's clerk; proprietor of the Castle at Walworth
characters.summary: He states as policy what everyone else in the novel does by accident: that the self at work and the self at home are different people and must not be confounded. At the office he collects portable property from condemned men; at Walworth he fires a gun at nine so his deaf father can feel it.
characters.clue: His house has a drawbridge, a moat four feet wide and a cannon, and his opinions change at the garden gate.

characters.name: Herbert Pocket
characters.role: Pip's friend and fellow lodger at Barnard's Inn
characters.summary: The pale young gentleman Pip fought in a garden, now the one person in London who improves him. He is hopeless at making money and excellent at everything else, and the best thing Pip does in the novel is to buy him a partnership in secret and never tell him.
characters.clue: He renames his friend after a piece of music, is perpetually looking about him for capital, and never learns who paid for his position.

characters.name: Dolge Orlick
characters.summary: He is what Pip's resentments would look like if they were acted on. He attacks Mrs Joe with the convict's leg-iron, and in the sluice-house he accuses Pip of the very things Pip accuses himself of — that he came between a man and his prospects, and that he was always the favourite.
characters.clue: He slouches about the forge, strikes a woman with a filed-off leg-iron, and later tells his enemy that everything wrong in his life was that enemy's doing.

themes.name: Gentility and what it costs
themes.summary: Becoming a gentleman in this book is not a moral improvement but a change of accent, boots and address, paid for by someone else. Dickens sets Pip's education against Joe's illiteracy and Biddy's self-teaching, and quietly notes that the least educated characters make the fewest mistakes about how to behave.
themes.development: The shame begins with a pair of hands in Chapter 8, becomes an income in Chapter 18, and is exposed as convict money in Chapter 39.

themes.name: Guilt, crime and complicity
themes.summary: Pip's first act is a theft committed under threat, and he never stops feeling like a criminal. The novel keeps him in the neighbourhood of the law — Newgate, the hulks, Jaggers's office, the condemned cell — so that the distance between the gentleman and the convict keeps failing to open up.
themes.development: The stolen pork pie leads to a man who takes the blame; the man leads to the money; the money leads Pip back to a prison, where he ends up praying for a dying convict.

themes.name: Class and money
themes.summary: Every fortune in the book has a source somebody would rather not name: Miss Havisham's brewery, Magwitch's sheep and speculation, Jaggers's fees from the dock. What the novel refuses is the idea that money can be laundered by manners, and Magwitch's return is the plot making that argument physically.
themes.development: Pip's debts rise with his status; his one honourable transaction, buying Herbert's partnership, is the one he keeps secret.

themes.name: Love as damage
themes.summary: Miss Havisham's instruction to Pip is to love Estella whatever it does to him, and to keep loving as it tears deeper. Estella tells him plainly that she has no heart and will hurt him. Love in this novel is repeatedly something done to a person rather than between two of them.
themes.development: The engineered attachment of the Satis House visits becomes an obsession Pip can defend only by admitting it is unreasonable, and Miss Havisham's collapse in Chapter 49 is the moment she recognises what she built.

themes.name: Parents, substitutes and making people
themes.summary: Nobody in the book is raised by the people who produced them. Pip has a sister, a brother-in-law, a guardian and two self-appointed benefactors; Estella has a jilted bride for a mother and a convict for a father. The recurring question is whether a child is made by design, and whether the designer can be blamed.
themes.development: Miss Havisham's 'what have I done' and Magwitch's 'I'm your second father' are the same claim from opposite ends — that a person can be manufactured — and the novel judges them differently.

themes.name: Memory and the older narrator
themes.summary: The story is told by a man who already knows the answer to every question the boy is asking. That gap is the novel's method: the reader gets the misjudgement and the verdict on it in the same sentence, which is why the snobbery can be shown at full strength without being endorsed.
themes.development: The narrator interrupts from the first chapter to name a memorable day and the long chain it begins, and keeps returning to the reader directly at the points where the younger Pip behaves worst.

techniques.name: Retrospective first person
techniques.definition: A narrator recalling their own past, so that experience and judgement arrive together.
techniques.inThisBook: The older Pip supplies verdicts the younger one could not reach — 'it is a most miserable thing to feel ashamed of home' — and occasionally addresses the reader outright to make the moral general.

techniques.name: Landscape as feeling
techniques.definition: Weather and place used to carry the emotional weight of a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: Mists rise as Pip leaves the forge and rise again in the last sentence of the book; the marshes are flat, wet and open, and the first thing they teach him is the identity of things.

techniques.name: Objects carrying the plot
techniques.definition: A physical thing that returns at intervals, gathering meaning each time.
techniques.inThisBook: The file stolen for Magwitch reappears in a stranger's hands, then as the weapon used on Mrs Joe; the bride-cake, the stopped clocks and the single shoe do the same work at Satis House.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: Two characters built so that each exposes something in the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Orlick voices Pip's own resentments back at him in the sluice-house; Magwitch and Miss Havisham are two benefactors making two children; Compeyson is the gentleman Magwitch is punished for not being.

techniques.name: Speech as class
techniques.definition: Giving each character a distinct vocabulary, grammar and rhythm.
techniques.inThisBook: Joe's tangled syntax, Magwitch's 'wittles', Jaggers's refusal of any sentence that is not evidence and Wemmick's two registers do more social work than any description in the novel.

techniques.name: Weekly serial structure
techniques.definition: Chapters shaped to end an instalment with a reason to return.
techniques.inThisBook: Written for thirty-five weekly numbers rather than monthly parts, the book is unusually tight for Dickens, and its two great reversals both fall at the close of a stage.

quotations.text: My father’s family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip. So, I called myself Pip, and came to be called Pip.
quotations.context: The opening sentences of the novel.
quotations.analysis: He names himself in the first line, which is the only act of self-creation in the book that works. Everything after this is somebody else's attempt to name him — Handel, my boy, sir, a gentleman — and the final clause, 'came to be called', already concedes that identity is something other people do to you.

quotations.text: My first most vivid and broad impression of the identity of things seems to me to have been gained on a memorable raw afternoon towards evening.
quotations.context: Introducing the churchyard on the marshes.
quotations.analysis: A child's first understanding of the world is dated to the afternoon a man threatened to cut his throat, and the phrase for it is legal and exact rather than emotional. 'The identity of things' is what the rest of the novel systematically takes away from him: nothing turns out to be what it was labelled.

quotations.text: “Hold your noise!” cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from among the graves at the side of the church porch. “Keep still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!”
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: The convict's first appearance, in the churchyard.
quotations.analysis: The man rises out of the family graves, which puts him structurally in the place of Pip's dead parents some four hundred pages before the plot gets there. He is also, at this moment, simply a voice — Dickens gives the sound before the body, so that the marshes seem to produce him.

quotations.text: “You get me a file.” He tilted me again. “And you get me wittles.” He tilted me again. “You bring ’em both to me.”
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: Giving Pip his instructions while holding him upside down.
quotations.analysis: The repeated stage direction between clauses turns a threat into a rhythm, and the two objects demanded — one to eat, one to cut iron — are the whole of what the man needs from the world. Both come back: the file resurfaces in a stranger's hand and then as the weapon used on Pip's sister.

quotations.text: “He calls the knaves Jacks, this boy!” said Estella with disdain, before our first game was out. “And what coarse hands he has! And what thick boots!”
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: Playing beggar my neighbour at Satis House.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences, three separate grounds of contempt: vocabulary, body and clothing. She never speaks to Pip in this scene, only about him, and the whole novel's machinery of shame is installed here with a card game and a piece of vocabulary Joe taught him.

quotations.text: I took the opportunity of being alone in the courtyard to look at my coarse hands and my common boots. My opinion of those accessories was not favorable. They had never troubled me before, but they troubled me now, as vulgar appendages.
quotations.context: Alone in the yard at Satis House, immediately after the card game.
quotations.analysis: He has adopted her adjectives within a page, and the word 'accessories' shows the change happening in his vocabulary before it happens in his conduct. 'They had never troubled me before' is the older narrator marking the exact moment a happy childhood was converted into a grievance.

quotations.text: “There’s one thing you may be sure of, Pip,” said Joe, after some rumination, “namely, that lies is lies. Howsever they come, they didn’t ought to come, and they come from the father of lies, and work round to the same.
quotations.speaker: Joe Gargery
quotations.context: After Pip has invented a coach, a flag and black velvet to describe Satis House.
quotations.analysis: The grammar is wrong in every clause and the reasoning is unanswerable, which is Dickens's standing joke about Joe and also his argument. Joe then adds that Pip is uncommon already, in learning and in size — he refuses the whole category the boy has just started to judge himself by.

quotations.text: Pause you who read this, and think for a moment of the long chain of iron or gold, of thorns or flowers, that would never have bound you, but for the formation of the first link on one memorable day.
quotations.context: Closing the chapter on Pip's first visit to Satis House.
quotations.analysis: The narrator stops the story to address the reader directly, and reaches for a chain — the image already attached to leg-irons, and in Dickens's own earlier Christmas book to a dead man's punishment. Offering iron or gold, thorns or flowers, he declines to say which Pip's turned out to be.

quotations.text: Miss Havisham would embrace her with lavish fondness, murmuring something in her ear that sounded like “Break their hearts my pride and hope, break their hearts and have no mercy!”
quotations.speaker: Miss Havisham
quotations.context: Watching Estella after one of Pip's visits.
quotations.analysis: Pip reports it as something that 'sounded like' the words, so the most damning line in Estella's upbringing reaches the reader through a child who did not quite catch it. The endearments and the instruction are in the same breath: pride and hope are what she calls the girl she is training to be unable to love.

quotations.text: It is a most miserable thing to feel ashamed of home. There may be black ingratitude in the thing, and the punishment may be retributive and well deserved; but that it is a miserable thing, I can testify.
quotations.context: After a year in which the forge has come to look coarse and common to him.
quotations.analysis: The older narrator concedes the charge against the boy in full — ingratitude, deserved punishment — and then insists on the misery anyway, in the language of a witness box. It is the book's characteristic move: guilt admitted so completely that pity becomes possible.

quotations.text: “Mr. Pip,” he replied, with gravity, “Walworth is one place, and this office is another. Much as the Aged is one person, and Mr. Jaggers is another. They must not be confounded together.
quotations.speaker: Wemmick
quotations.context: Pip asks for advice in Little Britain that Wemmick has already given at Walworth.
quotations.analysis: He states as a rule of hygiene what the rest of the novel suffers as a problem: that the person you are at work and the person you are at home are not obliged to agree. Pip has spent the book trying to keep the forge and London apart and calling it shame; Wemmick does the same thing and calls it an address.

quotations.text: he would wash his hands, and wipe them and dry them all over this towel, whenever he came in from a police court or dismissed a client from his room
quotations.context: Describing the closet in Jaggers's room.
quotations.analysis: The ritual is Pilate's, performed several times a day by a man who never states an opinion about guilt. Dickens attaches the smell of the soap to him everywhere he goes, so that the reader is reminded of what is being washed off at exactly the moments Jaggers is at his most impressive.

quotations.text: “Love her, love her, love her! If she favors you, love her. If she wounds you, love her. If she tears your heart to pieces⁠—and as it gets older and stronger it will tear deeper⁠—love her, love her, love her!”
quotations.speaker: Miss Havisham
quotations.context: Holding Pip's head down to hers in the chair at Satis House.
quotations.analysis: Nine imperatives in three sentences, with the conditions arranged so that being hurt and being favoured produce the same instruction. She is not describing love but prescribing a wound, and Pip lies awake that night converting her command into a declaration of his own, which is the point at which the training takes.

quotations.text: “You must know,” said Estella, condescending to me as a brilliant and beautiful woman might, “that I have no heart⁠—if that has anything to do with my memory.”
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: Explaining to Pip why she does not remember what he remembers.
quotations.analysis: She is answering a question about memory, and the qualification at the end is the sharp part: she suspects that feeling and recollection are the same organ, and that she was denied both at once. Pip hears a coquette's line and misses the diagnosis.

quotations.text: I knew to my sorrow, often and often, if not always, that I loved her against reason, against promise, against peace, against hope, against happiness, against all discouragement that could be.
quotations.context: The narrator interrupting to describe what loving Estella was actually like.
quotations.analysis: Six repetitions of 'against', each one naming something a sensible man would have chosen instead, and the sentence never supplies a reason on the other side. This is the older Pip refusing the conventional account of love as a mistake to be explained, and admitting it as a fact he could not argue with.

quotations.text: “So,” said Estella, “I must be taken as I have been made. The success is not mine, the failure is not mine, but the two together make me.”
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: Answering Miss Havisham's complaint that she is cold to her.
quotations.analysis: The passive voice is exact and deliberate: she has been made, and she declines both the credit and the blame. It is also an answer to the whole Victorian plot of self-improvement that Pip is living out three streets away — one character is trying to make himself, and the other knows she was manufactured.

quotations.text: “Yes, Pip, dear boy, I’ve made a gentleman on you! It’s me wot has done it! I swore that time, sure as ever I earned a guinea, that guinea should go to you.
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: Revealing himself as Pip's benefactor in the rooms by the river.
quotations.analysis: The grammar Pip has spent three hundred pages learning to be ashamed of is the grammar that paid for the lessons. 'Made a gentleman on you' is a maker's claim over an object, and Pip's horror is not only at the source of the money but at being the thing that was made.

quotations.text: “Look’ee here, Pip. I’m your second father. You’re my son⁠—more to me nor any son. I’ve put away money, only for you to spend.
quotations.speaker: Magwitch
quotations.context: Continuing the revelation, in Pip's chambers at night.
quotations.analysis: He claims a relationship rather than a debt, and the claim is unanswerable because it is true — no one else has spent a life on Pip. 'Second father' also places him behind Joe in the queue, which is the one piece of accounting in the scene that Pip is in no position to dispute.

quotations.text: “Out of my thoughts! You are part of my existence, part of myself. You have been in every line I have ever read since I first came here, the rough common boy whose poor heart you wounded even then.
quotations.speaker: Pip
quotations.context: At Satis House, on learning that Estella will marry Bentley Drummle.
quotations.analysis: He describes her as an editorial presence in everything he has read, which for a man whose education was the whole point of his fortune is a devastating admission about what the education was for. He also calls himself the rough common boy in the same sentence, taking back Estella's word at the one moment he is speaking as an equal.

quotations.text: “O!” she cried, despairingly. “What have I done! What have I done!”
quotations.speaker: Miss Havisham
quotations.context: After Pip's account of his feelings for Estella has shown her what she made.
quotations.analysis: The question repeats twenty and fifty times in a page, and the novel says she never changed the order of the three sentences she was left with by the end. She had asked Pip to forgive her in writing, under her name — the whole scene is a woman trying to get a sentence exactly right, having spent twenty-five years refusing to finish one.

quotations.text: I thought of the two men who went up into the Temple to pray, and I knew there were no better words that I could say beside his bed, than “O Lord, be merciful to him a sinner!”
quotations.context: At Magwitch's death in the prison infirmary.
quotations.analysis: Pip has just told a dying man that his daughter is alive, a lady and loved — the only lie in the novel that costs nobody anything. The prayer he then chooses is the publican's rather than the Pharisee's, which quietly settles the question of who in this book has been standing at the front of the temple.

quotations.text: “Lookee here, old chap,” said Joe, bending over me. “Ever the best of friends; ain’t us, Pip?”
quotations.speaker: Joe Gargery
quotations.context: Nursing Pip through the fever, having paid his debts.
quotations.analysis: The same sentence he used in Chapter 7 to comfort a crying child, produced again fifty chapters later without a word of reproach in between. Joe's vocabulary has not moved at all while Pip's has been expensively remade, and the novel's judgement is contained in which of the two turns out to have needed changing.

quotations.text: “I have been bent and broken, but⁠—I hope⁠—into a better shape.
quotations.speaker: Estella
quotations.context: In the ruined garden of Satis House, eleven years later.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor belongs to the forge: iron is bent and broken into shape by heat and hammering, and the woman raised in a brewer's house finishes the novel speaking Joe's trade. The hesitation marked by the dashes is the only uncertainty she has ever expressed.

quotations.text: as the morning mists had risen long ago when I first left the forge, so the evening mists were rising now, and in all the broad expanse of tranquil light they showed to me, I saw no shadow of another parting from her.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel, as published.
quotations.analysis: The sentence closes a loop opened in Chapter 19, where mists rose as Pip walked away from the forge towards London. What it does not do is say they marry: 'no shadow of another parting' is a negative, seen in mist, by a narrator who has been wrong about every prospect he has ever surveyed.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Thirty-five weekly instalments in All the Year Round, the journal Dickens owned and edited.

atAGlance.label: Book form
atAGlance.note: Chapman and Hall, in three volumes.

atAGlance.label: Divisions
atAGlance.note: The text itself announces the end of the first and second stages of Pip's expectations.

atAGlance.label: Endings
atAGlance.note: Dickens wrote one ending, then replaced it before publication after Bulwer-Lytton read the manuscript.

atAGlance.label: Narration
atAGlance.note: His second novel told wholly in the first person, after David Copperfield.

criticalViews.position: A novel about the gentleman as a fiction
criticalViews.summary: The central reading treats gentility as the book's target: Pip's education buys him accent, address and debt, while the people who behave best in the novel are a blacksmith, a village schoolmistress and a transported felon.
criticalViews.counter: The ending softens the case — Pip is rewarded with a clerkship, a friendship and a scene in a garden, none of which examine the system that produced the shame.

criticalViews.position: The two endings
criticalViews.summary: A long-running textual argument. The manuscript ending kept Pip and Estella apart; the published one brings them together in the ruined garden in terms carefully hedged with mist. Which is the better novel, and which the more honest, has been debated since the first readers learned there were two.
criticalViews.counter: The published ending is not the reconciliation it is often taken for: it promises only that Pip saw no shadow of another parting, which is a statement about his eyesight.

criticalViews.position: Crime, empire and the source of money
criticalViews.summary: Later criticism has followed the money: an English gentleman is funded by a sheep farmer in New South Wales, whose capital comes from a penal colony. The novel's plot makes visible a connection between metropolitan respectability and transportation that most Victorian fiction leaves offstage.
criticalViews.counter: Magwitch is also the novel's most loving character, and readings that treat him chiefly as economic evidence can lose what the deathbed scene is doing.

criticalViews.position: Pip as an unreliable witness against himself
criticalViews.summary: Criticism of the narration notes that every harsh judgement of Pip in the book is made by Pip, which makes the reader's disapproval hard to separate from the narrator's self-punishment.
criticalViews.counter: Biddy, Joe and Herbert are all given chances to say what they think, and none of them is as severe as the narrator — which may mean he is exaggerating, or that they are being kind.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens present the idea of the gentleman?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, money and conduct
plan: Begin with Chapter 8: the whole apparatus of shame installed by a card game, a pair of hands and a pair of boots.
Contrast Joe's conduct with Pip's manners — Joe is the only person in the novel whose behaviour is never governed by who is watching.
Use Magwitch's claim to have made a gentleman to show that the title is something bought, and by whom.
Bring in Compeyson, the gentleman who received the lighter sentence, as the novel's hardest evidence.
Ask what Pip ends with: a clerkship, a friendship and no fortune, and whether that counts as an answer or an evasion.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Miss Havisham and Estella.
essayQuestions.focus: Damage, design and responsibility
plan: Set out what Miss Havisham has staged: stopped clocks, one shoe, the bride-cake left for the mice.
Read Estella's warnings as accurate rather than flirtatious — she says plainly that she has no heart.
Use 'I must be taken as I have been made' to argue about how much responsibility a manufactured person carries.
Turn on Chapter 49, where Miss Havisham sees what she did by watching Pip's face, and asks the same question fifty times.
Weigh two verdicts: a Gothic monster of a woman, or the novel's clearest case of damage repeating itself down a generation.

essayQuestions.question: What use does Dickens make of the marshes and the river?
essayQuestions.focus: Setting, structure and mood
plan: Open with Chapter 1, where the flat marsh country teaches a child the identity of things.
Track the mists: rising as Pip leaves the forge in Chapter 19, and rising again in the novel's last sentence.
Set the openness of the marshes against the enclosure of Satis House and the crowding of Smithfield.
Follow the Thames from the hulks at the start to the failed escape by rowing boat in Chapter 54.
Conclude on the pattern: Pip goes up the river to become a gentleman and comes back down it with a dying man.

essayQuestions.question: 'The novel is told by a man judging his younger self.' How far does that shape the reader's response?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration and sympathy
plan: Establish the double voice with 'it is a most miserable thing to feel ashamed of home', where the charge and the plea arrive together.
Note the direct addresses to the reader, which generalise Pip's case at the points where he behaves worst.
Compare what other characters say about Pip — Biddy, Joe, Herbert — with what he says about himself.
Consider Orlick in Chapter 53, who voices the accusations from outside and is not believed because of who is making them.
Decide whether the retrospection earns the reader's sympathy or simply forecloses criticism by getting there first.

discussionQuestions: Pip is ashamed of Joe and knows it is contemptible. Does knowing make it better or worse?
Magwitch says he has made a gentleman. Is he a benefactor, an owner, or both?
Estella warns Pip repeatedly and he ignores her. Whose failure is that?
Dickens replaced his first ending after a friend objected. Should a reader prefer the published one?
Wemmick keeps his feelings at Walworth and his judgement in Little Britain. Is that cowardice or common sense?

timeline.label: Dickens born in Portsmouth
timeline.detail: Pip's childhood belongs roughly to the same decade as Dickens's own.

timeline.label: The blacking warehouse
timeline.detail: Dickens's father was imprisoned for debt and the boy was sent out to work, an episode behind the novel's shame about hands, clothes and company.

timeline.label: Transportation to New South Wales ends
timeline.detail: The system that sent Magwitch to Australia, and the sentence he risks hanging by breaking.

timeline.label: David Copperfield completed
timeline.detail: Dickens re-read it before starting Great Expectations, to be sure he was not repeating himself in the first person.

timeline.label: Dickens moves to Gad's Hill Place
timeline.detail: In the Kent country the novel's marshes and estuary are drawn from.

timeline.label: Serialisation begins
timeline.detail: The first weekly instalment appeared in All the Year Round in December; Dickens took the novel on partly to lift the journal's sales.

timeline.label: The ending is changed
timeline.detail: Bulwer-Lytton read the manuscript ending and objected; Dickens wrote the replacement that has been printed ever since.

timeline.label: Serial ends and the book appears
timeline.detail: The last instalment ran in August, and Chapman and Hall published the novel in three volumes.

timeline.label: Dickens dies at Gad's Hill
timeline.detail: Great Expectations was his penultimate completed novel, followed by Our Mutual Friend.

timeline.label: David Lean's film
timeline.detail: Its graveyard opening and Satis House interiors have shaped how the novel is imagined ever since.

timeline.label: Alfonso Cuarón's film
timeline.detail: Relocated to Florida and New York, with Pip as a painter, which tests how much of the novel is the plot and how much the class system.

timeline.label: Mike Newell's film
timeline.detail: A return to period adaptation, with Ralph Fiennes as Magwitch and Helena Bonham Carter as Miss Havisham.

places.name: Cooling, Kent
places.note: The marsh churchyard with its row of small graves, usually taken as the model for the opening chapter.

places.name: Rochester
places.note: The market town behind Pip's, and the brewery and old houses behind Satis House.

places.name: Gad's Hill Place, Higham
places.note: Dickens's house, a few miles from the marshes he was writing about.

places.name: Smithfield and Little Britain, London
places.note: Jaggers's office, in sight of Newgate and the meat market Pip arrives at, smeared with filth and fat.

places.name: Walworth
places.note: Wemmick's castle, drawbridge and nine o'clock gun.

places.name: Hammersmith
places.note: Matthew Pocket's house on the river, where Pip is educated alongside Drummle and Startop.

related.why: Dickens seventeen years earlier on money, memory and whether a settled character can be remade.
The other great first-person Victorian account of a childhood turned into a case against the adults who managed it.
Written for the same journal circle, and the clearest demonstration of what serial suspense does to a plot.
The next generation's version of the same question: what a person's origins are allowed to decide about their life.
A boy narrator, a fugitive on a river and a conscience formed against everything he has been taught.

books.title: Hamlet
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Elsinore, the Danish royal castle, with journeys to Paris, Wittenberg and England reported rather than shown
books.lengthNote: The longest play in the canon; no surviving early text has ever been performed uncut as a matter of routine
books.summary: A prince comes home to a court that has already buried his father and married his mother, and a ghost tells him the new king is the murderer. What follows is not a hunt but an investigation: Hamlet has to decide what would count as proof of something no witness saw, and every answer he reaches arrives late or costs a life he did not mean to spend.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Hamlet
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering of a conflated text. The three early witnesses — Q1, Q2 and the Folio — differ, and modern editions number accordingly.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A dead king speaks before the living one is questioned
structure.summary: The Ghost walks twice before Hamlet is told about it, so the audience knows Denmark is disturbed before it meets the man who will be blamed for disturbing it. Claudius disposes of mourning, marriage and a foreign war in a single speech; by the end of the act Hamlet has a murder accusation from a source he cannot classify, and a plan to behave strangely on purpose.

scenes.title: The watch
scenes.summary: Sentries and Horatio see the Ghost and connect it to Denmark's rearmament against Fortinbras.

scenes.title: The court
scenes.summary: Claudius performs state business fluently; Hamlet refuses the performance, and hears that his father has been seen.

scenes.title: Advice and prohibition
scenes.summary: Laertes leaves for Paris with a lecture from Polonius, who then forbids Ophelia to see Hamlet.

scenes.title: The platform
scenes.summary: Hamlet meets the Ghost in the cold and follows it against his friends' advice.

scenes.title: The Ghost's account
scenes.summary: Poison in the ear, a command to revenge, an exemption for Gertrude, and an oath of silence.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The court turns observation into policy
structure.summary: Polonius sends a man to France to spread lies about his own son in order to hear the truth about him, which is the method of the whole court in miniature. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are hired to do the same to Hamlet. The act ends with Hamlet inventing a better version of the same technique: a play staged to be watched by one man.

scenes.title: Reynaldo and the report
scenes.summary: Polonius teaches an informer to invent small vices; Ophelia describes Hamlet's silent visit.

scenes.title: Friends, ambassadors, players
scenes.summary: The schoolfellows are recruited, the Norwegian crisis is settled offstage, and the players give Hamlet an idea.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A play catches a king; a sword misses one
structure.summary: Two scenes of arranged watching sit either side of the Mousetrap. Claudius reacts, which Hamlet reads as proof, and then kneels to pray, which Hamlet reads as a bad moment to kill him. Within a hundred lines Hamlet does kill, through a curtain, without looking, and the man behind it is Ophelia's father.

scenes.title: The nunnery scene
scenes.summary: Hamlet's most famous soliloquy is spoken into a trap, and Ophelia is the bait he then turns on.

scenes.title: The Mousetrap
scenes.summary: Advice to the players, then a murder play; Claudius rises and calls for light.

scenes.title: The prayer
scenes.summary: Claudius finds he cannot repent; Hamlet postpones the killing on theological grounds.

scenes.title: The closet
scenes.summary: Polonius dies behind the arras, and the Ghost returns to a room where only Hamlet can see it.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Grief is converted into political weapons
structure.summary: Hamlet is exported. In his absence the play shows what happens to the people he has damaged: Ophelia goes mad and drowns, Laertes comes home with a mob behind him, and Claudius spends one long scene turning a young man's grief into a poisoned foil. The act runs on offstage events reported by letters and messengers.

scenes.title: The report
scenes.summary: Gertrude tells Claudius of the killing and describes her son as mad.

scenes.title: The sponge
scenes.summary: Hamlet refuses to say where the body is and tells Rosencrantz what a courtier is for.

scenes.title: Supper of worms
scenes.summary: Claudius, working in public calm, sends Hamlet to England with a sealed order for his death.

scenes.title: The army crossing
scenes.summary: Fortinbras marches for a worthless patch of Poland; Hamlet measures himself against it.

scenes.title: Ophelia's songs
scenes.summary: Madness set to old tunes and flowers, then Laertes at the door with an armed crowd.

scenes.title: Pirates
scenes.summary: Horatio receives the letter that returns Hamlet to Denmark by accident.

scenes.title: The plot
scenes.summary: Claudius arranges the unbated sword and the poisoned cup; Gertrude reports the drowning.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Death becomes ordinary work, then arrives
structure.summary: A man who digs graves for a living sings at it, and Hamlet finally talks about death without metaphor, holding the skull of somebody he knew. The duel is a rigged fencing match that goes wrong in every direction at once; four people die of a plot designed to kill one, and the last Danish voice in the play gives the throne to a Norwegian.

scenes.title: The graveyard
scenes.summary: Gravediggers argue law and precedence; Yorick's skull; a funeral turns into a fight in the grave.

scenes.title: The duel
scenes.summary: Hamlet tells how he rewrote the commission, accepts the match, and the poison finds everyone.

characters.name: Hamlet
characters.role: Prince of Denmark, son of the murdered king
characters.summary: A student called home into a job he has no evidence for and no appetite for. His delay is usually described as a flaw, but the play keeps showing him doing the work of proof: testing the Ghost, staging the play, reading the commission. What he cannot do is act while he is still thinking, and the two things almost never stop at the same time.
characters.clue: He wears black at a wedding, talks to a skull, and stages a play in order to watch one man's face.
traits: unable to act and think at once

relationships.label: kills the father of, then fights

characters.name: Claudius
characters.role: King of Denmark, the dead king's brother
characters.summary: The most competent politician in the play and the only character who tells the audience outright that he is guilty. He settles a foreign crisis by letter, manages a rebellion by talking to it, and never once mishandles a room — which is what makes the prayer scene devastating, because it is the single thing he cannot negotiate.
characters.clue: He opens with a speech that makes a funeral and a wedding sound like one piece of administration, and later cannot pray.

characters.name: Gertrude
characters.summary: She is given very few lines in which to be anything other than the subject of other people's speeches about her. The play never says whether she knew about the murder, and the closet scene is the one place where she is asked directly and answers in a way that settles nothing. Her clearest moment is the speech describing Ophelia's drowning.
characters.clue: Her marriage is the scandal the play opens on, and her longest speech is a description of a drowning she did not witness.

relationships.label: hoped to have as a daughter-in-law

characters.name: Ophelia
characters.summary: Every scene she appears in before her madness has been arranged by a man: her father tells her what to feel, her brother tells her what to fear, and she is placed in a corridor with a book to be watched. When she loses her reason she is finally allowed to speak first and at length, and the court cannot stop her singing.
