Stevenson makes the failure repeat until it becomes the subject: the response to Hyde is social and instinctive before it is visual, which leaves a reader to wonder what these respectable observers think they are recognising.
themes.development: Enfield cannot specify it, Utterson cannot, Poole cannot, and Jekyll finally explains it as evil written plainly on a face — an explanation from the least reliable source available.

themes.name: Appetite and habit
themes.summary: The story keeps the pleasures vague and the mechanics of dependence very precise. Jekyll starts taking the draught for enjoyment, then to be himself again, then in double doses, then at any hour; the last crisis is a failed supply of a chemical. It reads less like a fable about sin than a careful account of a habit.
themes.development: An occasional escape becomes an involuntary change in Regent's Park, and the final chapter turns on a drawer of salt that cannot be replaced.

techniques.name: Multiple narrators
techniques.definition: A story assembled from several voices, each limited to what that person knows.
techniques.inThisBook: Eight chapters follow Utterson, who is wrong; the last two are written by Lanyon and Jekyll, who are right and dead. The truth arrives only when it can no longer be tested.

techniques.name: Delayed revelation
techniques.definition: Withholding the central fact so that earlier scenes must be reread once it lands.
techniques.inThisBook: Stevenson never shows a transformation until chapter nine. Every adaptation that opens with one is telling a different story, because the novella's suspense is built on a reader sharing Utterson's blindness.

techniques.name: Doors and thresholds
techniques.definition: Physical barriers used to carry an idea about what is concealed behind them.
techniques.inThisBook: A blistered door with neither bell nor knocker, a cabinet door broken with an axe, a window shut mid-sentence: the plot advances by things being locked, forced or closed.

techniques.name: Legal and professional diction
techniques.definition: The vocabulary of contracts, cases and clinical reports used for uncanny material.
techniques.inThisBook: The title itself is a case report, the will's phrasing is quoted verbatim, and the confession is a statement of the case — the supernatural is handled entirely in the language of offices.

techniques.name: Understatement
techniques.definition: Saying less than the situation warrants, so that the omission carries the weight.
techniques.inThisBook: Enfield's it was hellish to see, Lanyon's refusal to name what he witnessed, and Utterson's habit of noticing something and going home are all places where the prose declines to elaborate.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: Pairing characters or spaces so that each exposes something about the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Jekyll and Hyde are the obvious pair, but so are the two fronts of one house, the two doctors, and Utterson and Enfield, who walk together every Sunday without speaking.

quotations.text: I let my brother go to the devil in his own way.
quotations.speaker: Gabriel John Utterson
quotations.context: The narrator's summary of Utterson's usual joke about himself, on the first page.
quotations.analysis: It is offered as tolerance and it is also a policy of non-intervention, stated before any of the events. Cain's question was whether he was his brother's keeper; Utterson has decided in advance that he is not, and the plot then hands him a friend going to the devil and eight chapters in which he never quite intervenes.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Story of the Door

quotations.text: It was two storeys high; showed no window, nothing but a door on the lower storey and a blind forehead of discoloured wall on the upper; and bore in every feature, the marks of prolonged and sordid negligence.
quotations.context: The first description of the door in the by-street, before anyone connects it to Jekyll.
quotations.analysis: Blind forehead gives the building a face that cannot look back, which is exactly the problem every witness will have with Hyde. The whole description is of absences — no window, nothing but a door, neither bell nor knocker — so the reader meets the concealed half of Jekyll's house as a subtraction from an ordinary street.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Story of the Door

quotations.text: It sounds nothing to hear, but it was hellish to see. It wasn’t like a man; it was like some damned Juggernaut.
quotations.speaker: Richard Enfield
quotations.context: Enfield describing how Hyde walked over the fallen child.
quotations.analysis: Enfield reaches for a Hindu temple car brought back by imperial travellers because ordinary English will not do the job, and he flags the failure himself: it sounds nothing to hear. The comparison makes Hyde mechanical rather than cruel — something that continues rather than something that decides.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Story of the Door

quotations.text: I never saw a circle of such hateful faces; and there was the man in the middle, with a kind of black, sneering coolness
quotations.speaker: Richard Enfield
quotations.context: The crowd that gathers around Hyde after the child is knocked down.
quotations.analysis: The hateful faces here are the respectable ones. Enfield has just described a doctor turning sick with the desire to kill, and women as wild as harpies, and the calm figure is the man who trampled a child. Stevenson keeps arranging scenes in which the decent majority looks worse than it means to.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Story of the Door

quotations.text: There is something wrong with his appearance; something displeasing, something downright detestable. I never saw a man I so disliked, and yet I scarce know why.
quotations.speaker: Richard Enfield
quotations.context: Utterson has asked what Hyde looks like.
quotations.analysis: Three attempts at a noun and not one physical detail: the sentence describes Enfield's reaction and calls it a description. Every witness in the book will repeat the pattern, and since the reader only ever gets these reports, Hyde stays permanently unillustrated — which is why he is so easy for adaptations to invent.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Story of the Door

quotations.text: the person that drew the cheque is the very pink of the proprieties, celebrated too, and (what makes it worse) one of your fellows who do what they call good
quotations.speaker: Richard Enfield
quotations.context: Explaining why he assumes the cheque means blackmail.
quotations.analysis: What makes it worse is the whole novella in four words: the scandal is not the violence but the signature attached to it. Enfield's parenthesis assumes that public charity and private vice go together as a matter of course, which is the assumption Jekyll's confession will confirm from the inside.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Story of the Door

quotations.text: disappearance or unexplained absence for any period exceeding three calendar months
quotations.context: The clause in Jekyll's will that has offended Utterson for years.
quotations.analysis: A will normally provides for death; this one provides for a man ceasing to be present without dying. Utterson reads it as evidence that Hyde has a hold over his friend, which is a reasonable professional inference and completely wrong. The clause is in fact the most honest sentence Jekyll writes before his confession.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Search for Mr. Hyde

quotations.text: If he be Mr. Hyde,” he had thought, “I shall be Mr. Seek.
quotations.speaker: Gabriel John Utterson
quotations.context: Utterson, having begun to haunt the by-street at night.
quotations.analysis: The one joke the lawyer makes in the book, and it treats the name as a pseudonym rather than a person. He is right that the name is a description and wrong about what it describes, and Stevenson lets the pun stand as the high point of an investigation that never gets any closer than this.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Search for Mr. Hyde

quotations.text: He began to go wrong, wrong in mind; and though of course I continue to take an interest in him for old sake’s sake as they say, I see and I have seen devilish little of the man.
quotations.speaker: Dr Hastie Lanyon
quotations.context: Lanyon, over wine, explaining his estrangement from Jekyll.
quotations.analysis: The repetition of wrong — first moral, then mental — is Lanyon trying to be charitable and failing. He has diagnosed his colleague as mad rather than immoral, which is the most generous verdict orthodox science can offer, and it will be overturned in one night by a demonstration he asked for.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Search for Mr. Hyde

quotations.text: if ever I read Satan’s signature upon a face, it is on that of your new friend.
quotations.speaker: Gabriel John Utterson
quotations.context: Utterson's private reflection after meeting Hyde in the street for the first time.
quotations.analysis: A lawyer reaches for the one thing in his professional world that settles a question — a signature — and applies it to a face. The metaphor concedes that he has no evidence, only a reading, and the book has already shown him that handwriting is precisely what cannot be trusted here.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Search for Mr. Hyde

quotations.text: He was wild when he was young; a long while ago to be sure; but in the law of God, there is no statute of limitations.
quotations.speaker: Gabriel John Utterson
quotations.context: Walking home, constructing a theory of blackmail out of Jekyll's youth.
quotations.analysis: He translates damnation into the only jurisdiction he practises in, and in doing so he arrives at a theory that is wrong in fact and exactly right in spirit. Jekyll's statement will confirm the wild youth and the absence of any limitation period; it will simply put the punishment inside the man rather than in an extortionist's hands.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Search for Mr. Hyde

quotations.text: the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde.
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
quotations.context: Reassuring Utterson after dinner, and asking him to let the matter sleep.
quotations.analysis: Every word of it is true when he says it and false within the year — this is the sentence of a man describing an escape he has not yet failed to make. Choose is the load-bearing word, and the final statement is largely an account of the point at which choosing stopped being available.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease

quotations.text: And next moment, with apelike fury, he was trampling his victim under foot and hailing down a storm of blows, under which the bones were audibly shattered and the body jumped upon the roadway.
quotations.context: A maidservant at an upstairs window watching the killing of Sir Danvers Carew.
quotations.analysis: The violence is graded by sound and motion rather than by injury: audibly shattered, and a body that jumps. Apelike is the closest the book comes to the Victorian idea that the lower nature is an earlier one, and it is worth noticing that the observation belongs to a witness who faints, not to the narrator.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Carew Murder Case

quotations.text: The stick with which the deed had been done, although it was of some rare and very tough and heavy wood, had broken in the middle under the stress of this insensate cruelty
quotations.context: The police examine the scene the following morning.
quotations.analysis: The cane was a present from Utterson, and half of it will be found in Jekyll's house: the murder weapon travels from the lawyer to the victim's body to the respectable friend's rooms. Stevenson measures the violence indirectly, by what it did to a piece of hardwood, which is more frightening than a description of the body would have been.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Carew Murder Case

quotations.text: It is one thing to mortify curiosity, another to conquer it
quotations.context: After Lanyon's death, with the sealed envelope locked in Utterson's safe.
quotations.analysis: Mortify is the word used earlier for Utterson's habit of drinking gin instead of the wine he loves, and here it covers a lawyer choosing not to open a packet he is legally entitled to hold. The novella's plot could end at this sentence if one respectable man broke one seal, and the point is that he does not.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Remarkable Incident of Dr. Lanyon

quotations.text: there before my eyes⁠—pale and shaken, and half fainting, and groping before him with his hands, like a man restored from death⁠—there stood Henry Jekyll!
quotations.speaker: Dr Hastie Lanyon
quotations.context: The end of Lanyon's account of the midnight visit.
quotations.analysis: The transformation the whole book has been withholding is given in a single clause, and it is the restoration rather than the change: Hyde becoming Jekyll, not the other way round. Lanyon's narrative then stops. He tells Utterson what he saw and refuses to write what he was told afterwards, which is the last act of professional discretion in the story.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Dr. Lanyon's Narrative

quotations.text: man is not truly one, but truly two. I say two, because the state of my own knowledge does not pass beyond that point.
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: The opening argument of the confession.
quotations.analysis: The second sentence undoes the first: he admits that two is the limit of his evidence, not a finding, and guesses that man will turn out to be a polity of many. The famous formula is offered by its own author as provisional, which is a warning about how much weight the rest of the confession can carry.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: Though so profound a double-dealer, I was in no sense a hypocrite; both sides of me were in dead earnest
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: Explaining the double life he led long before any chemistry was involved.
quotations.analysis: This is the confession's central plea in mitigation, and it is a distinction with real content: he is not pretending to be good, he is genuinely both. It also quietly establishes that the division existed years before the drug, which means the experiment did not cause his condition — it only supplied a second body to keep the accounts in.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: the unjust might go his way, delivered from the aspirations and remorse of his more upright twin; and the just could walk steadfastly and securely on his upward path
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: The daydream that preceded the experiment.
quotations.analysis: Read the order: the unjust is delivered first and at greater length, and the just merely continues walking. Jekyll's utopia is arranged for the benefit of the half he claims to want rid of, and the sentence gives away whose freedom the experiment was actually designed to secure.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: And yet when I looked upon that ugly idol in the glass, I was conscious of no repugnance, rather of a leap of welcome. This, too, was myself.
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: Seeing Hyde's reflection for the first time.
quotations.analysis: Everyone else who looks at that face reports disgust; the one person who is it reports welcome. The admission destroys the defence Jekyll spends the rest of the chapter building, since a man cannot claim that Hyde was an alien invader and also that he recognised him instantly with pleasure.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: all human beings, as we meet them, are commingled out of good and evil: and Edward Hyde, alone in the ranks of mankind, was pure evil.
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: Accounting for the physical revulsion Hyde provokes in strangers.
quotations.analysis: It is the most convenient sentence in the confession, and it is contradicted by the plot: Hyde is frightened, he weeps, he negotiates, he writes letters and he wants to live. Pure evil is what Jekyll needs Hyde to be if the responsibility is to sit anywhere but with him.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: Edward Hyde would pass away like the stain of breath upon a mirror
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: Describing the security of the arrangement in its early months.
quotations.analysis: The image is of something that was never a substance in the first place, which is how Jekyll would like the arrangement understood. Note what follows it in the sentence: a man quietly at home who could afford to laugh at suspicion. The comfort being described is not moral relief but immunity from consequences.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: My devil had been long caged, he came out roaring.
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: Explaining the murder of Sir Danvers Carew after two months of abstinence.
quotations.analysis: The possessive is the admission: my devil, not the devil. He has just spent two months living virtuously, and the account he gives is that the abstinence itself loaded the violence — which makes the Carew murder the direct consequence of his attempt to reform.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: I was slowly losing hold of my original and better self, and becoming slowly incorporated with my second and worse.
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: After the involuntary transformation in Regent's Park.
quotations.analysis: The difficulty has reversed: at the start it took a drug to become Hyde, and now it takes one to stay Jekyll. Slowly appears twice in a single sentence, and the repetition turns a supernatural condition into something with the shape of a habit, measured in doses that stop working.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

quotations.text: Here then, as I lay down the pen and proceed to seal up my confession, I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.
quotations.speaker: Dr Henry Jekyll
quotations.reference: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novella.
quotations.analysis: He writes about himself in the third person and hands the ending to a sealing-wax, not to a death: the act that finishes Henry Jekyll is the closing of a document. It is also a disclaimer — what is to follow concerns another than myself — so the book ends with its narrator declining responsibility for his own body.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: At Skerryvore, the house in Bournemouth Stevenson took for his health.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By Longmans, Green and Co. in London; a New York edition appeared at about the same time.

atAGlance.label: Title
atAGlance.value: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
atAGlance.note: No opening The, and no full stop after Dr — the phrasing of a case report rather than a novel.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.value: Ten chapters, two of them sealed documents
atAGlance.note: Eight chapters of investigation, then Lanyon's narrative and Jekyll's statement arrive after both men are dead.

criticalViews.position: A fable about the divided self
criticalViews.summary: The reading the title has given the language: two natures in one man, one of them released by chemistry. It takes Jekyll's own theory as the book's, and it is the version almost every adaptation dramatises.
criticalViews.counter: The theory belongs to a narrator with every reason to prefer it, and the novella's own evidence — Hyde's fear, his letters, his negotiations — keeps failing to match the claim that he is pure evil.

criticalViews.position: A study of Victorian respectability
criticalViews.summary: On this account the subject is not the laboratory but the club: a professional class in which discretion is a virtue, questions are impolite, and a man's reputation is a shared asset that several people work to protect.
criticalViews.counter: It risks making the story sociology. The horror in the last night chapter is not about reputation at all; it is about a voice behind a door.

criticalViews.position: A book about addiction
criticalViews.summary: Readers have long noticed how precisely the middle chapters describe tolerance, escalating doses, involuntary relapse and a failed supply. The crisis is finally chemical: a batch of salt with an impurity that cannot be reproduced.
criticalViews.counter: Stevenson never names a substance or a habit, and the reading can quietly replace the moral question — what Jekyll wanted — with a medical one.

criticalViews.position: A story about the limits of description
criticalViews.summary: Attention has turned to what the book refuses to show: the pleasures are unspecified, the deformity is unnamed, and eight chapters pass without a transformation. What is frightening is generated by the gaps rather than by any image.
criticalViews.counter: A reader can also find the gaps evasive rather than artful, and the unspecified pleasures have carried very different meanings for different generations.

essayQuestions.question: How does Stevenson control what the reader is allowed to know?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, narration and delayed revelation
plan: Establish that eight chapters follow a man whose professional imagination cannot reach the answer.
Use the will and the handwriting comparison to show evidence arriving in a form Utterson can misread.
Examine Lanyon's narrative: the one eyewitness account, and its deliberate stopping point.
Read the final statement as a document with an author and a purpose rather than as the truth.
Conclude with adaptation: what is lost when a production shows the transformation in its first scene.

essayQuestions.question: Is Hyde a separate person, or a permission?
essayQuestions.focus: Duality, responsibility and the evidence of the confession
plan: Set out Jekyll's own theory of two natures and note where he admits its limits.
Gather the moments that undercut the theory: the leap of welcome at the mirror, my devil, the memory that carries across.
Use the Carew murder and its timing after two months of virtue.
Consider Hyde's ordinary behaviour — cheques, lodgings, letters — as evidence against pure evil.
Decide whether the novella endorses Jekyll's defence or supplies the material to dismantle it.

essayQuestions.question: What does respectability cost in this novella?
essayQuestions.focus: Reputation, silence and professional discretion
plan: Begin with Enfield and Utterson agreeing never to mention the door again.
Trace the pattern through Utterson's suppression of the letter in a murder investigation.
Weigh Lanyon's sealed envelope, held unopened while there is still time to act.
Set Poole against the professionals: a servant who believes the evidence of his ears.
Close on Jekyll's admission that he was in no sense a hypocrite, and ask what that distinction is worth.

essayQuestions.question: How does Stevenson use London?
essayQuestions.focus: Setting, architecture and the divided map
plan: Start with the single building that has a comfortable square at the front and a blistered door at the back.
Contrast the descriptions of the by-street on a Sunday with Soho under fog.
Track the thresholds: the door with no knocker, the window shut mid-sentence, the cabinet door taken down with an axe.
Consider Edinburgh behind the London geography, and what Stevenson gains by moving it south.
Conclude with Regent's Park, where the safest and most public space produces the change.

discussionQuestions: Utterson never opens Lanyon's envelope while it could still do any good. Is that decency or cowardice?
Nobody can describe Hyde's deformity. What do you think the witnesses are actually responding to?
The novella never says what Hyde's pleasures are. Does that make the book stronger or evasive?
Jekyll's statement is the only full account of what happened. How much of it would you accept?
Almost every adaptation shows the transformation early. What is lost, and is anything gained?

timeline.label: Deacon William Brodie is hanged in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: A respected cabinetmaker and town councillor by day and a burglar by night; Stevenson grew up with the story and later wrote a play about him.

timeline.label: Robert Louis Stevenson is born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: Into a family of lighthouse engineers, in a city of respectable New Town squares and old closes.

timeline.label: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
timeline.detail: One source of the late-Victorian habit of describing the worse half of a man as an earlier one.

timeline.label: The novella is written at Bournemouth
timeline.detail: By Stevenson's own account it began in a dream and was drafted at great speed; the household story that he burned a first version has been repeated ever since.

timeline.label: Published in London by Longmans, Green and Co.
timeline.detail: Issued as a cheap shilling shocker in January and taken up almost at once by pulpits and reviewers.

timeline.label: Kidnapped published in the same year
timeline.detail: Stevenson's most productive period, and a reminder that the man writing about a divided self was also writing adventure fiction.

timeline.label: Richard Mansfield stars in the authorised stage version
timeline.detail: Thomas Russell Sullivan's adaptation, first at the Boston Museum; the transformation is performed in front of the audience, reversing Stevenson's method.

timeline.label: Mansfield brings the play to London during the Whitechapel murders
timeline.detail: The coincidence fixed a link between the story and the idea of a respectable Londoner who kills, and the production closed early.

timeline.label: Stevenson dies at Vailima in Samoa
timeline.detail: Aged forty-four, with Weir of Hermiston unfinished.

timeline.label: Rouben Mamoulian's film for Paramount
timeline.detail: Fredric March won an Academy Award for the dual role, and the film's subjective camera made the transformation the centrepiece.

places.name: Soho, London
places.note: Hyde's rooms, reached through a fog that Utterson describes as a district of some city in a nightmare.

places.name: Cavendish Square
places.note: Lanyon's house, the address of orthodox and prosperous medicine.

places.name: Regent's Park
places.note: Where Jekyll changes into Hyde on a bench, in daylight, without taking anything.

places.name: Bournemouth
places.note: Skerryvore, the house where Stevenson wrote the novella in 1885.

places.name: Edinburgh
places.note: Stevenson's own divided city, and the town where Deacon Brodie kept two lives in one reputation.

related.why: The other late-Victorian case file, where the danger is again reconstructed from documents by professional men.
Published five years later, and the same arrangement in reverse: the respectable face stays intact while the hidden thing takes the damage.
The earlier experiment carried out alone and in secret, and the earlier confession delivered by a dying man.
The same London of fog, cabs and respectable clients with unrespectable problems, investigated by someone who is much better at it than Utterson.
Another short book whose whole effect depends on a single narrator's account and on what is never shown.

books.title: King Lear
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: A pre-Christian Britain of dukedoms and earldoms, moving from a palace to open heath and finally to the cliffs and camps around Dover
books.lengthNote: Around 3,300 lines in a conflated text; the quarto and the Folio each contain several hundred lines the other lacks
books.openingLine: I thought the king had more affected the Duke of Albany than Cornwall.
books.summary: An old king asks his three daughters to say how much they love him, and disinherits the one who will not perform. Within two acts he has no soldiers, no roof and no title, and the play spends the next three watching what is left of a man when the offices are taken away. A second family repeats the mistake with sons, and by the end both fathers have learned to see and neither survives the knowledge.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of King Lear
sourceText.note: The Globe numbering follows a conflated text. The 1608 quarto and the 1623 Folio differ in hundreds of readings, and the Folio omits a whole scene that many editions print as 4.3.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A ceremony that cannot be undone
structure.summary: Lear turns the handover of a kingdom into a public competition in flattery, and punishes the one daughter who declines to compete. The same act shows Edmund forging a letter and persuading his father of the opposite of the truth. Both fathers act on speech alone, and both are wrong within a hundred lines of hearing it.

scenes.title: The love test
scenes.summary: Cordelia says nothing, is disinherited and married to France; Kent objects and is banished.

scenes.title: The forged letter
scenes.summary: Edmund persuades Gloucester that Edgar plots against him, using a document he wrote himself.

scenes.title: Goneril's instructions
scenes.summary: She tells her steward to treat the old king and his knights coldly on purpose.

scenes.title: A hundred knights
scenes.summary: Kent returns in disguise, the Fool arrives, and Lear curses Goneril with sterility.

scenes.title: Leaving for Regan
scenes.summary: The Fool works on Lear's mistake; Lear names the fear that will occupy the rest of the play.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The retinue is bargained down to nothing
structure.summary: Edmund stages an attack on himself and inherits his brother's place. Kent is put in the stocks — an insult to the king through his servant — and Lear arrives to find the two sisters auctioning his household downwards from a hundred knights to none. He walks out into weather rather than accept the last offer.

scenes.title: Edmund's wound
scenes.summary: A staged skirmish sends Edgar into flight and makes Edmund the loyal son.

scenes.title: Kent in the stocks
scenes.summary: A servant of the king is punished by a duke, and Gloucester's protest is overruled.

scenes.title: Poor Tom
scenes.summary: Edgar decides that the only safe identity left to him is that of a mad beggar.

scenes.title: What need one?
scenes.summary: The sisters reduce the retinue by arithmetic; Lear goes out into the storm.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Weather, and a mock trial in a hovel
structure.summary: Lear shouts at the elements, then does something he has never done before: he thinks about people who have no shelter on any night of the year. The scenes alternate between the heath and Gloucester's castle, so the king's disintegration is cut against the machinery of a coup, and the act ends with a duke pulling out an old man's eyes in his own house.

scenes.title: News of France
scenes.summary: Kent tells a gentleman of the division between the dukes and of forces landing.

scenes.title: The storm
scenes.summary: Lear commands the weather, and the Fool answers him in riddles and rhyme.

scenes.title: Gloucester's secret
scenes.summary: He confides his loyalty to the king to the son who immediately reports it.

scenes.title: The hovel
scenes.summary: Lear meets Poor Tom, and tears off his own clothes to match him.

scenes.title: The betrayal rewarded
scenes.summary: Edmund is made Earl of Gloucester for the information he has just given.

scenes.title: The mock trial
scenes.summary: Lear arraigns a joint-stool as Goneril before a beggar, a fool and a disguised earl.

scenes.title: The blinding
scenes.summary: Cornwall puts out Gloucester's eyes; a servant kills him for it and is killed.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Two ruined fathers, one led and one found
structure.summary: A blind man is guided towards a cliff by the son he disowned, and survives a fall that never happens. A mad king wanders through a field preaching about justice to a man with no eyes. The act ends with the one scene of repair the play allows: Cordelia's army has landed, and Lear wakes up in clean clothes not sure whether he is dead.

scenes.title: Led by Poor Tom
scenes.summary: Gloucester asks a beggar to take him to Dover, not knowing he has hired his son.

scenes.title: Albany turns
scenes.summary: Albany names his wife a fiend; news arrives of Cornwall's death.

scenes.title: Cordelia's grief reported
scenes.summary: A gentleman describes how she received the letters — a scene the Folio does not print.

scenes.title: The search
scenes.summary: Cordelia sends a hundred soldiers to find her father in the high-grown corn.

scenes.title: Regan's jealousy
scenes.summary: Regan interrogates Oswald about Goneril's letters to Edmund.

scenes.title: The cliff at Dover
scenes.summary: The fall that is not a fall, then Lear crowned with weeds on justice, authority and adultery.

scenes.title: Waking
scenes.summary: Lear comes back to himself, kneels to Cordelia, and asks her to forget and forgive.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The battle is won by the wrong side of the argument
structure.summary: The British army defeats the French, so the reunion of Act IV lasts one scene. Edmund's counter-order for Cordelia's death outlives the duel that kills him, by minutes. The play refuses to convert any of this into consolation: the last thing Lear does is ask five people to look at his daughter's lips.

scenes.title: Before the battle
scenes.summary: Edmund calculates between two sisters; Edgar delivers a letter to Albany.

scenes.title: The defeat
scenes.summary: Lear and Cordelia are taken; Edgar tells his father that ripeness is all.

scenes.title: The end
scenes.summary: Prison, a challenge, a duel, two dead sisters, a reprieve too late, and Lear with Cordelia's body.

characters.name: King Lear
characters.summary: A man who has never in his life been contradicted and cannot tell the difference between love and the language of love. What the play takes from him is not power — he gives that away in the first scene — but the assumptions that came with it, and what is left underneath turns out to be capable of pity for the first time at eighty.
characters.clue: He asks three women to say how much they love him, and ends the play carrying the one who refused.

characters.name: Cordelia
characters.summary: She speaks about a hundred lines in the whole play and is absent from the middle three acts, which is part of the design: the play keeps taking her away. Her refusal in the first scene is not defiance but an unwillingness to price a relationship, and it costs her a kingdom in under fifty lines.
characters.clue: Asked to bid for a third of a kingdom, she offers a word that means nothing, and is believed.

characters.name: Goneril
characters.role: Lear's eldest daughter, Duchess of Albany
characters.summary: She wins the first scene by saying what is wanted and spends the rest of the play being right about her father's knights and wrong about everything else. The play gives her a real grievance and then lets her overrun it: by Act IV she is poisoning her sister and writing to a man about killing her husband.
characters.clue: She tells her steward to grow cold to the old man on purpose, and later poisons her own sister.

characters.name: Regan
characters.role: Lear's second daughter, Duchess of Cornwall
characters.summary: She follows her sister's lead in Act I and outruns her afterwards. It is Regan who suggests plucking out the second eye, and Regan who kills the servant who objects. Widowed in the same scene, she immediately begins competing for Edmund, and dies of her sister's poison without ever suspecting it.
characters.clue: She asks what need her father has of even one attendant, and later calls for the other eye.

characters.name: Earl of Gloucester
characters.role: Lear's courtier, father of Edgar and Edmund
characters.summary: He jokes about his illegitimate son's conception in the play's opening exchange and never notices that the son is listening. His plot rhymes with Lear's without repeating it: Lear cannot read speech, Gloucester cannot read a document, and it is Gloucester who is punished physically for a loyalty he only just found the nerve to act on.
characters.clue: He believes a forged letter, loses both eyes in his own house, and asks a beggar to lead him to a cliff.

characters.name: Edmund
characters.summary: The only character who tells the audience his plan and keeps to it. He argues that the law's distinction between his brother and himself is arbitrary, which is true, and then uses the point to justify anything at all. His attempt to do one good thing arrives about ninety seconds too late to save Cordelia.
characters.clue: He forges a letter in his brother's hand, cuts his own arm to prove his loyalty, and is loved by two sisters at once.

characters.name: Edgar
characters.summary: He is tricked out of his name in Act I and spends four acts wearing other people's, of which Poor Tom is only the first. His care for his father is real and strangely cruel — he lets Gloucester believe in a miracle rather than tell him who is holding his arm — and he ends the play holding a kingdom nobody would want.
characters.clue: He blackens his face, takes the name of a Bedlam beggar, and leads his blind father to a cliff that is not there.

characters.name: Earl of Kent
characters.role: Lear's banished servant, disguised as Caius
characters.summary: He contradicts the king to his face in the first scene, is banished for it, and comes back in disguise the same week to carry on doing the job. His loyalty is not sentimental: he trips Oswald, insults Cornwall and gets himself locked in the stocks. At the end he declines the kingdom because he has an appointment elsewhere.
characters.clue: Banished for telling the truth, he shaves his beard, changes his voice and takes service with the man who banished him.

characters.name: The Fool
characters.summary: He arrives after Cordelia leaves and vanishes after the mock trial, which has made some readers connect them. His jokes are all one joke, repeated until it stops being funny: you gave away the thing that made you worth obeying. He is the only person allowed to say it, and he keeps saying it through the worst of the weather.
characters.clue: He tells the king that he is an O without a figure, and disappears from the play after a trial held in a hovel.

themes.name: Nothing, and the price of language
themes.summary: The word runs through both plots like a fault line: Cordelia's answer, Lear's reply, Edmund's 'nothing' as he pockets a forged letter, the Fool's arithmetic of noughts. The play sets speech that performs feeling against speech that measures it, and shows a state making irreversible decisions on the strength of the first.
themes.development: A refusal in 1.1, a joke through Act I, a fact by Act III, when Lear has nothing left to compare with, and an answer in 5.3 where a father asks a dead daughter to speak.

themes.name: Sight, blindness and judgement
themes.summary: Kent tells Lear to see better in the first scene, and the play spends five acts taking the metaphor literally. Gloucester says he stumbled when he saw; Lear, mad, tells a blind man that a man may see how this world goes with no eyes. Understanding in this play is consistently something that arrives after the organ of understanding has been destroyed.
themes.development: Figurative in Act I, appallingly literal in 3.7, and reversed in 4.6, where the blind man and the mad king conduct the play's clearest analysis of power.

themes.name: Nature and the unnatural
themes.summary: Everyone in the play appeals to nature and they mean incompatible things by it. Lear calls on it to make his daughter sterile; Edmund makes it his goddess and means appetite without law; Gloucester reads it in eclipses. The storm is the argument brought on stage, and it answers nobody.
themes.development: Invoked as authority in Acts I and II, unanswering in Act III, and reduced in 3.4 to a bare forked animal with nothing owed to it.

themes.name: Justice and authority
themes.summary: The play holds two trials. The first is a mock one in a hovel, where a madman arraigns a stool; the second is a duel between brothers decided by force. In between, Lear works out that a dog is obeyed in office and that the difference between the justice and the thief is a change of places — the most radical political speech Shakespeare ever gives a king.
themes.development: Ceremonial in 1.1, parodied in 3.6, dismantled in 4.6, and finally left to a chivalric combat that settles a private quarrel and saves nobody.

themes.name: Age, need and dependence
themes.summary: The quarrel that drives Lear onto the heath is about a number: a hundred knights, then fifty, then twenty-five, then what need one. The daughters' case is not obviously wrong, and the play knows it. What Lear finds in answer is that need is not the measure of a life, an argument he can only make once he has lost the argument.
themes.development: Negotiated downwards through Act II, answered in 2.4, and turned outwards in 3.4, where the same reasoning is applied to people who never had anything to lose.

themes.name: Service and loyalty
themes.summary: The play's decency is almost entirely in its servants. Kent takes a beating for a master who sacked him; an unnamed servant of Cornwall's draws a sword to stop a blinding and dies for it; an old tenant leads Gloucester when his family cannot. Rank organises the tragedy, but obligation runs the other way.
themes.development: Punished in 2.2, fatal in 3.7, and finally the only bond left standing in 5.3, where Kent follows his master out of the play.

techniques.name: The double plot
techniques.definition: Two parallel stories staged so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Shakespeare's only tragedy with a fully developed subplot: Lear misreads speech, Gloucester misreads a document, and the two ruined fathers meet in 4.6 so that the comparison happens on stage rather than in the reader's head.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Language that reduces people to beasts, appetite or prey.
techniques.inThisBook: Pelicans, kites, wolves, serpent's teeth, a dog obeyed in office, and finally the bare forked animal: the play measures how far a person can be stripped by how much animal vocabulary is used about them.

techniques.name: Disguise
techniques.definition: A character adopting another identity in full view of the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Kent and Edgar are both disguised for most of the play, and both keep the secret from the people it would comfort — Edgar's refusal to tell his father who he is turns a convention of comedy into an act of prolonged, well-meant cruelty.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Shifting between metre and prose to mark status, sanity or intimacy.
techniques.inThisBook: Lear's verse breaks down into prose on the heath and in the Dover fields, so the collapse can be heard before it is stated; the Fool works almost entirely in prose and rhyme.

techniques.name: The storm as antagonist
techniques.definition: Weather staged as an active force rather than a background.
techniques.inThisBook: Lear addresses the storm directly, commands it, and then concedes that it owes him nothing — a three-stage argument with the sky that no amount of thunder machinery can win for him.

techniques.name: Riddle and aside
techniques.definition: Speech aimed past its apparent hearer, at the audience or at nobody.
techniques.inThisBook: The Fool's riddles say to the theatre what nobody at court may say to the king; Edgar's asides during 4.1 let the audience hold a piece of knowledge that would change everything if it were spoken aloud.

quotations.text: Unhappy that I am, I cannot heave My heart into my mouth: I love your majesty According to my bond; nor more nor less.
quotations.speaker: Cordelia
quotations.context: Her explanation after answering the love test with a single word.
quotations.analysis: 'Bond' is a legal term, and she uses it deliberately: she is offering an obligation that can be relied on instead of a quantity that cannot be checked. 'Nor more nor less' is the sentence her father hears as coldness and the play treats as the only honest accounting in the scene.

quotations.text: Nothing will come of nothing: speak again.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: After Cordelia has twice said 'Nothing'.
quotations.analysis: He states a law of physics and applies it to affection, which is exactly the category error the play is about. The second half of the line is the important half: he gives her another turn, so the disaster that follows is not a misunderstanding but a decision taken with a chance to reconsider.

quotations.text: See better, Lear; and let me still remain The true blank of thine eye.
quotations.speaker: Kent
quotations.context: Refusing to leave after being told to get out of the king's sight.
quotations.analysis: The blank is the white centre of an archery target, so Kent is asking to be the thing his master aims at — a servant volunteering to be a mark. He also drops the royal address and uses the king's name, which in this court is the offence.

quotations.text: Thou, nature, art my goddess; to thy law My services are bound. Wherefore should I Stand in the plague of custom, and permit The curiosity of nations to deprive me,
quotations.speaker: Edmund
quotations.context: The opening of his first soliloquy, holding the letter he has just forged.
quotations.analysis: He borrows the vocabulary of service and law and points it at a goddess who has neither. The argument about primogeniture is genuinely good — an accident of birth order and marriage decides everything about him — which is why the play lets him make it before it lets him act on it.

quotations.text: Now, gods, stand up for bastards!
quotations.speaker: Edmund
quotations.context: The closing line of the soliloquy, as Gloucester comes in.
quotations.analysis: A prayer shouted at the top of an exit line, immediately before the trick it asks help with begins. The word he has just spent twenty lines objecting to is the one he plants at the end for emphasis, which tells you he intends to keep it rather than escape it.

quotations.text: Who is it that can tell me who I am?
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: In Goneril's house, finding that his own knights are being treated as an inconvenience.
quotations.analysis: The Fool answers 'Lear's shadow', and the answer is exact: without the retinue, the ceremony and the obedience, there is no test he can apply to himself. The question is asked in irony and turns out to be the play's real subject by the third act.

quotations.text: How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is To have a thankless child!
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: The end of the curse he lays on Goneril, before storming out.
quotations.analysis: He has just asked nature to make her barren, and this is the sentence he finishes on — a father's grievance dressed as a proverb. The comparison is with a bite, which keeps the whole speech inside the play's animal vocabulary, and he leaves the stage without waiting for a reply.

quotations.text: O, reason not the need: our basest beggars Are in the poorest thing superfluous: Allow not nature more than nature needs, Man's life's as cheap as beast's:
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Answering Regan's question, 'What need one?'
quotations.analysis: It is the best argument he makes in the play and he makes it in defence of a hundred armed men he does not need. The reasoning, though, is general and survives the occasion: measure a person by need and you have already agreed they are livestock. Two acts later he applies it to people with no roof at all.

quotations.text: Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! rage! blow!
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: His first line on the heath, in the storm.
quotations.analysis: Four imperatives in a line, addressed to weather that cannot obey and does not need to: he is still issuing orders because giving orders is the only register he has. The cheeks belong to the wind-heads on old maps, so the command is aimed at a picture of the world rather than the world.

quotations.text: I am a man More sinn'd against than sinning.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Ending the speech in which he summons hidden criminals to confess.
quotations.analysis: The comparative is doing the pleading: he does not claim innocence, only a favourable balance. It is also the first time in the play he calls himself a man rather than a king, and the sentence is only three words longer than it needs to be because the meter of his self-defence keeps shortening.

quotations.text: Poor naked wretches, whereso'er you are, That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm,
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Outside the hovel, having sent the Fool in first.
quotations.analysis: The first sentence in the play in which he thinks about anyone who is not in the room. He addresses people he cannot see and has never considered, and the admission that follows — that he has taken too little care of this — is the nearest thing to a moral turn the play grants him.

quotations.text: Thou art the thing itself: unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor bare, forked animal as thou art.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Looking at Poor Tom, who is naked in the storm; Lear then starts tearing off his own clothes.
quotations.analysis: It is prose, and the prose matters: the king's verse has gone. 'Forked' is a stage direction as much as an image — two legs, nothing else — and the speech ends not in a conclusion but in an action, which is why the scene is usually remembered as something seen rather than something said.

quotations.text: Lest it see more, prevent it. Out, vile jelly!
quotations.speaker: Cornwall
quotations.context: Putting out Gloucester's second eye, after his own servant has been killed trying to stop him.
quotations.analysis: The reason given is precautionary rather than vengeful, which makes it worse: an eye is destroyed because of what it might otherwise witness. Calling it jelly turns an organ into a substance, and Shakespeare puts the whole thing on stage rather than reporting it, so the audience is made to sit in the room.

quotations.text: I have no way, and therefore want no eyes; I stumbled when I saw:
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Blinded, told by an old tenant that he cannot see his way.
quotations.analysis: 'Want' means lack and need at once, and he uses it to argue himself out of pitying his own condition. The line states the play's central reversal as a plain past tense: the error happened while the eyes were working, so the eyes were never the instrument he needed.

quotations.text: As flies to wanton boys, are we to the gods. They kill us for their sport.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Spoken to the man he has just hired to lead him, who is his son.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted theology in the play is a man's response to a private disaster, not a conclusion the play endorses; forty lines earlier he was blaming eclipses, and by Act V he dies of joy. Note who hears it: Edgar, in disguise, who could disprove at least part of it by saying his own name.

quotations.text: And the creature run from the cur? There thou mightst behold the great image of authority: a dog's obeyed in office.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Mad, crowned with weeds, talking to the blinded Gloucester in the fields near Dover.
quotations.analysis: Authority is reduced to a reflex in a beggar's legs, and the argument is built from a scene anyone in the audience would have watched in a street. It is prose, spoken by a king who has lost his reason, and it is the most exact political sentence in the play — which is the point of putting it there.

quotations.text: You do me wrong to take me out o' the grave: Thou art a soul in bliss; but I am bound Upon a wheel of fire, that mine own tears Do scald like moulten lead.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Waking in the French camp, seeing Cordelia for the first time since Act I.
quotations.analysis: He wakes into a private hell and assumes his daughter is in heaven, so his first response to rescue is to apologise for being alive near her. The wheel is a torture from an older iconography than this play's Britain, and his own tears are the instrument — nothing is being done to him from outside.

quotations.text: I am a very foolish fond old man, Fourscore and upward, not an hour more nor less; And, to deal plainly, I fear I am not in my perfect mind.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Kneeling to Cordelia, who has told him not to.
quotations.analysis: Three admissions in four lines, each one plainer than anything he has said before: his age, his foolishness, the state of his mind. 'To deal plainly' is the manner he punished Cordelia for in the first scene, and he has arrived at it by way of a heath, a hovel and a field.

quotations.text: Men must endure Their going hence, even as their coming hither; Ripeness is all: come on.
quotations.speaker: Edgar
quotations.context: Getting his father off the battlefield after the British victory.
quotations.analysis: Consolation offered under pressure by a son still refusing to give his name, and it is a stoic commonplace rather than an answer. The last three words undo the grandeur: this is something said to keep a man walking, not a philosophy the play has arrived at.

quotations.text: The wheel is come full circle: I am here.
quotations.speaker: Edmund
quotations.context: Dying, after Edgar has told him who beat him in the duel.
quotations.analysis: He is the only character in the play to describe his own downfall as a shape, and he sounds almost pleased by the neatness of it. The wheel belongs to Fortune, whose authority he rejected in 1.2 in favour of nature — at the end he accepts the older machinery because it gives his ending a form.

quotations.text: Howl, howl, howl, howl! O, you are men of stones: Had I your tongues and eyes, I'ld use them so That heaven's vault should crack.
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: Entering with Cordelia dead in his arms.
quotations.analysis: The first word can be an order to the men on stage or a sound he is making himself, and productions have to decide. Either way the line begins outside language, and the accusation that follows — you have tongues and eyes and are not using them — indicts everybody standing there, including the audience.

quotations.text: Why should a dog, a horse, a rat, have life, And thou no breath at all? Thou'lt come no more, Never, never, never, never, never!
quotations.speaker: King Lear
quotations.context: His last speech, over Cordelia's body.
quotations.analysis: Five stressed nevers make a line of pure trochaic beats, the only one like it in Shakespeare, and it works because the metre has stopped doing anything except repeat. The question before it is the play's animal vocabulary turned inside out: the beasts are alive and the daughter is not, and no account of nature explains it.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After Harsnett's Declaration of 1603, which supplied Edgar's fiends, and before the recorded court performance of 1606.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: As a True Chronicle Historie, printed for Nathaniel Butter; the Folio of 1623 calls it a tragedy.

atAGlance.label: Two early texts
atAGlance.note: The Folio adds more than a hundred lines and drops around three hundred. Editors must choose, conflate or print both.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two full plots — Lear's daughters and Gloucester's sons — running in parallel and colliding on the heath.

criticalViews.position: The play as a Christian pattern of suffering
criticalViews.summary: A long tradition reads Lear's progress as a purgation: pride stripped away by storm and loss until, in 4.7, the king kneels and is reconciled. On this account the tragedy is a form of instruction.
criticalViews.counter: The ending resists it. Cordelia dies after the reprieve has been sent, for no reason the plot requires, and Lear's last words are a demand that four men look at her lips.

criticalViews.position: The play as a political and material tragedy
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the mid-twentieth century has emphasised the play's interest in property, need and power: a division of land, a negotiation over how many servants a pensioner deserves, and a king who works out that office is what makes obedience happen.
criticalViews.counter: It can flatten the family material, which the play stages with as much care as the politics — the arithmetic of 2.4 only devastates because it is done by daughters.

criticalViews.position: Two plays rather than one
criticalViews.summary: Because the 1608 quarto and the 1623 Folio differ so widely, many textual scholars argue that the Folio represents a later revision and that conflating the two produces a text no early audience heard.
criticalViews.counter: The conflated tradition is what four centuries of readers and actors have worked with, and some of the play's best-known material survives only because editors refused to choose.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use the Gloucester plot?
essayQuestions.focus: Double plot, parallel and difference
plan: Set the two opening deceptions side by side: Lear misreads speech in 1.1, Gloucester misreads a document in 1.2.
Distinguish rather than equate — Gloucester's suffering is physical and undeserved by anything he does on stage, Lear's is the consequence of his own ceremony.
Use 3.7 and 4.1 to show the subplot outpacing the main plot: the blinding is the most violent thing in the play and happens to the secondary father.
Analyse 4.6, where the two ruined men meet and the comparison is made on stage instead of by the audience.
Conclude with the endings: Gloucester dies offstage of joy and grief mixed, Lear on stage of neither.

essayQuestions.question: 'The play is about sight, not madness.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Seeing, knowing and judgement
plan: Start with Kent's 'See better, Lear' and the eye imagery running through the first scene.
Follow the metaphor into literal action at 3.7, and note what reason Cornwall gives for the second eye.
Read 4.1: Gloucester's claim that he stumbled when he saw, and what it implies about the value of evidence in this play.
Set 4.6 against both — a blind man and a mad king conducting the clearest analysis of authority in the text.
Weigh the counter-case: Lear's madness produces insight that his sanity never did, so the two strands may not be separable.

essayQuestions.question: Are Goneril and Regan given a case?
essayQuestions.focus: Justice, need and the presentation of the sisters
plan: Reconstruct their argument from 1.3, 1.4 and 2.4: a hundred armed men in someone else's house, and a father who curses one daughter with sterility.
Notice how much of their behaviour before 3.7 is administrative rather than cruel, and where exactly the line is crossed.
Use 'O, reason not the need' to show the play answering them at the level of principle rather than fact.
Consider the later plot — the poisoning, the letters to Edmund — and ask whether it convicts them or simply disposes of them.
Decide whether the play gives them a case it then refuses to let them keep.

essayQuestions.question: How far does King Lear offer any consolation?
essayQuestions.focus: The ending, justice and the gods
plan: Collect the appeals to the gods across the play and note that none of them is answered on stage.
Treat 4.7 as the play's best offer: reconciliation, clean clothes, a kneeling king, a daughter who says no cause.
Show how 5.3 dismantles it — the reprieve is sent, and arrives too late by a matter of lines.
Weigh Edgar's 'Ripeness is all' and Albany's closing couplet as attempts to supply a moral that the stage picture contradicts.
Compare Tate's ending, and use it to say precisely what Shakespeare's ending refuses to do.

discussionQuestions: Cordelia could have said something warm and true and kept her third of the kingdom. Why does she not?
The Fool disappears after the mock trial and is never mentioned again. What does the play gain by losing him there?
Edgar keeps his identity from his father for four acts. Is that kindness?
Gloucester says the gods kill us for their sport. Does the play agree with him?
Nahum Tate let Lear live for a hundred and fifty years of English theatre. What exactly does that version lose?

timeline.label: The second edition of Holinshed's Chronicles
timeline.detail: Carries the story of King Leir and his three daughters, drawn from Geoffrey of Monmouth, with a restoration that Shakespeare removes.

timeline.label: Sidney's Arcadia
timeline.detail: Supplies the blinded father and the wronged son that Shakespeare builds into the Gloucester plot.

timeline.label: The anonymous King Leir performed
timeline.detail: An older, more openly Christian play on the same story; printed in 1605, and probably known to Shakespeare.

timeline.label: Harsnett's Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures
timeline.detail: The source of the fiends Poor Tom names, and evidence that the play was written after it appeared.

timeline.label: Performed before King James at Whitehall
timeline.detail: The Stationers' Register record and the quarto title page both point to St Stephen's night in the Christmas holidays.

timeline.label: The First Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Printed for Nathaniel Butter as a True Chronicle Historie, and linking the play to the King's Men at the Globe.

timeline.label: The Pavier quarto
timeline.detail: A reprint that keeps the 1608 date on its title page; its true year was not established until the twentieth century.

timeline.label: The First Folio text
timeline.detail: Printed as The Tragedie of King Lear, with over a hundred lines the quarto lacks and around three hundred fewer of the quarto's.

timeline.label: Nahum Tate's History of King Lear
timeline.detail: Removes the Fool, marries Cordelia to Edgar and lets Lear live. It held the English stage for more than a century.

timeline.label: Macready restores the Fool and the tragic ending
timeline.detail: Priscilla Horton played the restored Fool; Shakespeare's ending returned to public stage memory.

timeline.label: Peter Brook's film
timeline.detail: Made from his 1962 Stratford production, with Paul Scofield as Lear and almost every trace of comfort stripped out.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn's RSC production with Ian McKellen
timeline.detail: A stormy, thrust-stage staging that included an on-stage hanging of the Fool.

places.name: Dover
places.note: The cliff Gloucester means to die from, and the coast where Cordelia's army lands.

places.name: Gloucester
places.note: The earldom of the second family, and the title Edmund is given for betraying his father.

places.name: Cornwall
places.note: Regan's dukedom, and the source of the play's most casual cruelty.

places.name: Kent
places.note: The earldom of the man who is banished for honesty in the first scene and comes back disguised.

places.name: Albany
places.note: The old name for the land north of the Forth, and Goneril's husband's title — a duke who slowly changes sides.

places.name: Burgundy
places.note: The suitor who withdraws when Cordelia's dowry disappears, leaving France to take her without one.

related.why: Written within a year or two, and the other Jacobean tragedy in which a kingdom is described as a body that has gone wrong.
The earlier tragedy of a court that cannot tell performance from feeling, and a hero who tests what others simply believe.
Another play in which a credulous man is talked into destroying the person who loves him, and the machinery is entirely verbal.
A later play about an old ruler, a daughter and the giving up of power, written as though the ending of Lear could be answered.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller material on the quarto and Folio texts, criticism and stage history.

books.title: Macbeth
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Eleventh-century Scotland, with one scene at the English court
books.lengthNote: Around 2,100 lines — the shortest of the major tragedies
books.openingLine: When shall we three meet again In thunder, lightning, or in rain?
books.summary: Three witches greet a victorious general with a prophecy that he will be king. Within a day he has murdered the king who trusts him, and the rest of the play watches him kill to keep a crown that gives him nothing. It is Shakespeare's fastest tragedy, and the speed is the argument: Macbeth is never allowed the time to become a different kind of man.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Macbeth
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Modern editions vary by a line or two.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A prophecy, and a decision made in the dark
structure.summary: Macbeth and Banquo meet the witches on the heath and hear that Macbeth will be thane of Cawdor and king. When the first title arrives within minutes, the second stops being an absurdity. Lady Macbeth reads his letter, judges him too decent to take the nearest way, and has the murder arranged before he reaches the door.

scenes.title: Thunder
scenes.summary: Three witches agree to meet Macbeth on the heath.

scenes.title: The report
scenes.summary: A wounded sergeant describes Macbeth carving his way through a rebel army.

scenes.title: The prophecy
scenes.summary: The witches hail Macbeth as Glamis, Cawdor and king hereafter, and tell Banquo he will father kings.

scenes.title: Malcolm named heir
scenes.summary: Duncan thanks Macbeth and then names his own son Prince of Cumberland, putting a step in Macbeth's way.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth's letter and calls on the spirits to strip her of pity.

scenes.title: The welcome
scenes.summary: Duncan arrives at Inverness and praises the sweetness of the air.

scenes.title: The argument
scenes.summary: Macbeth decides against the murder; his wife changes his mind in under fifty lines.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The murder, and the noise that follows it
structure.summary: Macbeth sees a dagger that is not there, kills Duncan offstage, and comes back unable to say 'Amen'. The knocking at the gate, the Porter's drunken joke about hell, and the discovery of the body turn a private act into a public emergency. Malcolm and Donalbain run, which conveniently makes them suspects.

scenes.title: The dagger
scenes.summary: Banquo confesses uneasy dreams; alone, Macbeth follows a dagger he cannot grasp.

scenes.title: After
scenes.summary: Macbeth returns with the grooms' daggers, hearing a voice cry sleep no more.

scenes.title: The knocking
scenes.summary: The Porter plays hell's gatekeeper; Macduff discovers the body and Macbeth kills the grooms.

scenes.title: Unnatural signs
scenes.summary: Ross and an Old Man report horses eating each other; Macbeth goes to Scone to be crowned.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Killing to keep what killing won
structure.summary: Banquo suspects and says nothing. Macbeth, who now fears the second half of the prophecy more than the first, hires murderers without telling his wife. Fleance escapes, the ghost sits in Macbeth's chair at the banquet, and the marriage that planned the first murder comes apart over the third.

scenes.title: Banquo's suspicion
scenes.summary: Banquo weighs what Macbeth has gained; Macbeth hires two murderers.

scenes.title: Scorpions
scenes.summary: Macbeth keeps his wife ignorant of the plan for the first time.

scenes.title: The ambush
scenes.summary: Banquo is killed and Fleance escapes into the dark.

scenes.title: The banquet
scenes.summary: Banquo's ghost takes Macbeth's seat and the state dinner collapses.

scenes.title: Hecate
scenes.summary: Hecate rebukes the witches — a scene most scholars think was added later.

scenes.title: Rumour
scenes.summary: Lennox speaks in careful irony; Macduff has gone to England.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Apparitions, and a household murdered
structure.summary: Macbeth demands more prophecy and is given three riddles that sound like safety. He orders the killing of Macduff's wife and children, an act with no strategic purpose at all. In England, Malcolm tests Macduff by pretending to be worse than the tyrant, and the news from home arrives.

scenes.title: The apparitions
scenes.summary: Beware Macduff; none of woman born shall harm Macbeth; he is safe till Birnam wood moves.

scenes.title: Fife
scenes.summary: Lady Macduff and her son are murdered on stage.

scenes.title: The English court
scenes.summary: Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty; Ross brings the news from Fife.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The riddles come true, and mean nothing
structure.summary: Lady Macbeth washes hands that are clean. Macbeth, told of her death, can find no more feeling in it than a line about tomorrow. Birnam wood moves because the army carries it; the man not of woman born was delivered by caesarean section. Every guarantee holds and every one betrays him.

scenes.title: Sleepwalking
scenes.summary: A doctor and gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth relive the murders in her sleep.

scenes.title: The march
scenes.summary: The Scottish lords join Malcolm's army near Birnam.

scenes.title: The yellow leaf
scenes.summary: Macbeth clings to the apparitions and asks the doctor to cure his wife's mind.

scenes.title: Branches
scenes.summary: Malcolm orders each soldier to cut a bough for cover.

scenes.title: Tomorrow
scenes.summary: The queen is dead; a messenger reports that the wood is moving.

scenes.title: The assault
scenes.summary: The army throws down its screen of branches.

scenes.title: Young Siward
scenes.summary: Macbeth kills a man he cannot fear and begins to look for Macduff.

scenes.title: The end
scenes.summary: Macduff reveals his birth, kills Macbeth, and Malcolm is hailed king.

characters.name: Macbeth
characters.role: Thane of Glamis, then Cawdor, then king of Scotland
characters.summary: A soldier praised for a savagery the state approves of, who discovers that the same nerve is unbearable when he uses it for himself. He imagines every murder in full before he commits it and feels every consequence afterwards, which is why the play is a tragedy rather than a case study.
characters.clue: A soldier whose imagination is his conscience: he sees the dagger before he uses it and hears the voice that will not let him sleep afterwards.

relationships.label: married to
relationships.note: Partners in the first murder, strangers by the third.

characters.name: Lady Macbeth
characters.summary: She reads her husband accurately in a single speech and organises the murder he cannot organise himself. Her strength is a performance she has to summon, and once the crown is won she has no further part to play, which is where the sleepwalking begins.
characters.clue: She calls on spirits to unsex her, tells her husband to look like the innocent flower, and later cannot get a spot off a clean hand.

characters.name: Banquo
characters.summary: He hears the same prophecy and does nothing with it, which makes him the play's control experiment. His silence after Duncan's death is not innocence either: he suspects Macbeth of foul play and keeps quiet because the prophecy also promised something to him.

characters.name: Duncan
characters.summary: Generous, trusting and a poor judge of faces — he says as much about the last thane of Cawdor moments before promoting the next traitor. Shakespeare makes him gentler than the historical king so that the murder costs the audience something.

characters.name: Macduff
characters.summary: He discovers the body, refuses the coronation, and leaves for England without warning his household — a decision the play does not let him off. His grief in 4.3 is the one moment where a man is allowed to feel a loss fully before acting on it.

characters.name: Malcolm
characters.role: Duncan's elder son, Prince of Cumberland
characters.summary: Named heir in 1.4, which is the political fact that makes the prophecy inconvenient. He flees, learns caution, and tests Macduff with a portrait of himself as a worse tyrant than Macbeth — a scene that shows a king being manufactured rather than born.

characters.name: The Weird Sisters
characters.summary: They tell the truth in a form designed to be misheard. Nothing they say compels anybody to do anything, which is the difficulty: the play never settles whether they cause the future or merely describe it accurately enough to be dangerous.

characters.name: Lady Macduff
characters.summary: She gets one scene, and uses it to say the thing nobody else will: that a man who leaves his wife and children unguarded has behaved like a traitor to them, whatever his politics. She is killed on stage, which is rare in Shakespeare and deliberate here.

characters.name: Fleance
characters.summary: He speaks eleven words and then escapes into the dark, and the whole second half of the play runs on that escape. James VI and I's line claimed descent from Banquo, so Fleance running offstage is also the future sitting in the audience.

themes.name: Ambition
themes.summary: The play is careful to show that ambition is not the same as wanting power. Macbeth has power already and is praised for it; what the witches give him is a way of picturing more, and the picture will not leave him alone. Shakespeare gives the desire a body — a spur, a leap, a fall — and no destination.
themes.development: Suggested in 1.3, argued over in 1.7, and by 3.4 it has become momentum rather than choice: he is so far in blood that going back is as tedious as going on.

themes.name: Guilt and conscience
themes.summary: Guilt in this play is physical. It stops a man saying 'Amen', it will not wash off, it takes a seat at dinner, and it eventually walks the corridors at night with a candle. Nobody is punished for the murders by the state; they are punished by their own nervous systems.
themes.development: Macbeth's imagination runs ahead of his conscience in Acts I and II, and his wife's runs behind hers — she is unshaken at the murder and destroyed by it five acts later.

themes.name: Kingship and the state
themes.summary: Scotland is described as a body: bleeding, sick, needing a physician. Malcolm's list of the king-becoming graces in 4.3 sets out what Macbeth is not, and the play's interest is less in who deserves the crown than in what happens to a country when its head is afraid.
themes.development: Duncan's Scotland rewards loyalty in public; Macbeth's rewards silence; Malcolm's begins with a promise of order that the audience has been given reason to doubt.

themes.name: Fate, prophecy and equivocation
themes.summary: Every prophecy in the play is true and every one misleads. The apparitions promise safety in terms that are technically exact and practically worthless, which is the same trick the Jesuit doctrine of equivocation was accused of in the Gunpowder Plot trials of 1606.
themes.development: First a prediction, then a riddle, then a trapdoor: Birnam wood does move, and the man not of woman born does exist.

themes.name: Appearance and reality
themes.summary: The play opens by declaring that fair is foul, and then spends five acts proving it operationally: a welcoming castle, a loyal host, an innocent flower, a safe prophecy. Reading the play is largely a matter of watching characters fail to read each other.
themes.development: Duncan cannot find the mind's construction in the face; by Act IV Malcolm will not trust a face at all, and tests Macduff with a false one of his own.

themes.name: Manhood and gender
themes.summary: 'When you durst do it, then you were a man' is an argument, not an insult, and it works. The play keeps asking what manhood is supposed to license: Macduff's answer in 4.3 — that he must also feel the loss as a man — is offered as a correction to everything Macbeth has been told.
themes.development: Lady Macbeth asks to be unsexed in 1.5; Macbeth asks his wife to bring forth men-children only in 1.7; Macduff refuses the equation in 4.3.

techniques.name: Equivocation
techniques.definition: Saying something literally true in a form designed to be understood wrongly.
techniques.inThisBook: The witches' apparitions and the Porter's joke about the equivocator who could not equivocate to heaven belong to the same 1606 argument about oaths and mental reservation.

techniques.name: Blood imagery
techniques.definition: A repeated image used to bind separate scenes into one idea.
techniques.inThisBook: Blood arrives as heroism in 1.2, becomes a stain in 2.2, a debt in 3.4 and a hallucination in 5.1 without ever leaving the stage.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Macbeth's soliloquies are where the murders actually happen; by Act V they have thinned to a report on how little he feels.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Balancing opposed terms against each other inside one line.
techniques.inThisBook: 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' sets the pattern, and the play keeps pairing terms that should exclude each other — lost and won, innocent flower and serpent.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: Duncan praising the sweetness of the air at Inverness is the clearest case: the audience has just heard what is waiting inside.

techniques.name: Disordered nature
techniques.definition: Weather and animal behaviour made to answer human action.
techniques.inThisBook: Horses eat each other, an owl kills a falcon and darkness strangles the day after Duncan's murder: the killing of a king is reported as a fault in the world.

quotations.text: Fair is foul, and foul is fair: Hover through the fog and filthy air.
quotations.speaker: The Witches
quotations.context: The closing couplet of the first scene, spoken by all three witches together.
quotations.analysis: Twelve lines into the play, the audience is handed its instructions: nothing here will be safely readable.
