The chiasmus turns two opposed words into a closed loop, and the shift into rhymed trochaic tetrameter sets the witches apart from every other voice in the play before they have done anything at all.

quotations.text: All hail, Macbeth, thou shalt be king hereafter!
quotations.speaker: Third Witch
quotations.context: The third of three greetings on the heath, after Glamis and Cawdor.
quotations.analysis: The sentence does not contain an instruction, a condition or a route. It is the flat future tense that does the damage: Macbeth is told what will be, and spends the play converting a prediction into a plan while believing he is only keeping an appointment.

quotations.text: It is too full o' the milk of human kindness To catch the nearest way.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Reading Macbeth's letter about the prophecy, alone.
quotations.analysis: She diagnoses him in a single image, and the image is not an insult — it grants him a nature she considers a practical obstacle. 'The nearest way' is the whole murder rendered as a route on a map, which is exactly the kind of euphemism the couple will need for the next two acts.

quotations.text: Come, you spirits That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here, And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full Of direst cruelty!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, after learning that Duncan will arrive that night.
quotations.analysis: The cruelty she wants has to be sent for, which tells the audience she does not already possess it. 'Crown to the toe' puts the crown on her body as well as on Duncan's head, and the request to be unsexed treats womanhood as a set of feelings — pity, remorse, the milk she later names — that would get in the way.

quotations.text: Look like the innocent flower, But be the serpent under't.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Instructing Macbeth as Duncan approaches the castle.
quotations.analysis: The advice is a compressed piece of stage direction: a face to wear and a thing to be. It also answers Duncan's complaint sixty lines earlier that there is no art to find the mind's construction in the face — the play has just supplied the art, and given it to the other side.

quotations.text: If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well It were done quickly.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, leaving the banquet at which Duncan is his guest.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of 'done' in twelve words, and not one of them names the act. The line is thinking in circles because the speaker will not let the word 'murder' into it, and the soliloquy goes on to reject the plan entirely on grounds of consequence rather than conscience.

quotations.text: I have no spur To prick the sides of my intent, but only Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself And falls on the other.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The end of the soliloquy in which he decides not to kill Duncan.
quotations.analysis: He can find no reason for the murder except the wanting of it, and he says so as though that settled the matter. The rider who over-leaps the saddle is a comic image for a catastrophic one, and the sentence breaks off before it lands — the falling is left to the rest of the play.

quotations.text: Is this a dagger which I see before me, The handle toward my hand?
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at night, moving towards Duncan's chamber.
quotations.analysis: The dagger is offered to him handle first, as a servant would offer it — the hallucination is helpfully arranging the murder. He asks a question rather than making a claim, and keeps asking: the speech is a man conducting an experiment on his own mind and losing.

quotations.text: Methought I heard a voice cry 'Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep'.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Immediately after the murder, still holding the daggers.
quotations.analysis: He reports the sentence rather than owning it, and the voice uses his name as though he were already a story being told about someone else. Sleep is the first of the ordinary things the murder takes away, and the play keeps the receipt: Lady Macbeth will be walking in her sleep three acts later.

quotations.text: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather The multitudinous seas in incarnadine, Making the green one red.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Looking at his hands after Duncan's murder.
quotations.analysis: The scale inverts inside four lines: an ocean cannot clean one hand, so the hand stains the ocean. 'Incarnadine' and 'multitudinous' are Latinate and enormous; 'making the green one red' is four monosyllables and a colour. Shakespeare gives the man the grand version and then the plain one, and the plain one is worse.

quotations.text: O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Speaking to Lady Macbeth while concealing the plan to kill Banquo.
quotations.analysis: The endearment and the scorpions arrive in the same breath, and he tells her about the state of his mind precisely in order to avoid telling her its contents. This is the scene where the marriage stops being a partnership: from here he acts and she is informed afterwards, if at all.

quotations.text: It will have blood; they say, blood will have blood.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: After the guests have been sent away from the ruined banquet.
quotations.analysis: He quotes a proverb, which is the closest he now comes to a moral framework: murder is described as a creature with an appetite of its own. The grammar has no agent in it anywhere, and that is the point — by Act III he has stopped experiencing his killings as things he decides to do.

quotations.text: Macbeth shall never vanquish'd be until Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill Shall come against him.
quotations.speaker: Third Apparition
quotations.context: The third apparition, a crowned child holding a tree.
quotations.analysis: The prophecy hands him an impossibility and he accepts the gift without examining the wrapping — a child holding a branch has already shown him how the wood will move. Equivocation works here not by lying but by offering a picture the listener would rather keep.

quotations.text: Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak Whispers the o'er-fraught heart and bids it break.
quotations.speaker: Malcolm
quotations.context: To Macduff, on hearing that his wife and children are dead.
quotations.analysis: The one piece of straightforwardly good advice in the play, and it is about language. Set it against Macbeth, who has spent four acts refusing to name what he is doing; the play's cure for grief is the opposite of the habit that produced it.

quotations.text: Out, damned spot! out, I say!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Sleepwalking, watched by a doctor and her gentlewoman.
quotations.analysis: She told her husband in 2.2 that a little water clears us of this deed, and she is now scrubbing a hand that has nothing on it. The speech is in prose, which for a queen at this point in a tragedy is itself a diagnosis, and it is broken into fragments that move between all three murders at once.

quotations.text: My way of life Is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf; And that which should accompany old age, As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends, I must not look to have.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at Dunsinane as the English army approaches.
quotations.analysis: He itemises exactly what he has lost, in order, and the list is entirely made of relationships. It is the most accurate self-assessment anyone makes in the play, and it changes nothing — a few lines later he is shouting at a servant about the colour of his face.

quotations.text: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow, Creeps in this petty pace from day to day To the last syllable of recorded time.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: On being told that the queen is dead.
quotations.analysis: Asked to feel something about his wife's death, he produces a theory of time instead. The repetition flattens the future into a queue, and 'syllable' quietly turns all of history into something merely said aloud — which sets up the walking shadow and the poor player five lines later.

quotations.text: Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player That struts and frets his hour upon the stage And then is heard no more.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is aimed at the actor saying it, in a theatre, to people who will go home in an hour. It is the bleakest thing in the play and also the most theatrically self-aware: the man who wanted to be remembered as king describes existence as a performance nobody will recall.

quotations.text: Macduff was from his mother's womb Untimely ripp'd.
quotations.speaker: Macduff
quotations.context: In single combat with Macbeth, answering the claim that no man of woman born can harm him.
quotations.analysis: The last guarantee fails on a technicality, and the technicality is a birth. Macbeth's response — that the word has 'cow'd my better part of man' — admits the whole trick: he had been fighting on the strength of a sentence rather than an army.

quotations.text: Our fears do make us traitors.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macduff
quotations.context: To Ross, on learning that her husband has fled to England.
quotations.analysis: Six words that convict Macduff of the thing the whole play is about — acting on fear and calling it strategy. She is defending nobody, least of all herself, and the scene that follows makes her the only character permitted to be simply right.

quotations.text: More needs she the divine than the physician.
quotations.speaker: Doctor
quotations.context: After watching Lady Macbeth sleepwalk.
quotations.analysis: Medicine hands the case over: what is wrong with her is not a condition. The line pairs with Macbeth's demand two scenes later that the same doctor pluck a rooted sorrow from the memory, and with Scotland itself, repeatedly described as a patient nobody can treat.

quotations.text: Stars, hide your fires; Let not light see my black and deep desires.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Aside, immediately after Duncan names Malcolm his heir.
quotations.analysis: The first thing he does after the obstacle appears is ask the universe to look away. Light and dark run through the whole play as a moral lighting rig, and here Macbeth is operating it himself — he wants not to be seen, including by himself.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Soon after the Gunpowder Plot trials, and three years into James VI and I's English reign.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto survives. The First Folio is the only early text.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare compresses decades of Scottish history into a matter of months.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two of the five acts are over before the murder is half an hour old on stage.

criticalViews.position: Macbeth as a study in conscience
criticalViews.summary: The oldest and still the most common reading: the play's interest is psychological, and its subject is a man who knows exactly what he is doing at every stage and does it anyway.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the witches decorative, when the play gives them the first and last word on what Macbeth becomes.

criticalViews.position: Macbeth as a Jacobean political play
criticalViews.summary: Read alongside the Gunpowder Plot, Daemonologie and the Stuart claim of descent from Banquo, the play looks less like a tragedy of character and more like an argument about legitimate rule addressed to a particular king.
criticalViews.counter: The flattery reading struggles with Act IV: a play written to please James spends a long scene teaching an audience to distrust the man who will be king.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of manhood
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1980s has focused on how consistently violence is licensed by the word 'man' — in Lady Macbeth's taunt, in Macbeth's answer to the murderers, and in Macduff's refusal of the equation in 4.3.
criticalViews.counter: Lady Macbeth's collapse can then be read as the play retreating into a conventional punishment for a woman who overreached.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Macbeth responsible for his own downfall?
essayQuestions.focus: Fate, choice and the limits of prophecy
plan: Open with the fact that nothing the witches say is an instruction: the prophecy is in the future tense, not the imperative.
Use 1.3 and 1.7 to show Macbeth reasoning his way to a decision and then reversing it under pressure from his wife.
Turn the argument at Act III: Banquo's murder is planned without prophecy, without his wife, and without hesitation.
Test the counter-case with 4.1 — the apparitions do not compel Fife, and the play offers no motive for it at all.
Close on 5.5: the man who blamed nobody reduces his own life to a story told by an idiot.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Lady Macbeth.
essayQuestions.focus: Gender, power and collapse
plan: Begin with 1.5: she has to send for cruelty, which means she does not start with it.
Read her control of 1.7 as rhetorical rather than temperamental — the argument she wins is about the meaning of the word 'man'.
Mark the hinge at 3.2, where Macbeth stops telling her things, and note how little she says at the banquet by comparison.
Use 5.1 to show the same material returning as prose, fragments and a clean hand that will not come clean.
Weigh two readings: a psychological collapse, or a play that gives a woman power and then takes it back.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use the supernatural in Macbeth?
essayQuestions.focus: Prophecy, equivocation and staging
plan: Set out what the supernatural actually does: it predicts, it never commands, and it is always accurate.
Compare Banquo's response to the same prophecy as a control on Macbeth's.
Examine the apparitions in 4.1 as equivocation in the strict 1606 sense, alongside the Porter in 2.3.
Consider the dagger and the ghost, which may be supernatural or may be symptoms, and which the play refuses to settle.
Conclude with staging: a production that makes the witches literal and one that makes them internal produce two different plays.

essayQuestions.question: 'A play about the health of a country, not the guilt of a man.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Kingship, the state and Act IV Scene 3
plan: Gather the imagery of Scotland as a body: bleeding, sick, in need of a physician.
Set Duncan's public rewards against Macbeth's rule by informer and Lennox's careful irony in 3.6.
Use Malcolm's list of the king-becoming graces in 4.3 as the play's explicit standard.
Test the statement against 5.1 and 5.5, which are as private as the play gets.
Decide whether the ending restores order or simply installs a more careful politician.

discussionQuestions: The witches never tell Macbeth to do anything. Does that make them innocent?
Why does Shakespeare kill Lady Macduff and her son on stage, when almost every other death happens offstage?
Macbeth hears of his wife's death and talks about time. Is that grief, or the absence of it?
Malcolm pretends to be worse than Macbeth in order to test Macduff. What does the scene suggest about the skills a king needs?
The play is the shortest of the major tragedies. What would be lost if it were longer?

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth becomes king of Alba
timeline.detail: He ruled for seventeen years, a reign Shakespeare compresses to a few violent months.

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth is killed at Lumphanan
timeline.detail: Not at Dunsinane, and not by Macduff.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's chief source for the Scottish material, including the meeting with the three weird sisters.

timeline.label: James VI publishes Daemonologie
timeline.detail: The future king of England writes a dialogue on witchcraft six years before inheriting the English throne.

timeline.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England
timeline.detail: A Scottish king in London, claiming descent from Banquo, changes what a Scottish play on a London stage can mean.

timeline.label: The Gunpowder Plot
timeline.detail: The conspiracy and its trials put the word equivocation into everyday London use.

timeline.label: Macbeth most likely written and first performed
timeline.detail: The Porter's equivocator is the strongest internal evidence for the date.

timeline.label: Simon Forman records seeing Macbeth at the Globe
timeline.detail: The earliest surviving eyewitness account of the play in performance.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early printed text of the play, and a short one.

timeline.label: Verdi's Macbeth premieres in Florence
timeline.detail: Revised for Paris in 1865, it becomes a performance tradition of its own.

timeline.label: Orson Welles directs the Federal Theatre Project's Black-cast Macbeth
timeline.detail: Staged at the Lafayette Theatre in Harlem and relocated to a Caribbean island.

places.name: Inverness
places.note: Macbeth's castle, where Duncan is murdered while a guest.

places.name: Forres
places.note: Duncan's court, where Macbeth is thanked and Malcolm is named heir.

places.name: Dunsinane Hill
places.note: Macbeth's fortress in the last act, and the hill Birnam wood must reach.

places.name: Birnam
places.note: The wood the soldiers cut for cover, about twelve miles from Dunsinane.

places.name: Fife
places.note: Macduff's household, murdered in 4.2.

places.name: Iona
places.note: Colmekill, where Duncan's body is carried for burial among his ancestors.

related.why: The other tragedy built almost entirely out of soliloquy, and the opposite case: a man who cannot act.
Written within a year or two, and equally interested in a kingdom that comes apart at the top.
An earlier study of a usurper who enjoys the audience's company, where Macbeth cannot bear it.
Political murder argued out in advance, and the same discovery that killing a ruler does not settle anything.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller textual, critical and performance material.

books.title: Much Ado About Nothing
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Messina, in and around Leonato's house, over about a week
books.lengthNote: Around 2,500 lines, the greater part of them in prose
books.openingLine: I learn in this letter that Don Peter of Arragon comes this night to Messina.
books.summary: Two couples are made by the same method. Beatrice and Benedick are talked into love by friends who arrange for them to overhear flattering lies; Claudio is talked out of it by a stranger at a window. The play's comedy and its near-catastrophe run on identical machinery, and it takes a pair of incompetent constables to notice the difference.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Much Ado About Nothing
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts the prose scenes continuously. Modern editions vary.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Soldiers arrive and two people start arguing
structure.summary: Don Pedro's company returns from a war that cost almost nothing, and the house fills with young men with time on their hands. Claudio decides within minutes that he loves Hero; Beatrice and Benedick resume a quarrel that predates the play; and Don John, newly and unconvincingly reconciled to his brother, announces that he would rather be disliked than pretend.

scenes.title: The messenger
scenes.summary: Beatrice asks after Benedick before he arrives; Claudio asks Don Pedro to court Hero for him.

scenes.title: Half a rumour
scenes.summary: Antonio brings Leonato a garbled report that the prince loves Hero himself.

scenes.title: Plain-dealing villain
scenes.summary: Don John states his character outright and begins looking for something to spoil.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A masked dance and a plan to make two people fall in love
structure.summary: At the masked ball the wooing is done by proxy and briefly believed to be a betrayal. Once that is cleared up, Don Pedro proposes the only labour of Hercules he thinks worth attempting: getting Beatrice and Benedick to admit they like each other. The gulling of Benedick, staged in an orchard, works within a dozen lines.

scenes.title: The masque
scenes.summary: Beatrice abuses Benedick to his masked face; Claudio believes briefly that Don Pedro has taken Hero for himself.

scenes.title: Borachio's offer
scenes.summary: Don John is told how a window, a borrowed name and a willing servant can undo the match.

scenes.title: Benedick in the arbour
scenes.summary: A song, then three men loudly discussing Beatrice's hopeless love, and a bachelor converted.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The second trap, and the one that is not a joke
structure.summary: Hero and Ursula perform the same trick on Beatrice, and it works even faster because it accuses her of pride rather than of weakness. Meanwhile Don John shows Claudio a scene at a window, and the watch — half asleep and entirely illiterate in the ways of their betters — arrest the two men who staged it.

scenes.title: Beatrice in the garden
scenes.summary: She overhears herself described as too scornful to be loved, and surrenders in rhyme.

scenes.title: A changed Benedick
scenes.summary: His friends mock his shaved beard and perfume; Don John invites Claudio to see proof.

scenes.title: The watch
scenes.summary: Dogberry instructs his men to avoid trouble, and they arrest Borachio bragging about the deception.

scenes.title: Dressing
scenes.summary: Hero's women joke about husbands and heaviness on the morning of the wedding.

scenes.title: Too late
scenes.summary: Dogberry tries to tell Leonato what his watch has found and is sent away to hold the examination himself.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A wedding turned into an accusation
structure.summary: Claudio waits until the ceremony to denounce Hero, which is not an outburst but a plan. She faints, her father believes the accusers, and a friar proposes to report her dead. Left alone in the empty church, Beatrice and Benedick admit they love each other, and she immediately asks him to kill his best friend.

scenes.title: The church
scenes.summary: The public shaming, the swoon, the Friar's plan, and 'Kill Claudio'.

scenes.title: The examination
scenes.summary: Dogberry conducts an inquiry he cannot follow and gets the confession anyway.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Grief, confession and a second wedding
structure.summary: Leonato challenges the men who broke his daughter, and is laughed at for being old. The truth arrives not through the gentlemen's investigation but through the constables' paperwork. Claudio mourns at a tomb, agrees to marry a cousin sight unseen, and is given Hero back.

scenes.title: Old men and swords
scenes.summary: Leonato and Antonio challenge Claudio and Don Pedro; Benedick does the same in earnest; Borachio confesses.

scenes.title: Bad verses
scenes.summary: Benedick tries to write a love poem, fails, and learns Hero is cleared.

scenes.title: The monument
scenes.summary: Claudio reads an epitaph and hangs a scroll on a tomb that contains nobody.

scenes.title: The masked brides
scenes.summary: Hero unmasks, the lovers are caught out by their own handwriting, and Don John is reported taken.

characters.name: Beatrice
characters.summary: She has the fastest tongue in Shakespearean comedy and uses it, by her own admission, as armour: the play hints at an earlier hurt from Benedick that she will not describe. Her anger after the wedding is the point at which the comedy nearly stops being one.
characters.clue: She would rather hear her dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves her, and her first request of the man she finally admits loving is that he kill his friend.

characters.name: Benedick
characters.role: A lord of Padua, of Don Pedro's company
characters.summary: His anti-marriage act is loud enough to be a performance, and the gulling scene works by letting him surrender without losing face. He is the only man in the play who takes Beatrice's account of the wedding seriously, and he changes sides for her at real cost.
characters.clue: He swears he will die a bachelor, is talked out of it by three friends shouting in a garden, and ends up challenging his commander's favourite.

characters.name: Hero
characters.summary: She speaks little in the first half and is discussed constantly, which is precisely what makes her vulnerable: her reputation exists entirely in other people's mouths. In 3.1 she runs the trick that catches Beatrice, so the play does show her capable of managing a scene when she is given one.
characters.clue: Her value is agreed by everyone before she has said fifty words, and it is destroyed in public by a man who never asks her a question.

relationships.label: betrothed to, denounced by, married to

characters.name: Claudio
characters.summary: He falls in love by report, asks another man to do his courting, and believes an accusation on the evidence of a window at night. His cruelty at the wedding is not hot temper but a rehearsed public performance, and the play makes him accept a wife sight unseen before it forgives him.
characters.clue: He never speaks to the woman he loves without an intermediary, and he saves his accusation until the altar so that everybody can hear it.
traits: conventional to the point of cruelty

characters.name: Don Pedro
characters.summary: He arranges everything: Claudio's marriage, the gulling of two friends, and, without meaning to, the conditions in which a lie about Hero can be believed. He ends the play with no partner and one line of consolation offered to him, which several productions have made the quietest moment in the last scene.
characters.clue: He courts one woman on another man's behalf, invents the plot that marries two enemies, and is left standing alone at the end of it.

characters.name: Don John
characters.summary: He announces that he is a villain in his third scene and offers no reason beyond his position, which is the interesting thing about him: a defeated bastard brother in a household where legitimacy is everything. He needs to invent almost nothing, because the men around him are ready to believe it.
characters.clue: He calls himself a plain-dealing villain and says he is trusted with a muzzle; his whole plot amounts to arranging for two people to be seen at a window.

characters.name: Leonato
characters.summary: Hospitable, pleased with his household, and the first person in the church to believe the accusation against his own daughter. His grief in 5.1 produces the best serious verse in the play, and it is directed at the men who wronged her only after a friar has told him she is innocent.
characters.clue: He welcomes a prince, gives away a daughter, and at the altar wishes aloud that somebody would lend him a dagger.

characters.name: Dogberry
characters.summary: He reverses almost every word he uses and is right about almost every fact. The play's crime is solved by men the gentry cannot be bothered to listen to, and the running joke about being written down an ass carries a real grievance about who is believed.
characters.clue: He instructs his watchmen to let thieves go rather than risk a scuffle, and then demands to be recorded, in writing, as an ass.

relationships.label: tries and fails to report to

characters.name: Margaret
characters.summary: She stands at the window in her mistress's clothes and is the physical cause of the catastrophe, and the play excuses her in a line and a half without asking what she thought she was doing. Her bawdy jokes on the wedding morning are the last cheerful thing said before the church scene.
characters.clue: She wears her mistress's gown at a window one night, and the play forgives her in half a sentence without ever letting her explain.

themes.name: Noting, overhearing and evidence
themes.summary: Nobody in this play learns anything by being told it directly. Information arrives by eavesdropping, by report, by a scene arranged for a particular watcher, and the play's title puns on the word for it. Both love plots and the slander plot use exactly the same device, which is the argument the comedy is making.
themes.development: Two staged overhearings in Act II and Act III produce a marriage; a third staged sight in Act III nearly produces a death.

themes.name: Reputation and public honour
themes.summary: Hero's worth is established by other people's praise and destroyed by other people's testimony; she is never asked to give an account of herself until it is too late to matter. Messina is a small enough world for a name to be the whole of a person's estate.
themes.development: The accusation is deliberately staged at the altar, and the repair is staged there too — the second wedding is as public as the first because the damage was.

themes.name: Wit as defence
themes.summary: Beatrice and Benedick talk brilliantly in order not to be caught out, and the friends who trick them understand this exactly: both are given permission to love by being told they are already loved. Wit in this play is protective clothing, and the plot works by removing it.
themes.development: Their prose skirmishing in 1.1 becomes rhymed resolve in 3.1, awkward confession in 4.1, and a scrap of bad poetry produced as evidence in 5.4.

themes.name: Men, women and what manhood licenses
themes.summary: Beatrice's fury in the church is that manhood has been melted into courtesy: the men have the swords and the credit, and they use both to destroy a girl. 'Kill Claudio' asks whether a man's loyalty to another man can be outweighed by his loyalty to the truth.
themes.development: Benedick's answer is not immediate — he refuses first, then agrees, and the challenge he eventually delivers is spoken quietly and in prose.

themes.name: Benign and malicious deception
themes.summary: The play refuses a clean line between a kind lie and a cruel one. Don Pedro's trick is a gift and Don John's is an attack, but both rely on the target's existing self-image, and both work because being watched makes people believe what they are shown.
themes.development: The Friar's plan in 4.1 is a third kind: a false report used to undo the effect of another false report.

themes.name: Repair, and what it cannot mend
themes.summary: The comedy ends with the right people married and the villain caught, but Shakespeare does not pretend the wedding scene never happened. Claudio is given a penance rather than an argument, and Hero's first words to him afterwards correct him about who she is.
themes.development: The tomb scene, the second veiled bride and Benedick's call for a dance are three separate attempts to close the play, and the last one has to talk over Don John's arrest.

techniques.name: Prose as the main medium
techniques.definition: Unmetered speech carrying the substance of a play rather than its low comedy.
techniques.inThisBook: Most of the play is prose, and the lovers' most important exchanges are in it; verse arrives for ceremony, grief and the moment Beatrice surrenders in rhyme at the end of 3.1.

techniques.name: The staged eavesdrop
techniques.definition: A scene performed by characters who know they are being overheard, for a listener who thinks he is not seen.
techniques.inThisBook: Shakespeare builds the same scene twice, once for each lover, and gives the audience the pleasure of watching a performance and its dupe at the same time.

techniques.name: Malapropism
techniques.definition: Using a word that sounds like the intended one and means something else, usually the opposite.
techniques.inThisBook: Dogberry's comparisons are odorous and his suspects are full of piety; the joke works because the errors keep accidentally telling the truth about Messina.

techniques.name: The nothing/noting pun
techniques.definition: A double meaning carried by two words that sounded almost identical in early modern English.
techniques.inThisBook: The title names both the fuss over a non-event and the play's real mechanism, observation; the same pun runs through Balthasar's scene about musical notes in 2.3.

techniques.name: The crime kept offstage
techniques.definition: Withholding the decisive action from the audience and showing only its report.
techniques.inThisBook: The window scene that ruins Hero is never staged; the audience hears it planned and hears it described, which places them alongside the watch rather than alongside Claudio.

techniques.name: Song as commentary
techniques.definition: A lyric that states the play's theme from outside the action.
techniques.inThisBook: Balthasar's 'Sigh no more, ladies' advises women to expect men to be deceivers, and it is sung to distract Benedick immediately before he is deceived.

quotations.text: There is a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick and her: they never meet but there's a skirmish of wit between them.
quotations.speaker: Leonato
quotations.context: Explaining Beatrice to the messenger, who has just heard her insult a man she claims not to care about.
quotations.analysis: The phrase frames the relationship as a spectacle the household enjoys, which is exactly why the two of them cannot drop it: an audience is watching. Note that it is the uncle who supplies the label, before either of them is on stage together — their love is a matter of public commentary before it is a matter of feeling.

quotations.text: What, my dear Lady Disdain! are you yet living?
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: His first words to Beatrice in the play, after she has interrupted him.
quotations.analysis: He greets her with an allegorical title, as though she were a figure in a morality play rather than a person, and she takes the personification off him in her reply and feeds it. Neither of them uses the other's name in this whole exchange, which is the shape of the defence they have both agreed to.

quotations.text: I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Agreeing, competitively, with Benedick's claim that he loves no woman.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is precise: both are noise made by a creature that does not mean anything by it. She says this in front of her uncle and a room of guests, which makes it a position she will have to be seen to abandon — and the friends who trick her know it.

quotations.text: Can the world buy such a jewel?
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Asking Benedick what he thinks of Hero, minutes after arriving in Messina.
quotations.analysis: Benedick has just asked whether he means to buy her, and Claudio's answer accepts the vocabulary without noticing it. He values Hero as a possession whose worth is set by general agreement, which is why a general agreement that she is worthless can destroy her in one scene.

quotations.text: it must not be denied but I am a plain-dealing villain. I am trusted with a muzzle and enfranchised with a clog;
quotations.speaker: Don John
quotations.context: To Conrade, who has advised him to look more cheerful now that he is reconciled to his brother.
quotations.analysis: He claims the one virtue available to him — not pretending — and describes his pardon as a muzzle and a chained block. The imagery is of a dangerous animal on a lead, and it is his own; the play gives him no motive beyond the position his birth has left him in.

quotations.text: Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more, Men were deceivers ever, One foot in sea and one on shore, To one thing constant never:
quotations.speaker: Balthasar
quotations.context: The song sung in Leonato's orchard while Benedick hides in the arbour.
quotations.analysis: The song tells women to stop grieving over men who are unreliable by nature, and it is performed as cover for three men about to tell an elaborate lie. Its advice is also the play's plot in advance: Claudio will be exactly the deceiver described, and the ladies will be told to let him go.

quotations.text: No, the world must be peopled. When I said I would die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I were married.
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Alone in the orchard, immediately after the gulling.
quotations.analysis: He reverses a public vow in two sentences and gives a reason of cosmic scale for a decision of purely private appetite. The joke in the second sentence is a genuine piece of self-knowledge dressed as a quibble: he did not expect to live long enough to be caught out, and he has been.

quotations.text: Contempt, farewell! and maiden pride, adieu! No glory lives behind the back of such. And, Benedick, love on; I will requite thee, Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand:
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Coming forward after overhearing Hero and Ursula discuss her pride.
quotations.analysis: She surrenders in rhymed verse, the only time she speaks it, and the metrical shift does the work a soliloquy would do elsewhere. The falconry image — a wild bird taken to the hand — is one she chooses herself, and it concedes rather more than the trick actually asked for.

quotations.text: Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.
quotations.speaker: Hero
quotations.context: The closing line of the scene in which she and Ursula trap Beatrice.
quotations.analysis: Hero, who is usually spoken about rather than speaking, gets the couplet that names the play's method. A trap is not an arrow: it requires planning, bait and a victim who walks in, and every match in Messina is made that way, including the one that goes wrong.

quotations.text: Comparisons are odorous: palabras, neighbour Verges.
quotations.speaker: Dogberry
quotations.context: Trying to tell Leonato what his watch has arrested, on the morning of the wedding.
quotations.analysis: He means odious, and the mistake is funnier than the word he wanted; but the scene is also the play's most painful piece of timing, because Leonato is in a hurry and sends him away. The catastrophe of Act IV is entirely preventable, and it is prevented by nobody because of who is speaking.

quotations.text: O, what men dare do! what men may do! what men daily
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: In the church, beginning the accusation, having so far refused to say the word 'marry'.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation is about men, not about Hero, and it is the nearest the scene comes to self-knowledge: what men dare do is precisely what Claudio is about to do to a girl in front of her father. The line breaks off mid-sentence, and the completed thought never arrives.

quotations.text: Give not this rotten orange to your friend; She's but the sign and semblance of her honour.
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Handing Hero back to Leonato at the altar.
quotations.analysis: The image is of fruit that looks sound and is spoiled inside, and it turns a person into damaged goods being returned to a supplier. 'Sign and semblance' is the play's own subject stated by its worst reader of signs: Claudio has believed a semblance, and he is accusing her of being one.

quotations.text: But fare thee well, most foul, most fair! farewell, Thou pure impiety and impious purity!
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: His last words to Hero before she faints.
quotations.analysis: Two lines of perfectly balanced antithesis produced by a man in what he presents as uncontrollable grief — the rhetoric is far too neat for the emotion it claims. Shakespeare gives him the figure twice over, with the nouns and adjectives swapped in the second half, so that the speech sounds composed in advance, because it was.

quotations.text: I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is not that strange?
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Alone with Beatrice in the empty church after Hero has been carried out.
quotations.analysis: The declaration arrives in the wreckage of somebody else's wedding, and he ends it with a question because he cannot say it without a shrug. 'Nothing' is the title word, and here it is doing honest work for once: he loves nothing so well, in a play where nothing has been the cause of all the trouble.

quotations.text: Kill Claudio.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Her answer when Benedick tells her to bid him do anything for her.
quotations.analysis: Two words, immediately after a page of elaborate prose, and the shortest speech either of them makes in the play. It is the point where the comedy's machinery — a lover offering extravagant service — is taken literally, and the audience's laughter, which almost always comes, is part of what the scene is testing.

quotations.text: O God, that I were a man! I would eat his heart in the market-place.
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Explaining to Benedick why Claudio is her enemy.
quotations.analysis: She says it three times in twenty lines, which is a measure of how completely her wit has failed her. 'In the market-place' is the detail that matters: Hero was destroyed in public, so the revenge Beatrice imagines is public too, and it has to be carried out by a man because the law and the sword both belong to men.

quotations.text: But manhood is melted into courtesies, valour into compliment, and men are only turned into tongue, and trim ones too
quotations.speaker: Beatrice
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, on the men of Messina.
quotations.analysis: It is a complaint about talk from the play's best talker, and it convicts her own weapon: wit is what the men have instead of action. The verbs are all of liquefaction and exchange — melted, turned — as though a substance had been swapped for a currency.

quotations.text: O that he were here to write me down an ass! But, masters, remember that I am an ass; though it be not written down, yet forget not that I am an ass.
quotations.speaker: Dogberry
quotations.context: In the prison, having been called an ass by Conrade during the examination.
quotations.analysis: His grievance is that the insult has not been entered in the record, and the joke is that he insists on the record being complete even when it damns him. Messina has just ruined a girl on unwritten testimony; the constable is the only person in the play who believes that what is said should be written down.

quotations.text: For there was never yet philosopher That could endure the toothache patiently,
quotations.speaker: Leonato
quotations.context: Refusing his brother's advice to bear his daughter's disgrace calmly.
quotations.analysis: He answers moral consolation with dentistry, and the deflation is the point: the men who counsel patience have not been in the chair. It is the best serious writing in the play and it is given to the man who, one scene earlier, wished his daughter dead rather than shamed.

quotations.text: Done to death by slanderous tongues Was the Hero that here lies:
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Reading the epitaph at Leonato's monument, believing Hero dead.
quotations.analysis: The penance is a poem, hung on a tomb containing nobody, read by the man whose tongue did most of the slandering — and the epitaph does not name him. Shakespeare gives the scene formal rhymed stanzas and a ritual, which is either the repair Messina needs or an exact measure of how cheap its rituals are.

quotations.text: for man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion.
quotations.speaker: Benedick
quotations.context: Explaining why nobody should mock him for marrying after swearing he never would.
quotations.analysis: He does not defend the reversal; he generalises it into a fact about the species and calls that a conclusion. It is the play's answer to its own machinery — people are talked into things, and the sensible response is to marry, dance, and not examine it too closely.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Placed by its style and by the company's records at the end of the 1590s.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The First Quarto, printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise and William Aspley.

atAGlance.label: Source tradition
atAGlance.note: The Hero plot belongs to a European story family found in Ariosto and in Bandello; Beatrice and Benedick are Shakespeare's own.

atAGlance.label: Title
atAGlance.note: The two words sounded close in early modern English, and almost every turn of the plot depends on somebody noting — watching, overhearing or reporting.

criticalViews.position: The play belongs to Beatrice and Benedick
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the inherited slandered-bride plot is the frame and the invented couple are the picture: the comedy's real subject is two intelligent people arguing themselves out of a defence.
criticalViews.counter: It leaves Act IV hard to account for, since the church scene is the longest and most serious writing in the play and Hero is at the centre of it.

criticalViews.position: A comedy about evidence
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long noticed that nothing here is learned first-hand. The same technique — a scene staged for a watcher — makes one marriage and nearly destroys another, which turns the play into an argument about how societies decide what is true.
criticalViews.counter: The resolution comes from a confession rather than from anybody reasoning better, so the play may be less confident about evidence than the reading suggests.

criticalViews.position: A play about what men are permitted to do
criticalViews.summary: Recent stage practice and criticism have concentrated on Claudio's public shaming of Hero, Leonato's readiness to believe it, and Beatrice's fury that revenge is a man's office. The comedy is then held open rather than closed by the second wedding.
criticalViews.counter: Hero herself is given no scene in which to judge Claudio, which makes it difficult to say what the play thinks the right ending would be.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use deception in Much Ado About Nothing?
essayQuestions.focus: Overhearing, evidence and the two plots
plan: Establish the pattern: nobody in this play learns anything except by watching or being told.
Compare the two gulling scenes, 2.3 and 3.1, and note that each accuses its target of the fault they most fear.
Set Don John's window scene against them, and observe that Shakespeare never stages it.
Add the Friar's false report of Hero's death as a third kind of lie, used as medicine.
Conclude on the watch: the truth arrives from the people nobody bothered to listen to in 3.5.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Beatrice.
essayQuestions.focus: Wit, anger and the limits of comedy
plan: Begin with 1.1, where she asks after Benedick before admitting she has any interest in him.
Read her wit as defence rather than temperament, using her hint at an earlier hurt.
Use the rhymed verse of 3.1.113 to show how completely the trick works, and how much she concedes in the image of the tamed bird.
Turn to 4.1: the repeated wish to be a man, and the demand that Benedick act because she cannot.
Close by asking whether the last scene's discovered sonnet restores the comedy or simply puts the armour back on.

essayQuestions.question: Is Claudio forgivable?
essayQuestions.focus: Reputation, repentance and the second wedding
plan: Note how he falls in love: by report, through a proxy, with a woman he has spoken to scarcely at all.
Show that the denunciation at 4.1.29 is staged rather than impulsive — he waits for the altar and an audience.
Weigh the mourning of 5.3 against the fact that he agrees to marry an unseen cousin the next morning.
Consider what the play withholds: Hero never accuses him, and no character demands that he explain himself.
Decide whether the comedy asks for forgiveness, or simply moves on and lets the audience decide.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Dogberry and the watch?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, language and who gets believed
plan: Set out the joke first: a constable who reverses his words and instructs his men to avoid arresting anyone.
Show that the watch nevertheless overhear the confession that solves the plot, in 3.3.
Make 3.5 the centre of the argument — Leonato is in a hurry and will not listen, and the wedding proceeds.
Read the 'write me down an ass' joke as a grievance about record and testimony as well as a gag.
Conclude on the reversal: the gentlemen read signs badly and the fools take statements accurately.

discussionQuestions: Both love plots are begun by a lie. Does the play think that matters?
Shakespeare never shows the scene at Hero's window. What does the play gain by keeping it offstage?
'Kill Claudio' usually gets a laugh. Should it?
Leonato believes the accusation against his own daughter before anyone else does. Is he forgiven too easily?
Don Pedro ends the play without a partner. What should a production do with him in the final dance?

timeline.label: Ariosto's Orlando Furioso first published
timeline.detail: Its story of Ginevra, falsely accused after a maid is seen at her window in her mistress's clothes, is the closest analogue to the Hero plot.

timeline.label: Bandello's Novelle
timeline.detail: Another version of the slandered bride, set in Messina, which brings the story to the city Shakespeare uses.

timeline.label: Sir John Harington translates Orlando Furioso
timeline.detail: The English verse translation makes the Ginevra episode available to readers and playwrights in London.

timeline.label: The play is most likely written
timeline.detail: Composition is usually placed in 1598 or 1599, at the end of the decade of comedies.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise and William Aspley; its title page links the play to the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

timeline.label: Performed at court
timeline.detail: Recorded among the plays given during the celebrations for the marriage of Princess Elizabeth.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, with some of the quarto's confusing speech prefixes regularised.

timeline.label: Peggy Ashcroft and John Gielgud at Stratford
timeline.detail: The pairing that began the modern tradition of the play as a vehicle for two major actors.

timeline.label: Judi Dench and Donald Sinden for the RSC
timeline.detail: One of the best remembered of the company's many Beatrice and Benedick pairings.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh's film
timeline.detail: Shot at the Villa Vignamaggio in Tuscany, with Emma Thompson as Beatrice; one of the most commercially successful Shakespeare films.

timeline.label: Iqbal Khan sets the play in contemporary Delhi
timeline.detail: An RSC production with Meera Syal as Beatrice, staged as part of the World Shakespeare Festival.

timeline.label: Kenny Leon's Public Theater production is filmed
timeline.detail: An all-Black cast in a contemporary American political setting, recorded for broadcast.

places.name: Messina
places.note: The whole play: Leonato's house, its orchard and garden, a church and a prison.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Benedick's city, named in the first scene along with the reputation that precedes him.

places.name: Florence
places.note: Claudio's city; the first scene introduces him as a young Florentine who has fought beyond the promise of his age.

places.name: Zaragoza
places.note: Chief city of Aragon, the kingdom Don Pedro is prince of and the source of the company's rank.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the 1600 quarto was printed and where the Lord Chamberlain's Men first played it.

related.why: The next of the great comedies, and the other one in which a joke played on a self-important man goes too far to be laughed off.
Written within a year or two, and the closest comparison for two people talking themselves into love in prose.
The same accusation of a faithful woman, taken seriously enough to kill a child and to need sixteen years to mend.
The slandered-wife plot again, with the malicious deceiver given a full part and no comic constables to stop him.
Shakespeare's other comedy of people made to love on someone else's instruction, with the trickery done by magic instead of gossip.

books.title: Pride and Prejudice
books.author: Jane Austen
books.setting: Hertfordshire, Kent, London and Derbyshire, in the years of the militia camps
books.lengthNote: Sixty-one chapters, first issued in three volumes
books.openingLine: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
books.summary: A family of five daughters, an estate entailed away from all of them, and a neighbourhood that treats every new arrival as an opportunity. Elizabeth Bennet is the best reader of character in the book and gets the two most important readings wrong, and Austen builds the plot so that correcting them costs her something. The comedy never lets go of the arithmetic underneath it: who has money, who will inherit, and who can afford to refuse.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Pride and Prejudice
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously from 1 to 61, as in the Standard Ebooks text; first editions divide the same chapters across three volumes.

structure.label: Chapters 1–12
structure.title: Netherfield taken, and everybody measured
structure.summary: A single man with four or five thousand a year moves into the neighbourhood and the Bennets begin calculating. The Meryton assembly fixes Darcy's reputation in one overheard sentence, and Jane's convenient illness keeps Elizabeth at Netherfield long enough for the two of them to start sparring in earnest.

structure.label: Chapters 13–23
structure.title: The heir, the officer and the practical marriage
structure.summary: Mr Collins arrives to inspect the estate he will inherit and the cousin he intends to marry; Wickham arrives with a grievance that flatters Elizabeth's judgement. Within three days Collins is refused, Charlotte Lucas accepts him, and the Bingleys leave for London taking Jane's prospects with them.

structure.label: Chapters 24–34
structure.title: Hunsford, Rosings and a proposal nobody wanted
structure.summary: Elizabeth visits Charlotte's parsonage and sees what a comfortable home actually costs. Lady Catherine presides, Colonel Fitzwilliam lets slip that Darcy separated Bingley from Jane, and Darcy proposes in terms that make refusing him easy and enjoyable.

structure.label: Chapters 35–42
structure.title: The letter, and a second reading
structure.summary: Darcy hands over a letter and walks away, and the novel changes direction without a single event taking place. Elizabeth reads it twice, reconstructs Wickham from the beginning, and arrives at the only self-accusation in the book that is not comic.

structure.label: Chapters 43–50
structure.title: Pemberley, and the news from Brighton
structure.summary: A house, a housekeeper and a set of grounds supply the evidence about Darcy that conversation could not. Then Lydia runs off with Wickham, and the family's standing, which has been a joke for forty chapters, becomes something that can actually be destroyed.

structure.label: Chapters 51–61
structure.title: What the settlement cost, and who paid it
structure.summary: Lydia returns married and unembarrassed, and the reader learns before Elizabeth does who bought the marriage. Lady Catherine's attempt to extract a promise produces the opposite of the one she wants, and the last chapters distribute incomes as carefully as affections.

characters.name: Elizabeth Bennet
characters.role: Second of the five Bennet daughters
characters.summary: Quick, funny and justly confident in her own judgement, which is exactly why the novel arranges for her to be wrong about the two men she is most certain of. Her wit is a form of courage in a household where nobody else will say anything true.
characters.clue: She refuses two proposals, walks three miles through mud to nurse her sister, and only discovers her own vanity by reading a letter twice.

relationships.label: closest friend, and a test of her principles

characters.name: Fitzwilliam Darcy
characters.summary: Ten thousand a year and no talent for a room full of strangers. Austen gives him the novel's worst opening sentence and then spends fifty chapters showing that his conduct has always been better than his manner, which is not quite the same as saying he was right.
characters.clue: He insults a woman within her hearing at a country dance, proposes to her against his own better judgement, and later pays a blackguard to marry her sister without telling anyone.

characters.name: Jane Bennet
characters.summary: Her determination to think well of everybody is presented as a moral achievement and a practical disaster: it makes her unreadable to Bingley, unreadable to Darcy, and defenceless against Caroline Bingley. The novel likes her and does not recommend her method.
characters.clue: She catches cold riding to dinner in the rain because her mother wanted her to stay the night, and forgives everyone involved.

characters.name: Charles Bingley
characters.summary: Amiable, rich and so willing to be guided that his friend can detach him from the woman he loves with a few words about her family. He is the novel's evidence that good nature without judgement is a kind of weakness.
characters.clue: He takes a house for the shooting, falls in love at the first assembly, and is talked out of it by a friend and a sister in a single winter.

characters.name: George Wickham
characters.summary: He tells Elizabeth a story about Darcy within an hour of meeting her, and she believes it because it is well told and because she wants to. His charm is a working method rather than a temperament, and the militia's presence in Meryton is what gives it a market.
characters.clue: The steward's son who was left a living in a will, sold it for ready money, and then complained for the rest of the book that he had been robbed of it.

relationships.label: elopes with, and is paid to marry
slanders and is bought off by

characters.name: Mr Collins
characters.role: Clergyman of Hunsford, heir to Longbourn
characters.summary: He proposes to two women in three days and is not embarrassed by either outcome, because the proposal was never about a person. Everything he says is addressed upwards to his patroness, even when he is standing in somebody else's parlour insulting their daughter.
characters.clue: He offers his hand as a favour to the family he will dispossess, and numbers his reasons for marrying like items in a sermon.

characters.name: Charlotte Lucas
characters.summary: Twenty-seven, without fortune, and the only character who states the terms of the marriage market out loud without either joking or complaining. Her parsonage is arranged so that she sees as little of her husband as the house allows, which is the closest the novel comes to a verdict on the bargain.
characters.clue: She accepts in three days the man her closest friend refused, and explains that she asks only a comfortable home.

characters.name: Lydia Bennet
characters.summary: Fifteen, unsupervised and encouraged, she does exactly what her upbringing has trained her to do, and the novel is careful to spread the blame across her mother's indulgence and her father's amused neglect. Her elopement is the one plot event that could not be undone by an explanation.
characters.clue: She is delighted to be married before her elder sisters and cannot understand why the family is not delighted too.

characters.name: Mr Bennet
characters.summary: He retreats to his library and treats his family as a source of entertainment, and the novel charges him for it: the daughter he never bothered to check runs away, and his best line about making sport for our neighbours is spoken just before he finds out what that costs.
characters.clue: He tells his least favourite daughter that one parent will refuse to see her again whichever way she answers a proposal.

characters.name: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
characters.summary: She gives orders about other people's carriages, shelves and marriages with the same confidence, and is the only character who states the class objection to the match in plain words. Her one decisive action in the plot is the one that brings the marriage about.
characters.clue: She drives to a small Hertfordshire village to demand a promise, and is told that she has no right to ask for one.

characters.name: Mrs Bennet
characters.summary: Ridiculous and not wrong. Her single subject is getting five daughters married before her husband dies, and the entail means that the alternative is genuine poverty, so the novel laughs at her method rather than her motive.
characters.clue: Her nerves are her oldest companions, and she can turn a wet evening into an engagement if the house is far enough from home.

themes.name: First impressions and judgement
themes.summary: The discarded title is still the working one. Almost every character forms a verdict in a single evening and then spends the book defending it, and Austen makes the reader do the same thing so that the correction lands on both at once.
themes.development: Fixed at the Meryton assembly, hardened by Wickham's story, dismantled by a letter in Chapter 35, and formally re-examined at Pemberley.

themes.name: Marriage and money
themes.summary: Every attachment in the novel is quoted with a figure attached, from Bingley's four or five thousand a year to the hundred pounds that settles Lydia. Austen does not treat this as vulgar; she treats it as the arithmetic within which affection has to operate.
themes.development: Stated as a joke in the first sentence, argued seriously by Charlotte in Chapter 22, and paid in cash by Darcy in the last volume.

themes.name: Rank and connection
themes.summary: The obstacle between Elizabeth and Darcy is not money on her side but relations on hers: an uncle in trade, an aunt in Cheapside, a mother who cannot be taken anywhere. The novel dismantles the objection by making the Gardiners the most sensible adults in it.
themes.development: Voiced by Caroline Bingley, formalised by Darcy's first proposal, and shouted by Lady Catherine in the last volume after it has stopped being true for anyone the reader trusts.

themes.name: Entail and female security
themes.summary: Longbourn passes to Mr Collins, so five daughters must find husbands or find lodgings. The legal fact sits under every comic scene, and it is why Charlotte's calculation is a calculation rather than a failure of feeling.
themes.development: Explained early and never forgotten: it makes Mrs Bennet's campaign rational, Collins's proposal a favour in his own eyes, and Lydia's ruin a threat to four other women.

themes.name: Reputation and family conduct
themes.summary: Character in this novel is public property. A sister's elopement is treated as a defect in every other sister, and Mary's moralising about a woman's irretrievable ruin is contemptible and, within the world of the book, accurate about the consequences.
themes.development: From the embarrassment of the Netherfield ball, through Darcy's letter about Jane's family, to the Brighton crisis where reputation becomes something that must be bought back.

themes.name: Self-knowledge
themes.summary: Both leading characters have to revise not an opinion but a habit of mind. Elizabeth discovers that she was flattered into belief; Darcy discovers that being brought up on good principles is not the same as being taught to apply them.
themes.development: Elizabeth's reckoning comes in Chapter 36, Darcy's is reported in Chapter 58, and the novel makes the two confessions echo each other's grammar.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Narration that takes on a character's vocabulary and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrative sits so close to Elizabeth that her errors arrive as facts; the reader distrusts Darcy on her evidence and has to re-read the first half after the letter.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: The famous first sentence states a truth nobody in the book holds and everybody acts on: it is the mothers, not the single men, who are in want of anything.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: Written documents inserted into a narrative as evidence and as plot.
techniques.inThisBook: Darcy's letter is the structural hinge, and Austen distinguishes her characters by their prose: Collins pompous, Jane over-careful, Lydia unpunctuated and untroubled.

techniques.name: Dialogue as exposure
techniques.definition: Letting characters convict themselves in their own speech rather than describing their faults.
techniques.inThisBook: Mr Collins numbers his reasons for marrying and Lady Catherine interrogates a stranger about her sisters' accomplishments; neither needs a word of narrative comment.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A generalisation compressed into a single balanced sentence.
techniques.inThisBook: Characters reach for maxims when they are least reliable — Mary on vanity and pride, Charlotte on happiness in marriage, Mary again on a woman's ruin.

techniques.name: Parallel courtships
techniques.definition: Running several versions of the same situation so that each comments on the others.
techniques.inThisBook: Five marriages are set side by side — Jane's, Charlotte's, Lydia's, Elizabeth's and the Bennets' own — so that the reader can see what each one was bought with.

quotations.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The sentence claims to report a consensus and names nobody who holds it; the passive construction hides the mothers who are the actual subject. Read strictly it is also false in the book that follows, where the single men are in want of nothing and the women are in want of an income.

quotations.text: You mistake me, my dear. I have a high respect for your nerves. They are my old friends. I have heard you mention them with consideration these twenty years at least.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Answering his wife's complaint that he has no compassion on her nerves.
quotations.analysis: The joke depends on treating an ailment as an acquaintance, and it establishes the marriage in a line: he has been amusing himself at her expense for two decades and has changed nothing. Twenty years is also the age of the eldest daughter, which quietly dates the arrangement.

quotations.text: She is tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At the Meryton assembly, refusing Bingley's suggestion that he dance with Elizabeth, who is sitting close enough to hear.
quotations.analysis: Eight words decide the first half of the book. The grammar is the insult: she is graded, then found insufficient for a purpose, with no verb that admits she is a person in the room. Elizabeth's response is to repeat it as a comic story, which is how a wound is kept fresh.

quotations.text: I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Discussing Darcy's behaviour at the assembly with Charlotte Lucas and her family.
quotations.analysis: She names the mechanism of her own prejudice and does not notice she has done it. The two pronouns are balanced against each other across the comma, which is the shape the whole novel will take: two kinds of pride meeting and neither able to see the other's.

quotations.text: Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used synonymously. A person may be proud without being vain. Pride relates more to our opinion of ourselves, vanity to what we would have others think of us.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: Mary offering the company the benefit of her reading.
quotations.analysis: The distinction is sound and the novel uses it: Darcy is proud and Wickham is vain, and the difference is exactly the one Mary draws. Austen's joke is that the book's dullest speaker supplies its most useful definition, and nobody in the room listens.

quotations.text: My good opinion once lost is lost forever.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At Netherfield, admitting to a resentful temper during an evening of sparring with Elizabeth.
quotations.analysis: He says this as a confession of a fault and plainly regards it as a standard. The novel then spends fifty chapters disproving it about him, since his good opinion of Elizabeth survives her refusal and her family; the line is a self-portrait that has stopped being accurate.

quotations.text: That will do extremely well, child. You have delighted us long enough. Let the other young ladies have time to exhibit.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Stopping Mary's second song at the Netherfield ball.
quotations.analysis: A father humiliates a daughter in public and the sentence is constructed so that the cruelty travels inside a compliment. It is the clearest instance of the habit Elizabeth will later have to judge: her father's wit is aimed at his own children and costs him nothing.

quotations.text: My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it a right thing for every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example of matrimony in his parish.
quotations.speaker: Mr Collins
quotations.context: Proposing to Elizabeth, having secured her mother's permission but not her attention.
quotations.analysis: He begins a proposal with an enumerated list and the first item is professional example. The woman is not in the sentence at all; she appears later, as the third reason, on the recommendation of somebody else. Austen lets the syntax do the whole characterisation.

quotations.text: An unhappy alternative is before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents. Your mother will never see you again if you do not marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you do.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Called in by Mrs Bennet to force Elizabeth to accept Collins.
quotations.analysis: He supports his daughter by pretending not to, which lets him defeat his wife and stay amusing at the same time. The sentence is perfectly balanced around the two parents, and the balance is the point: Elizabeth's rescue arrives as a joke, and the same detachment will let Lydia go to Brighton.

quotations.text: I am not romantic you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home; and considering Mr. Collins’s character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as fair, as most people can boast on entering the marriage state.
quotations.speaker: Charlotte Lucas
quotations.context: Telling Elizabeth that she has accepted Mr Collins.
quotations.analysis: She asks only for a house and states her odds like an actuary, and the novel never corrects her arithmetic. Set against the first sentence of the book, this is the same proposition with the irony taken out, spoken by the person whom the marriage market has priced most accurately.

quotations.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The first proposal, at the Hunsford parsonage, while Elizabeth is re-reading Jane's letters.
quotations.analysis: Four short sentences, three of them about his own resistance, and the declaration arrives only in the fourth. 'Struggled' and 'repressed' treat his feeling as an enemy position, so that by the time he reaches 'admire and love' he has already told her what the offer costs him.

quotations.text: I had not known you a month before I felt that you were the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Darcy, after he has asked why he is rejected with so little civility.
quotations.analysis: The superlative is a hostage to fortune and Austen collects on it twenty-six chapters later. Note the precision of 'a month': she dates her verdict exactly, which is what makes it possible for the novel to show her the evidence she had not yet seen.

quotations.text: Be not alarmed, Madam, on receiving this letter, by the apprehension of its containing any repetition of those sentiments, or renewal of those offers, which were last night so disgusting to you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The opening of the letter handed to Elizabeth in the park at Rosings.
quotations.analysis: He hands over the one form of speech she cannot interrupt, and opens by disclaiming any renewal of the offer, which is how he makes the document readable. From here the novel's evidence arrives in writing, and its turning point involves no event at all — only a second reading.

quotations.text: But vanity, not love, has been my folly. Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance, and driven reason away, where either were concerned. Till this moment, I never knew myself.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Alone, having read Darcy's letter twice and reconstructed everything Wickham told her.
quotations.analysis: She does not accuse herself of loving the wrong man but of a fault in method: she was pleased by one and slighted by the other, and let that do her thinking. 'Vanity, not love, has been my folly' applies Mary's distinction from Chapter 5 to herself, thirty chapters after it was laughed at.

quotations.text: I have never had a cross word from him in my life, and I have known him ever since he was four years old.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Reynolds
quotations.context: The Pemberley housekeeper showing the house to Elizabeth and the Gardiners.
quotations.analysis: The testimony that changes Elizabeth's mind comes from a servant with twenty years of observation and no reason to flatter a stranger. Austen makes the evidence economic rather than romantic: landlord and master are job titles, and Darcy is being assessed on how he treats people who cannot answer back.

quotations.text: In what an amiable light does this place him!
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Standing in the Pemberley gallery, hearing the housekeeper describe Darcy's care of his sister.
quotations.analysis: 'This place' is doing double duty: the phrase means this circumstance, and she is standing in the house itself. The estate is functioning as evidence — grounds, portraits, accounts of conduct over years — where conversation had produced only impressions.

quotations.text: Unhappy as the event must be for Lydia, we may draw from it this useful lesson; that loss of virtue in a female is irretrievable⁠—that one false step involves her in endless ruin⁠—that her reputation is no less brittle than it is beautiful⁠—and that she cannot be too much guarded in her behaviour towards the undeserving of the other sex.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: To Elizabeth, while the family waits for news of Lydia.
quotations.analysis: The consolation is monstrous and the description is correct, which is the difficulty the novel will not dissolve. 'Brittle' and 'beautiful' are yoked by alliteration into a single property that a woman owns and can break, and nothing in the plot disproves the account — only Darcy's money limits the damage.

quotations.text: Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?
quotations.speaker: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
quotations.context: In the Longbourn shrubbery, demanding that Elizabeth promise never to accept Darcy.
quotations.analysis: The objection has left the realm of income and become almost sacramental: a house has shades, and a marriage would defile them. It is the class argument in its purest and least answerable form, and the novel answers it by having the interview itself convince Darcy to propose again.

quotations.text: I am only resolved to act in that manner which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Lady Catherine the promise she has come for.
quotations.analysis: She claims the right to define her own happiness and denies her interrogator any standing at all, and she does it in the flattest, least witty sentence she speaks in the book. The wit is dropped because this is not a duel; it is a jurisdictional claim.

quotations.text: For what do we live but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our turn?
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Reading Mr Collins's letter aloud to Elizabeth, who cannot enjoy it.
quotations.analysis: It is the closest thing he has to a philosophy, and the novel has just finished showing what it costs: the daughter he did not watch has been retrieved with somebody else's money. The rhetorical question assumes an answer that the last hundred pages have withdrawn.

quotations.text: I have been a selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle. As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temper.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: Walking with Elizabeth after the second proposal has been accepted.
quotations.analysis: The distinction between practice and principle is the same one Elizabeth reached in Chapter 36, and Austen gives the two confessions a matching shape so that the marriage is founded on a shared diagnosis. He blames an upbringing and does not use it as an excuse, which is the difference between him and Wickham.

quotations.text: I am the happiest creature in the world. Perhaps other people have said so before, but not one with such justice. I am happier even than Jane; she only smiles, I laugh.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Writing to Mrs Gardiner, who had been at Pemberley with her.
quotations.analysis: She claims a superlative and then immediately audits it, which is exactly how she has argued all book. The comparison with Jane is not vanity but accuracy about temperament: the sister who thinks well of everyone smiles, and the one who has had to revise her judgements laughs.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Thomas Egerton, London, in three volumes, credited to the author of Sense and Sensibility.

atAGlance.label: Earlier title
atAGlance.note: The 1796–97 draft; the discarded title names the novel's central test more plainly than the published one.

atAGlance.label: Copyright
atAGlance.note: Austen sold the copyright to Egerton for £110 rather than publishing on commission, and so earned nothing from later editions.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The first proposal falls almost exactly at the centre of the book, and everything after it is re-reading.

criticalViews.position: A comedy of moral education
