criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading takes the novel at the word of its discarded title: two people form wrong first impressions, gather better evidence, and are rewarded with each other. On this account the book's subject is the discipline of judgement.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away how much of the reward is material, and why the plot is settled by Darcy's chequebook rather than by anybody's improved understanding.

criticalViews.position: An economic novel about women without money
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the entail reads the courtships as a survey of what is available to genteel women with no income: Charlotte's bargain, Lydia's disaster and Elizabeth's luck are three outcomes of one predicament.
criticalViews.counter: Pressed hard it can make Elizabeth's refusals look like bad economics rather than integrity, and it struggles with how funny the book is.

criticalViews.position: A study in narrative point of view
criticalViews.summary: Formalist and stylistic criticism has focused on Austen's free indirect style, arguing that the novel's real achievement is the reader's induced error: we misjudge Darcy because we are reading through Elizabeth without being told so.
criticalViews.counter: The technique is not applied evenly — several chapters step away from Elizabeth entirely — so the effect may owe as much to withheld information as to style.

essayQuestions.question: How does Austen present the relationship between marriage and money?
essayQuestions.focus: Entail, income and the price of refusal
plan: Start with the entail as a legal fact, not a theme: Longbourn passes to Collins, and five daughters must therefore marry or be dependent.
Read the first sentence as a joke whose real subject is the mothers, then set Charlotte's speech in Chapter 22 beside it as the same proposition without irony.
Compare the three completed bargains — Charlotte's comfort, Lydia's rescue, Elizabeth's Pemberley — and note what each one cost and who paid.
Test the romantic reading against Chapter 47: Lydia's ruin is averted by money, and the novel says so plainly.
Conclude on whether the ending endorses the system it has mocked, or simply gives one heroine an exemption from it.

essayQuestions.question: 'The novel is about learning to read people.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Judgement, evidence and revision
plan: Establish the pattern of instant verdicts: the assembly in Chapter 3, Wickham's history in Chapter 16, Mrs Bennet on Bingley's income.
Show how Austen implicates the reader through free indirect style, so that Elizabeth's misreadings arrive as narrative fact.
Make Chapter 35 the hinge: the evidence is written, it can be re-read, and nothing happens except a change of mind.
Use Pemberley in Chapter 43 to argue that the novel trusts long testimony and property over conversation and charm.
Weigh the counter-case: Jane reads everybody generously and is wrong about nobody's character, only about their conduct.

essayQuestions.question: Examine Austen's presentation of Mr Bennet.
essayQuestions.focus: Wit, detachment and paternal failure
plan: Open with the twenty-year joke about his wife's nerves: the marriage as a settled comic arrangement.
Show the wit turned on his own children in Chapter 18, and on Elizabeth's proposal crisis in Chapter 20, where it happens to help.
Trace the cost: Lydia goes to Brighton because refusing would have been tiresome, and the library is his habitual answer to every demand.
Read his line about making sport for our neighbours in Chapter 57 against the crisis that has just been paid for by Darcy.
Decide whether the novel forgives him, and what his brief self-reproach after Lydia's flight is worth.

essayQuestions.question: How far does Pride and Prejudice challenge the class system it describes?
essayQuestions.focus: Rank, connection and the Gardiners
plan: Separate money from rank: the Bennets are gentry without capital, the Gardiners have capital without rank, and Darcy has both.
Track the objection as it hardens: Caroline Bingley's sneers, Darcy's first proposal, Lady Catherine's shades of Pemberley.
Use the Gardiners as the novel's counter-argument — the tradesman's family are the most sensible adults in the book and the ones Darcy treats best.
Note the limits: no character crosses a class line without a fortune arriving to make it respectable, and Wickham's rise is punished.
Conclude on the ending's arithmetic, where affection is settled alongside incomes in the same sentences.

discussionQuestions: Charlotte Lucas asks only for a comfortable home. Does the novel think she is wrong?
Elizabeth changes her mind about Darcy after seeing his house. Is that a shallow reason or a sound one?
Mr Bennet is the funniest character in the book and arguably the most culpable. Can both be true at once?
Lydia's elopement is settled with money and never with an apology. What does the novel want us to feel about that?
The book was first called First Impressions. Which title describes it better, and what does the change cost?

timeline.label: Jane Austen born at Steventon
timeline.detail: The seventh child of a Hampshire rector, in a household that read aloud and wrote for each other.

timeline.label: First Impressions drafted
timeline.detail: Written in 1796–97, in Austen's early twenties. No manuscript of this version survives.

timeline.label: The manuscript is offered to Thomas Cadell
timeline.detail: Austen's father wrote to the London publisher, who declined without asking to see it. The novel waited more than a decade.

timeline.label: Sense and Sensibility published
timeline.detail: Austen's first published novel, issued anonymously, made a second Austen title commercially plausible.

timeline.label: Pride and Prejudice published
timeline.detail: Thomas Egerton issued it in three volumes on 28 January, credited to the author of Sense and Sensibility. A second edition followed the same year.

timeline.label: Mansfield Park published
timeline.detail: The first of Austen's novels written entirely after she had become a published author.

timeline.label: Emma published
timeline.detail: Issued by John Murray with an 1816 date on the title page.

timeline.label: Austen dies at Winchester
timeline.detail: She was forty-one. Her name had still not appeared on a title page.

timeline.label: Northanger Abbey and Persuasion published together
timeline.detail: Issued posthumously, with a biographical notice by her brother Henry that named her at last.

timeline.label: Richard Bentley reprints the novels
timeline.detail: Austen enters the cheap standard-novel market, and stays in print from this point on.

timeline.label: The Peacock edition
timeline.detail: George Allen publishes Hugh Thomson's illustrated edition, whose gilt peacock binding became the novel's most recognisable object.

timeline.label: MGM's Pride and Prejudice
timeline.detail: Directed by Robert Z. Leonard, with Greer Garson and Laurence Olivier, and costumed with cheerful disregard for the Regency.

timeline.label: BBC serial adapted by Andrew Davies
timeline.detail: Jennifer Ehle and Colin Firth in six episodes; the version against which most later screen Darcys are measured.

timeline.label: Joe Wright's film
timeline.detail: Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen, in a version that puts mud, livestock and noise back into Longbourn.

places.name: Hertfordshire
places.note: Longbourn, Meryton and Netherfield: a neighbourhood of twenty-four families, small enough that one new tenant changes everything.

places.name: Gracechurch Street, London
places.note: The Gardiners' house, within sight of their own warehouses — the address that Caroline Bingley finds fatal and the novel finds respectable.

places.name: Kent
places.note: Hunsford parsonage and Rosings Park, where Charlotte's bargain and Darcy's first proposal are both inspected at close range.

places.name: Derbyshire
places.note: Pemberley and the village of Lambton, reached on a tour that Elizabeth undertakes only because the Lakes proved too far.

places.name: Brighton
places.note: The militia's summer quarters, and the town Lydia is allowed to visit because refusing would have caused a scene.

places.name: Newcastle upon Tyne
places.note: Where Wickham's new regiment is quartered after the marriage: far north, and paid for by Darcy.

related.why: Austen's first published novel, and the same marriage market seen from the side of women who have already lost their income.
Another governess-adjacent heroine who refuses a proposal on principle, written thirty years later and with the comedy removed.
A hero who has to discover that his own judgement was bought for him, and that the money came from a source he despised.
The marriage market as farce, with the interrogation about income and connections played at full volume.
The opposite settlement of the same questions about property, rank and who may marry whom.

books.title: Romeo and Juliet
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Verona, with one day in Mantua, across roughly four days of high summer
books.lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines, and the whole of it takes four days
books.openingLine: Two households, both alike in dignity, In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
books.summary: A Chorus gives away the ending in fourteen lines, and the play then spends four days showing how quickly two children can reach it. Shakespeare took a story that had run over months in his sources and pressed it into a single hot week, so that every adult delay, every sealed-off street and every letter that fails to arrive lands on lovers who have no time to spare.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Romeo and Juliet
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which runs the Prologue as 1.0. Modern editions differ by a line or two.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A brawl, a feast, and a sonnet between strangers
structure.summary: Two servants start a street fight over nothing, the Prince threatens death for the next offence, and Romeo is in love with a woman who will not have him. At the Capulet feast he meets Juliet, and the two build a sonnet between them before either learns the other's name.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: The Chorus announces the feud, the lovers and their deaths in fourteen lines.

scenes.title: Coals and swords
scenes.summary: A servants' quarrel becomes a civic riot; the Prince sets death as the penalty for the next one.

scenes.title: Paris asks
scenes.summary: Capulet tells Paris his daughter is too young, and then invites him to the feast anyway.

scenes.title: Fourteen
scenes.summary: Lady Capulet raises marriage; the Nurse answers with a long, fond, indecent memory.

scenes.title: Queen Mab
scenes.summary: Mercutio's fantasy about the dreams of sleepers runs out of control on the way to the party.

scenes.title: The feast
scenes.summary: Romeo sees Juliet, Tybalt is restrained by Capulet, and the two lovers learn each other's surnames last.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A marriage arranged in a night and a morning
structure.summary: Romeo climbs the orchard wall and hears Juliet say aloud what she would never have told him. She proposes marriage herself, and by the following afternoon Friar Laurence has performed it, hoping a secret wedding will do what the Prince's threats cannot.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: A second Chorus sonnet marks the change from old love to new.

scenes.title: The wall
scenes.summary: Mercutio conjures for Romeo bawdily in the lane while Romeo hides on the other side.

scenes.title: The orchard
scenes.summary: Juliet, overheard, argues with a name; before the scene ends she has proposed marriage.

scenes.title: The cell
scenes.summary: Friar Laurence, gathering herbs, agrees to marry them for political reasons of his own.

scenes.title: Wit in the street
scenes.summary: Mercutio finds Romeo restored to sociable joking; the Nurse arrives on her errand.

scenes.title: The Nurse delays
scenes.summary: Juliet waits three hours for news and is teased with aching bones before she gets it.

scenes.title: The wedding
scenes.summary: The Friar warns against violent delights and marries them within the same speech.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Two deaths at noon and a banishment
structure.summary: Mercutio dies under Romeo's arm, Romeo kills Tybalt within minutes, and the Prince commutes death to exile. Juliet spends her wedding night with a husband who must leave at dawn, and wakes to a father who will disown her if she does not marry Paris on Thursday.

scenes.title: The street at noon
scenes.summary: Mercutio and Tybalt are killed in quick succession; Romeo is banished, not executed.

scenes.title: Juliet hears
scenes.summary: The Nurse's garbled news makes Juliet think Romeo dead, then curse him, then defend him.

scenes.title: On the floor
scenes.summary: Romeo will not hear the word banished; the Friar and the Nurse get him to Juliet.

scenes.title: Thursday
scenes.summary: Capulet fixes the wedding to Paris while his daughter is upstairs with her husband.

scenes.title: Dawn and after
scenes.summary: The lovers part; Capulet threatens to turn Juliet out, and the Nurse advises bigamy.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A drug, a false death and a house of mourning
structure.summary: Juliet takes the Friar's vial without telling anyone, and the scene in which she swallows it is the longest she is ever left alone. The Capulets wake to find her cold, and the household turns its wedding preparations into a funeral in the space of one scene.

scenes.title: The plan
scenes.summary: Juliet meets Paris at the Friar's cell and is given a potion and a forty-two-hour lie.

scenes.title: Obedience
scenes.summary: Juliet apologises to her father, who joyfully brings the wedding forward a day.

scenes.title: The vial
scenes.summary: Alone, Juliet imagines waking among bones, and drinks anyway.

scenes.title: Morning in the kitchen
scenes.summary: Capulet fusses over pastry and logs while his daughter lies drugged upstairs.

scenes.title: The discovery
scenes.summary: Formal lamentation from the family; the musicians stay behind to argue about their fee.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The message that does not arrive
structure.summary: Romeo in Mantua hears of Juliet's death from a servant before the Friar's letter can reach him, because the messenger is shut up in a plague house. He buys poison from a starving apothecary, kills Paris at the tomb door, and dies minutes before Juliet wakes.

scenes.title: Mantua
scenes.summary: Balthasar brings the wrong news; Romeo remembers an apothecary poor enough to break the law.

scenes.title: Quarantine
scenes.summary: Friar John explains that plague searchers sealed the house and the letter never left.

scenes.title: The tomb
scenes.summary: Paris, Romeo and Juliet die; the Friar confesses, and the two fathers agree on statues.

characters.name: Romeo
characters.summary: He arrives already in love, with a woman the audience never meets, and speaking a courtly idiom he has clearly borrowed. What Juliet does to him is mostly grammatical: he stops making balanced Petrarchan antitheses about himself and starts answering another person.
characters.clue: He comes to the party in a borrowed idiom of sighs and oxymorons, and leaves it speaking half a sonnet that somebody else finishes.

relationships.label: kinsman by marriage, then killer of

characters.name: Juliet
characters.summary: She is the practical one. She proposes the marriage, fixes the arrangements, questions the Friar's plan for flaws before she takes it, and dies without a speech. Her soliloquies are the only places in the play where somebody thinks a decision through before making it.
characters.clue: Not yet fourteen, she settles the wedding arrangements herself, cross-examines a friar's plan for holes, and then drinks it down alone.

characters.name: Mercutio
characters.role: Kinsman to the Prince, friend to Romeo
characters.summary: Related to neither house, which is why his death breaks the play open: the feud kills a man who had no stake in it. His Queen Mab speech is the longest flight of fancy Shakespeare had written to that point, and it collapses into bitterness before anyone can stop it.
characters.clue: He belongs to neither house, talks faster than anybody in Verona, and jokes about being a grave man while bleeding to death.

characters.name: Tybalt
characters.summary: He treats the feud as an identity rather than a grievance, and he is the only character who states a preference for hatred over peace. Capulet's refusal to let him act at the feast stores up the violence that arrives in the next act.
characters.clue: He hates the word peace as he hates hell, and is sent back to his seat at a party by an old man who wants no fuss.

characters.name: The Nurse
characters.summary: She has fed Juliet, buried her own daughter, and speaks the only unguarded prose in the Capulet house. Her advice after the banishment — marry Paris, the second match is better — is not treachery so much as a servant's realism, and Juliet ends the friendship on the spot.
characters.clue: She dates her memories by an earthquake and a weaning, and her practical advice about a second husband costs her a friendship of fourteen years.

characters.name: Friar Laurence
characters.summary: A herbalist who knows that the same plant heals and kills, and who applies the principle to politics: a secret marriage, he hopes, will cure a public feud. Every one of his interventions is well meant, improvised, and worse than the situation it was designed to fix.
characters.clue: He gathers herbs at dawn, knows that poison and medicine can share a flower, and runs out of the tomb when the watch arrives.

characters.name: Capulet
characters.role: Juliet's father, head of the house
characters.summary: In Act I he tells Paris his daughter is too young and that her consent matters; in Act III he threatens to throw her into the street. Nothing has changed except that he has been contradicted, which is the most frightening thing about the scene.
characters.clue: He begins by telling a suitor to wait two years for his daughter's consent, and ends by offering her a choice between a wedding and starvation.

characters.name: Lady Capulet
characters.summary: She cannot talk to her daughter without the Nurse in the room, and her one plan after Tybalt's death is to have Romeo poisoned in Mantua. She married young herself, which the play mentions once and does not press.
characters.clue: She needs a servant in the room to hold a conversation with her own daughter, and her idea of comfort is an offer to poison a man in Mantua.

characters.name: Benvolio
characters.summary: The play's witness: he tries to stop the first fight, reports the second accurately to the Prince, and then disappears from the text without explanation. His function is to want peace and to be ineffective at it.
characters.clue: He draws his sword only to beat other swords down, gives the Prince the fairest account of a killing, and then vanishes from the play.

characters.name: Paris
characters.role: A young nobleman, kinsman to the Prince
characters.summary: He is not a villain, and that is the difficulty: he courts Juliet through her father because that is how it is done, speaks to her kindly when they meet, and comes to her tomb with flowers. He dies asking to be laid beside her.
characters.clue: He asks the father rather than the daughter, brings flowers to a tomb, and is killed at its door by a man he takes for a vandal.

themes.name: Haste and timing
themes.summary: The play is built on a clock. Brooke's poem takes months; Shakespeare takes four days, and then fills them with deadlines — Thursday, the dawn, forty-two hours, three hours of waiting for a Nurse. Almost every disaster is a matter of minutes rather than of malice.
themes.development: The Friar's warnings against speed in 2.3 and 2.6 are ignored by everyone including himself, and by Act V the plot has been reduced to a race between a letter and a horse.

themes.name: The feud and civic order
themes.summary: Nobody in the play can say what the quarrel is about. It is inherited, not argued, and it is carried out mostly by servants and young men with nothing else to do. The Prince's authority works only in the scene in which he is standing.
themes.development: Three street brawls mark the play's three movements, and the last of them kills a man related to neither house.

themes.name: Love, desire and its languages
themes.summary: Verona offers several competing accounts of what love is: Mercutio's obscenity, the Nurse's memory of bruised knees, Paris's negotiation with a father, Romeo's Petrarchan sighing over Rosaline. The lovers have to invent something that fits none of them, and they do it inside fourteen lines.
themes.development: Romeo's borrowed oxymorons in Act I give way to shared speech in 1.5 and plain future-tense planning in 2.2.

themes.name: Parents, children and obedience
themes.summary: The adults in this play are not monsters; they are simply certain they know best and unable to be told otherwise. Capulet's swing from indulgence to threat in the space of two acts shows what paternal affection is worth in Verona once it is contradicted.
themes.development: Capulet asks for Juliet's consent in 1.2, ignores it in 3.4, and threatens to disown her in 3.5; her mother and her nurse both decline to intervene.

themes.name: Fate, stars and accident
themes.summary: The Prologue calls the lovers star-cross'd before they appear, and the characters keep blaming the heavens. What the play actually stages is a chain of contingencies: a servant who cannot read, a plague quarantine, a friar who arrives half a minute late.
themes.development: Romeo moves from a vague misgiving about the stars in 1.4 to defying them in 5.1, and the Friar's last word is that a greater power has thwarted the plan.

themes.name: Death as bridegroom
themes.summary: Juliet says her grave will be her wedding bed within minutes of meeting Romeo, and the play keeps the equation going: a bride laid out for a funeral, a tomb described as a lantern, a husband who imagines Death keeping his wife for a lover.
themes.development: What begins as courtly hyperbole in 1.5 is literalised in 4.5 when the wedding music is turned to a dirge, and again in 5.3.

techniques.name: Sonnet form in dialogue
techniques.definition: Fourteen lines of rhymed iambic pentameter, here divided between speakers rather than spoken by one voice.
techniques.inThisBook: The Chorus speaks a sonnet, and then Romeo and Juliet build one together at the feast, each taking a quatrain and sharing the couplet: the form itself performs the meeting.

techniques.name: Oxymoron
techniques.definition: Two contradictory terms yoked into a single phrase.
techniques.inThisBook: Romeo's loving hate and cold fire in Act I are a poet's exercise; by 3.2 Juliet's beautiful tyrant and damned saint are doing real work, because she has just been told her husband killed her cousin.

techniques.name: Light against dark
techniques.definition: A repeated contrast of brightness and night used to organise a play's images.
techniques.inThisBook: Every declaration happens at night and every catastrophe in daylight: torches, a jewel in an ear, the sun at the window, and a tomb that Romeo says is full of light because Juliet is in it.

techniques.name: Prose and bawdy
techniques.definition: Unmetered speech, often obscene, set against the verse of the main plot.
techniques.inThisBook: Sampson, Gregory, Mercutio and the Nurse keep a running physical commentary on sex that the lovers' verse never acknowledges; the two registers meet only when Juliet dismisses the Nurse.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something the characters on stage do not.
techniques.inThisBook: The Prologue removes suspense deliberately, so that the Nurse's teasing, Capulet's wedding plans and the whole of Act IV are watched by an audience already told how they end.

techniques.name: Stichomythia
techniques.definition: Rapid exchange of single lines between two speakers.
techniques.inThisBook: The pilgrim exchange at the feast and the dawn parting in 3.5 both run line for line, which is what makes the lovers sound like two halves of one speaker.

quotations.text: From forth the fatal loins of these two foes A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life;
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Prologue, spoken before any character appears.
quotations.analysis: 'Take their life' means both to be born and to kill themselves, so the sentence contains the whole plot in three words. Shakespeare gives away the ending on purpose: the audience is not being asked what happens but how long it takes, which is the question the rest of the play answers in days and hours.

quotations.text: What, drawn, and talk of peace! I hate the word, As I hate hell, all Montagues, and thee
quotations.speaker: Tybalt
quotations.context: To Benvolio, who has drawn his sword only to separate the fighting servants.
quotations.analysis: He hates a word, not a person — the grammar puts 'peace', 'hell', 'all Montagues' and 'thee' into the same list, as though they were the same kind of thing. It is the clearest statement in the play that the feud is not about a grievance but about an identity somebody would have to give up.

quotations.text: My child is yet a stranger in the world; She hath not seen the change of fourteen years, Let two more summers wither in their pride, Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride.
quotations.speaker: Capulet
quotations.context: Refusing, for the moment, Paris's request for Juliet's hand.
quotations.analysis: This is the same man who in Act III gives his daughter four days to marry or be turned out of doors, and he has not changed his opinion of her in between — only been contradicted. The play plants his reasonableness early so that the later scene registers as something other than a bad temper.

quotations.text: O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright! It seems she hangs upon the cheek of night Like a rich jewel in an Ethiope's ear; Beauty too rich for use, for earth too dear!
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: Seeing Juliet for the first time, across the Capulets' hall.
quotations.analysis: He does not know her name and is already making her a light source in a room full of torches. The imagery of brightness set in darkness runs from here to the tomb, where Romeo will call a burial vault a lantern; the play's love scenes are all lit against black.

quotations.text: If I profane with my unworthiest hand This holy shrine, the gentle fine is this: My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand To smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: The opening quatrain of the sonnet the lovers make between them at the feast.
quotations.analysis: Romeo offers a quatrain and Juliet answers with one in the same rhyme scheme, which means she has recognised the form and chosen to complete it. Two strangers producing a single sonnet is the most economical way Shakespeare ever found to show people discovering they think alike, and it happens before either knows the other's surname.

quotations.text: My only love sprung from my only hate! Too early seen unknown, and known too late!
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: On being told by the Nurse that the young man is a Montague.
quotations.analysis: The line is balanced on the word 'only', which does duty twice and means something different each time: sole love, sole hatred. 'Too early' and 'too late' inside one line is the play's own clock complaining, four scenes before there is anything to be late for.

quotations.text: It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: In the Capulet orchard, seeing a light at the window above.
quotations.analysis: Nine monosyllables and one name, which is unusually plain for a man who has spent Act I in elaborate paradoxes. The metaphor also quietly reverses the scene's conditions: it is the middle of the night, and he is describing a sunrise.

quotations.text: O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo? Deny thy father and refuse thy name; Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, And I'll no longer be a Capulet.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Alone at her window, unaware that Romeo is below.
quotations.analysis: 'Wherefore' means why, not where: she is asking why he has to be that particular man, and she answers her own question in the next three lines by offering to change her name instead. Within a minute of her first private speech she has proposed the practical solution the adults spend five acts failing to find.

quotations.text: What's in a name? that which we call a rose By any other name would smell as sweet;
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, arguing with the word 'Montague'.
quotations.analysis: The argument is philosophically sound and turns out to be false in Verona, where names cost lives. Juliet is testing whether language can be separated from the world, and the rest of the play is the experiment failing: a name gets Mercutio killed and a letter that never arrives kills the rest.

quotations.text: It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden; Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be Ere one can say 'It lightens.'
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Refusing to exchange vows on the spot, in the middle of the orchard scene.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of 'too' in two lines, and the simile is chosen for its speed: lightning is over before the word for it can be said. She sees the danger of haste more clearly than the Friar does, and proposes marriage thirty lines later anyway.

quotations.text: My bounty is as boundless as the sea, My love as deep; the more I give to thee, The more I have, for both are infinite.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Called away by the Nurse, returning to the window for the third time.
quotations.analysis: Verona runs on exchange — dowries, bonds of kinship, favours owed — and this is the one economy in the play that does not work by subtraction. The rhyme of 'sea' and 'thee' ties the scale of the image to the person it is addressed to, which is why the hyperbole does not sound like boasting.

quotations.text: Good night, good night! parting is such sweet sorrow, That I shall say good night till it be morrow.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: The end of the orchard scene, after three false exits.
quotations.analysis: The couplet is a joke about its own form: she says good night twice and then promises to keep saying it until morning, which is exactly what the preceding hundred lines have been doing. The oxymoron is conventional, but the staging makes it literal — she cannot leave, and the scene keeps restarting.

quotations.text: Virtue itself turns vice, being misapplied; And vice sometimes by action dignified.
quotations.speaker: Friar Laurence
quotations.context: Gathering herbs at dawn, before Romeo arrives to ask for a wedding.
quotations.analysis: He is talking about plants, and he has just said that the same flower cheers when smelt and kills when tasted. The couplet is also his own defence in advance: everything he does from here is a good thing misapplied, and he will use one of those flowers to fake a death.

quotations.text: Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.
quotations.speaker: Friar Laurence
quotations.context: The last line of the scene, as Romeo hurries him towards the wedding.
quotations.analysis: It is the exit line of a scene in which the Friar has just agreed to marry two teenagers who met the previous night. The advice is sound, the speaker ignores it, and the play stages the consequence twice over — a messenger who does not arrive and a friar who arrives half a minute late.

quotations.text: These violent delights have violent ends And in their triumph die, like fire and powder, Which as they kiss consume
quotations.speaker: Friar Laurence
quotations.context: Waiting for Juliet at the cell, immediately before he marries them.
quotations.analysis: The image is gunpowder meeting a flame, and the verb for their meeting is 'kiss'. He is warning against the wedding he is about to perform, which is the pattern of his whole part: accurate diagnosis followed immediately by the opposite action.

quotations.text: A plague o' both your houses! I am sped.
quotations.speaker: Mercutio
quotations.context: Stabbed under Romeo's arm as Romeo tries to part the fighters.
quotations.analysis: He curses both families, which is his right: he belongs to neither and is dying for a quarrel he has only ever mocked. He says it three times in twenty lines, and the play takes the curse literally — the next four deaths are Capulets and Montagues.

quotations.text: O, I am fortune's fool!
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: Standing over Tybalt's body, told to run before the Prince arrives.
quotations.analysis: Five words, and every one of them shifts the agency away from the man who has just done the killing. It is the play's habit in miniature: the characters keep describing as fate a sequence of things they have chosen, and the audience has watched Romeo choose this one.

quotations.text: And you be not, hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, For, by my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee,
quotations.speaker: Capulet
quotations.context: To Juliet, who has said she will not marry Paris.
quotations.analysis: Four verbs with nothing between them, each one a worse outcome than the last, from a man who two acts earlier wanted her consent before anything was agreed. Neither her mother nor her nurse contradicts him, and the scene ends with Juliet alone on stage for the first time since the orchard.

quotations.text: Go, counsellor; Thou and my bosom henceforth shall be twain.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Alone, after the Nurse has advised her to marry Paris and forget Romeo.
quotations.analysis: She ends fourteen years of intimacy in a line and a half, and she does it in verse to a woman who has just spoken prose. 'Twain' is a marriage word turned inside out: the one relationship in the play that predates the action is dissolved just as the Nurse becomes useless to her.

quotations.text: I have a faint cold fear thrills through my veins, That almost freezes up the heat of life
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: Alone in her chamber with the Friar's vial, having sent the Nurse away.
quotations.analysis: She describes the drug's effect before she has taken it, which is the point of the speech: she has already imagined waking among her ancestors' bones and is going through with it anyway. It is the longest she is left alone on stage, and she uses the time to test the plan for flaws rather than to hesitate.

quotations.text: Is it even so? then I defy you, stars!
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: In Mantua, on hearing from Balthasar that Juliet lies dead in the Capulet vault.
quotations.analysis: The Prologue called him star-cross'd; here he answers the Prologue directly, and the defiance takes the form of doing exactly what the stars were said to have arranged. He is acting on news that is fifteen minutes out of date, which is the only thing wrong with the whole plan.

quotations.text: O true apothecary! Thy drugs are quick. Thus with a kiss I die.
quotations.speaker: Romeo
quotations.context: In the tomb, having drunk the poison beside Juliet's body.
quotations.analysis: He praises the tradesman for the quality of the goods, which is a startling thing to do in the middle of a suicide, and the compliment is about speed. The last words turn the poison into the kiss, so that the drug and the marriage meet in one action.

quotations.text: Yea, noise? then I'll be brief. O happy dagger! This is thy sheath; there rust, and let me die.
quotations.speaker: Juliet
quotations.context: In the tomb, hearing the watch approach after the Friar has fled.
quotations.analysis: 'I'll be brief' is the shortest deathbed intention in Shakespeare, and she keeps to it: no lament, no speech to the body, twelve words and a stab. Calling her own body the dagger's sheath makes the suicide a consummation, and it is the only wedding night the play allows to finish.

quotations.text: For never was a story of more woe Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.
quotations.speaker: Prince
quotations.context: The last two lines of the play, over the bodies and the reconciled fathers.
quotations.analysis: The Prince calls it a story, not a crime, which is how Verona will be able to live with it: the fathers have just agreed to put up gold statues. Her name comes first and his is possessive — 'her Romeo' — the one moment the play's title order is reversed, and it is the closing rhyme.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Usually placed in Shakespeare's early to mid-1590s work, close to A Midsummer Night's Dream and Richard II.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: An Excellent conceited Tragedie of Romeo and Iuliet, printed by John Danter — much shorter than the text that followed.

atAGlance.label: The fuller text
atAGlance.note: Advertised as newly corrected, augmented and amended; it is the basis of later quartos, the Folio and most modern editions.

atAGlance.label: Chief English source
atAGlance.note: The Tragical History of Romeus and Juliet supplies the plot, the Friar, the Nurse, the potion and the tomb, spread over months rather than days.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of fate
criticalViews.summary: The Prologue's star-cross'd lovers, the omens, the Friar's greater power: on this reading the play is about a design nobody can escape, and the characters' choices are the means by which it is carried out.
criticalViews.counter: Every disaster in Act V has a mundane cause — a servant sent with the wrong news, a letter stopped by plague searchers, a friar who is a minute slow.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of haste and accident
criticalViews.summary: Shakespeare's most conspicuous change to Brooke was compression: months become four days. Read that way, the play is an experiment in what happens to ordinary bad decisions when nobody has time to reconsider them.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the feud incidental, when the play's first and last scenes are both about a quarrel between households rather than a mistake between lovers.

criticalViews.position: A play about patriarchal households
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has increasingly read the tragedy through Capulet's authority over a thirteen-year-old, the marriage market Paris enters, and the silence of both Juliet's mother and her nurse at the moment she most needs them.
criticalViews.counter: Juliet is also the play's most decisive agent, and reading her only as a victim of her father flattens the scenes in which she arranges her own marriage and tests her own escape.

essayQuestions.question: How far is the tragedy of Romeo and Juliet caused by chance rather than by character?
essayQuestions.focus: Fate, accident and decision
plan: Start with the Prologue: the audience is told the ending, so the play's question is mechanism rather than outcome.
List the accidents honestly — the illiterate servant in 1.2, the plague quarantine in 5.2, the Friar's late arrival — and note that none of them is supernatural.
Set against them the decisions: Romeo's choice to answer Tybalt's challenge in 3.1, Juliet's choice to take the vial in 4.3.
Use 3.1.138 and 5.1.25 to show Romeo describing as fortune two things he has just done himself.
Conclude on the Friar's 'greater power' in 5.3 and ask whether the play endorses it or lets him off.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Shakespeare's presentation of Juliet.
essayQuestions.focus: Agency, speech and isolation
plan: Open with her first scene, where she speaks eight short lines while her mother and the Nurse discuss her marriage around her.
Read 2.2 as a scene of practical arrangement, not rapture: she raises the marriage, sets the time and names the messenger.
Mark the turn at 3.5, where she dismisses the Nurse in a line and a half and is left without an ally.
Use 4.3 to show her testing the Friar's plan for flaws, including the possibility that he has poisoned her.
Close on the brevity of 5.3.177 and weigh it against the length of Romeo's death speech.

essayQuestions.question: What part does the feud play in the tragedy?
essayQuestions.focus: Civic violence and inherited hatred
plan: Establish that nobody in the play ever states the cause of the quarrel, and that the first fight is started by servants.
Track the Prince's three interventions and show that his authority lasts only as long as he is on stage.
Use Tybalt at 1.1.63 to show hatred presented as an identity rather than a grievance.
Argue that Mercutio's death is the hinge, because it kills a man related to neither house and drags Romeo in.
End with the gold statues in 5.3 and ask what the reconciliation actually costs the fathers.

essayQuestions.question: 'The adults in this play are more dangerous than the feud.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Parents, advisers and the failure of counsel
plan: Begin with Capulet's reasonableness at 1.2.8 so that the later threat registers as a change of temper, not of principle.
Follow the Nurse from confidante to the advice at 3.5 that ends the friendship.
Examine Friar Laurence's pattern: correct diagnosis at 2.3 and 2.6, reckless intervention immediately afterwards.
Consider Lady Capulet's plan to have Romeo poisoned as the family's own version of private violence.
Test the proposition against the fact that the lovers marry in secret before any adult refuses them anything.

discussionQuestions: The Prologue tells you the ending before the play starts. What does the play gain by giving up suspense?
Juliet is thirteen. How much does a production change if the lovers look their age?
Mercutio belongs to neither house. Why does Shakespeare make the play's turning point the death of an outsider?
Friar Laurence is never punished. Should he be?
The fathers end the feud by agreeing to build statues. Is that a reconciliation or an evasion?

timeline.label: Matteo Bandello publishes his Novelle
timeline.detail: His version of the Veronese lovers carries the story into the European collections that reach England.

timeline.label: Pierre Boaistuau adapts Bandello into French
timeline.detail: The Histoires tragiques supply the immediate source for the English versions.

timeline.label: Arthur Brooke, The Tragical History of Romeus and Juliet
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's chief English source: the feud, the Friar, the Nurse, the potion and the tomb, spread across months.

timeline.label: William Painter prints a prose version
timeline.detail: The Palace of Pleasure shows how far the Italian novella tradition had entered English reading.

timeline.label: First Quarto printed by John Danter
timeline.detail: An Excellent conceited Tragedie of Romeo and Iuliet; the title page claims frequent public performance by the Lord Hunsdon's Servants.

timeline.label: Second Quarto: 'newly corrected, augmented, and amended'
timeline.detail: Much fuller than Q1, and the basis of later quartos, the Folio text and modern editions.

timeline.label: The play is entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: A decade after the first quarto had already appeared in print.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed as The Tragedie of Romeo and Juliet, following the later quarto line.

timeline.label: David Garrick's acting version
timeline.detail: Restores more of Shakespeare's text than earlier adaptations while rewriting the ending for the eighteenth-century stage.

timeline.label: Gounod's Roméo et Juliette
timeline.detail: The opera makes the love plot the musical engine and gives the lovers extended duets.

timeline.label: Prokofiev composes the ballet score
timeline.detail: It becomes the basis of the best-known dance treatments, including Kenneth MacMillan's of 1965.

timeline.label: West Side Story opens
timeline.detail: The feud is transferred to New York gang conflict, with music by Leonard Bernstein and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim.

timeline.label: Zeffirelli's film
timeline.detail: Casting Leonard Whiting and Olivia Hussey as genuinely young leads changed what audiences expected the parts to look like.

timeline.label: Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's language kept intact inside a modern Verona Beach of guns, television and religious iconography.

places.name: Verona
places.note: The whole play but one scene: the public square, the Capulet house, the orchard, the friar's cell and the vault.

places.name: Mantua
places.note: Romeo's place of exile, about twenty-five miles away, and the apothecary's shop.

places.name: Vicenza
places.note: Home of Luigi da Porto, whose Italian novella stands early in the chain of sources behind Brooke.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the 1597 quarto was printed, its title page naming the Lord Hunsdon's Servants as the company.

related.why: Written around the same time, and containing a parody of exactly this plot in the Pyramus and Thisbe interlude.
The same city, the same rope-ladder elopement machinery, played for comedy instead.
The later tragedy of a young person trapped inside an adult household, and the opposite problem: too much delay rather than too little.
Another marriage made in secret against a father's will, and another catastrophe that turns on evidence arriving too late.
Shipwreck, disguise and mistaken identity handled as comedy, with the same interest in how quickly people fall in love with an idea.

books.title: Sense and Sensibility
books.author: Jane Austen
books.setting: Sussex, Devonshire, London and Somersetshire, in a household of reduced income
books.written: Begun in the 1790s, probably as Elinor and Marianne; revised for publication by 1811
books.lengthNote: Fifty chapters, first issued in three volumes
books.openingLine: The family of Dashwood had long been settled in Sussex.
books.summary: A will, a promise and a conversation between husband and wife reduce four women from Norland Park to a cottage in Devonshire, and the novel takes its shape from that arithmetic. Elinor keeps a secret she is bound not to share; Marianne tells everybody everything and is destroyed by a man who never wrote her a word she could show anyone. Austen's first published book is also her most interested in what silence costs the person keeping it.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Sense and Sensibility
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously from 1 to 50, as in the Standard Ebooks text; the 1811 first edition divides the same chapters across three volumes.

structure.label: Chapters 1–12
structure.title: A promise talked down, and a cottage in Devonshire
structure.summary: Old Mr Dashwood's will ties up Norland, and the second chapter reduces a deathbed promise to nothing across a single fireside conversation. The Dashwood women take Barton Cottage on a relation's charity, Marianne sprains her ankle in the rain, and Willoughby arrives carrying her downhill.

structure.label: Chapters 13–22
structure.title: An attachment everyone assumes, and a secret nobody expects
structure.summary: Willoughby and Marianne behave as though they were engaged and never say that they are; then he leaves for London without explanation. Lucy Steele, watching Elinor closely, discloses her four-year engagement to Edward Ferrars in a conversation designed to look like a confidence.

structure.label: Chapters 23–36
structure.title: London, and the letter Marianne has to read in public
structure.summary: In town Marianne writes to Willoughby and waits; he cuts her at a party and returns her letters with a note his fiancée dictated. Colonel Brandon supplies the history of the two Elizas, and the Ferrars family discovers Lucy, with consequences measured in pounds.

structure.label: Chapters 37–44
structure.title: What Elinor had been carrying, and what Willoughby came to say
structure.summary: Elinor finally tells Marianne how long she has known about Lucy and what it has cost to say nothing. At Cleveland Marianne walks in wet grass until she is dangerously ill, and Willoughby arrives at midnight to explain himself to the only person who will listen.

structure.label: Chapters 45–50
structure.title: A recovery, a misheard name, and two settlements
structure.summary: Marianne reconsiders her whole conduct without abandoning her capacity to feel. A servant's report that Mr Ferrars is married sends the household into mourning for the wrong brother, and the novel closes by arranging incomes at Delaford and a parsonage nearby.

characters.name: Elinor Dashwood
characters.summary: She is nineteen and already the family's counsellor, which tells the reader what her mother is like. Her self-command is a duty she has taken on rather than a coldness, and Austen is careful to show the bill: four months of knowing about Lucy while listening to her sister complain that she does not feel enough.
characters.clue: She keeps another woman's engagement secret for four months because she was told it in confidence, and is called cold-hearted for it by her own sister.

relationships.label: confided in, and quietly attacked by

characters.name: Marianne Dashwood
characters.summary: Everything but prudent, in the novel's own phrase. Her mistake is not that she feels too much but that she treats shared taste as evidence of shared character, which makes her the ideal audience for a man performing sensibility at her.
characters.clue: She runs down a hill in the rain, is carried home by a stranger, and later asks her sister whether her own conduct has been blameless.

characters.name: Edward Ferrars
characters.summary: Diffident, without a profession, and held in place by an engagement he made at nineteen to a woman he no longer loves. His honour consists entirely of refusing to break a promise that has become a trap, which is both admirable and the reason he is nearly absent from his own love plot.
characters.clue: He is disinherited rather than break an engagement, and is released only when the woman he is bound to elopes with his richer brother.
traits: with no occupation to fill his time

characters.name: John Willoughby
characters.role: Heir to Allenham, of Combe Magna in Somersetshire
characters.summary: He reads the right poets, rides the right horses and agrees with Marianne about everything, which is exactly how a fortune-hunter would behave and also how a man in love behaves. Austen's hardest decision is giving him a midnight scene in which his remorse is entirely genuine and entirely useless.
characters.clue: He carries a girl home through the rain, cuts her dead in a London drawing room, and turns up months later to explain himself to her sister while she lies ill upstairs.

characters.name: Colonel Brandon
characters.summary: Introduced as a joke about flannel waistcoats and old age, and revealed to be the only man in the book who has ever acted at real cost. The story of the two Elizas gives the novel its darker arithmetic: what happens to a woman with feeling and no protection.
characters.clue: Thirty-five, silent, and mocked for wearing flannel; he keeps a ward in the country and fights a duel he never mentions.

characters.name: Lucy Steele
characters.summary: Uneducated, sharp and the best tactician in the book. She turns a confidence into a weapon by making Elinor the one person who cannot repeat it, and she ends the novel richer than anybody except by abandoning the engagement she spent four hundred pages defending.
characters.clue: She tells her rival a secret in order to bind her to silence, and finally marries the brother with the money instead.
traits: illiterate on paper and expert in person

characters.name: Mrs Dashwood
characters.summary: She has her second daughter's temperament and none of a mother's caution, which is why nobody ever asks Marianne and Willoughby whether they are engaged. Her romantic delicacy is indistinguishable, in its effects, from neglect.
characters.clue: She refuses to ask her daughter a direct question about an engagement because asking would show a want of confidence.

characters.name: John Dashwood
characters.role: The sisters' half-brother, owner of Norland
characters.summary: He means to keep his promise to his dying father and is talked out of it in one conversation without ever noticing that he has changed his mind. He is the novel's demonstration that selfishness does not require a villain, only a wife with an argument and a husband who wants to be persuaded.
characters.clue: He promises his dying father to provide for his sisters, and reduces three thousand pounds to occasional presents of fish and game.

characters.name: Fanny Dashwood
characters.summary: She conducts the second chapter like a barrister, moving from three thousand pounds to five hundred to an annuity to nothing at all, and each step sounds more reasonable than the last. Austen gives her no soliloquy and no villainy — only impeccable argument in her own interest.
characters.clue: She observes that people always live for ever when there is an annuity to be paid them, and so the annuity is dropped.

characters.name: Mrs Jennings
characters.summary: Vulgar, inquisitive and the most practically kind person in the novel. She embarrasses both sisters constantly and is also the one who sits up with Marianne when she is dying, which is Austen's way of separating manners from goodness.
characters.clue: She jokes relentlessly about beaux and conquests, and then nurses a girl she barely knows through a fever nobody else can face.

themes.name: Sense and sensibility
themes.summary: The title looks like a contest and the novel refuses to hold one. Elinor's judgement leaves her carrying knowledge alone; Marianne's candour makes her legible to a man who reads her for profit. Each sister ends the book holding something she learned from the other.
themes.development: Set up in Chapter 1 as a contrast of temperaments, tested through four months of silence, and settled in Chapter 46 when Marianne judges her own conduct by her sister's standard.

themes.name: Money and inheritance
themes.summary: The plot is started by a will and finished by a settlement, and every important decision in between has a figure attached. Austen puts the numbers on the page — two thousand a year, five hundred pounds, a hundred a year — so that no reader can treat the feeling as separable from the income.
themes.development: From the second chapter's reduction of a promise to nothing, through Marianne's argument about competence in Chapter 17, to the livings and settlements distributed in the last chapters.

themes.name: Secrecy and silence
themes.summary: Almost every crisis in the book is caused by something withheld: an engagement kept for four years, an attachment never declared, a history told too late. Silence is variously honour, weapon and cowardice, and the novel distinguishes carefully between the three.
themes.development: Lucy's disclosure in Chapter 22 loads the gun; Elinor's four months of secrecy are detonated in Chapter 37; Brandon's history and Willoughby's confession arrive when they can no longer help.

themes.name: Dependence
themes.summary: The Dashwood women are not poor in any sense a labourer would recognise, and they have no power whatever over where they live, what they keep or whom they may marry. The novel's interest is in that specific genteel powerlessness, which looks comfortable and forecloses everything.
themes.development: Begins with the entail of Norland, continues at Barton on a relation's charity, and reaches its sharpest point in the two Elizas, who had feeling and no protection at all.

themes.name: Performance and sincerity
themes.summary: Willoughby's great advantage is that he is genuinely charming, so the performance of sensibility and the thing itself cannot be told apart by taste alone. The novel keeps asking what evidence of character is admissible, and keeps answering: conduct over time, and nothing else.
themes.development: Established in Marianne's first conversations with Willoughby about Cowper and dead leaves, and undone by the letter in Chapter 29 that he did not write.

themes.name: Illness and the body
themes.summary: Marianne's fever is not a metaphor that arrives conveniently; it is caused by wet feet, twice, and nearly kills her. Austen lets grief have physical consequences so that the reckoning that follows is forced on a body rather than reasoned out at leisure.
themes.development: Wet grass at Cleveland, a putrid fever, a night when Elinor expects her sister to die, and a recovery that produces the novel's only formal self-examination.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Narration that borrows a character's idiom and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.inThisBook: The narration sits mostly with Elinor, so the reader is kept as ignorant as she is and as bound by her discretion; Marianne is largely observed from outside, which is why her feelings arrive as events.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Wording that invites the reader to a judgement the speaker has not made.
techniques.inThisBook: The second chapter is conducted entirely in reasonable-sounding speech, and Austen never once says that John Dashwood is being mean; the arithmetic says it.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: Written documents used as plot, evidence and characterisation.
techniques.inThisBook: Marianne writes three unanswered notes and receives one cold reply that was dictated by another woman, and the physical returning of her letters and a lock of hair is what makes the break public.

techniques.name: Paired plots
techniques.definition: Running two versions of a situation side by side so that each measures the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Both sisters lose a man to a prior claim and a richer woman; one conceals it for four months and one collapses in a ballroom, and the novel refuses to declare a winner.

techniques.name: Embedded histories
techniques.definition: A second, older story told by a character to explain the present one.
techniques.inThisBook: Brandon's account of the two Elizas supplies the consequences the main plot is too polite to stage, and turns Willoughby from a disappointment into a danger.

techniques.name: Dialogue as exposure
techniques.definition: Allowing characters to convict themselves in their own speech.
techniques.inThisBook: Fanny Dashwood argues her husband down from three thousand pounds to nothing in a single conversation, and every step she takes sounds more reasonable than the one before.

quotations.text: possessed a strength of understanding, and coolness of judgment, which qualified her, though only nineteen, to be the counsellor of her mother
quotations.context: The narrator's first account of the eldest Dashwood sister.
quotations.analysis: A nineteen-year-old is described as her mother's counsellor, which characterises the mother as much as the daughter. The nouns are all about control — strength, coolness, judgment — and the clause that follows insists she also has strong feelings, so the novel cannot later be read as praising numbness.

quotations.text: She was sensible and clever; but eager in everything: her sorrows, her joys, could have no moderation. She was generous, amiable, interesting: she was everything but prudent.
quotations.context: The narrator introducing Marianne, immediately after the account of Elinor.
quotations.analysis: Three compliments and then the single withheld word. 'Everything but prudent' concedes that she lacks only one quality and structures the whole plot around its absence, and the list of generous, amiable, interesting is exactly what Willoughby will find useful.

quotations.text: people always live forever when there is an annuity to be paid them; and she is very stout and healthy, and hardly forty. An annuity is a very serious business; it comes over and over every year, and there is no getting rid of it.
quotations.speaker: Fanny Dashwood
quotations.context: Persuading her husband out of the last version of his promise to his dying father.
quotations.analysis: The objection to an annuity is that the recipients will be so inconsiderate as to survive. Notice the shift from a moral question to a bookkeeping one: 'a very serious business' and 'no getting rid of it' are the phrases of a woman describing a liability, and nobody in the room corrects her.

quotations.text: I think very highly of him⁠—that I greatly esteem, that I like him.
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Answering her mother and sister about her feelings for Edward Ferrars.
quotations.analysis: Three verbs in ascending order, each hedged, and none of them the one she means. It is not coldness but accuracy: she has no engagement and no declaration, so she claims only what she can defend — and her sister immediately treats the precision as an insult to love itself.

quotations.text: Esteem him! Like him! Cold-hearted Elinor! Oh! worse than cold-hearted! Ashamed of being otherwise. Use those words again, and I will leave the room this moment.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Bursting out at Elinor's careful account of her feelings for Edward.
quotations.analysis: She repeats her sister's two verbs as though quoting evidence at a trial, and the charge is not that Elinor feels nothing but that she is ashamed to say so. Forty chapters later Marianne will use the same word about her own conduct, and mean the opposite by it.

quotations.text: Oh! happy house, could you know what I suffer in now viewing you from this spot, from whence perhaps I may view you no more!⁠—And you, ye well-known trees!⁠—but you will continue the same.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Walking alone in front of the house on the family's last evening at Norland.
quotations.analysis: She addresses a house and then a stand of trees, and both refuse to answer, which she takes personally. The apostrophe is her method in miniature: feeling counts as real only when it is performed aloud, and the complaint that the trees will continue the same is a complaint that grief has no witness.

quotations.text: with me a flannel waistcoat is invariably connected with aches, cramps, rheumatisms, and every species of ailment that can afflict the old and the feeble.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Rejecting Mrs Jennings's suggestion that Colonel Brandon admires her.
quotations.analysis: A whole character is dismissed on the evidence of one garment, which is precisely the reasoning Marianne uses in the other direction about Willoughby. The novel remembers the joke: the last paragraph about her marriage returns to the flannel waistcoat, and by then the garment has stopped being funny.

quotations.text: with what transporting sensation have I formerly seen them fall! How have I delighted, as I walked, to see them driven in showers about me by the wind! What feelings have they, the season, the air altogether inspired! Now there is no one to regard them. They are seen only as a nuisance, swept hastily off, and driven as much as possible from the sight.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Told by Elinor that the walks at Norland are thick with dead leaves.
quotations.analysis: Three exclamations about her own past sensations, and then a grievance: the leaves are now swept up by people who do not feel them. Elinor's one-line reply, that not everyone shares her passion for dead leaves, is the driest thing she says in the book, and it lands because Marianne has just claimed a monopoly on noticing.

quotations.text: What have wealth or grandeur to do with happiness?
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Objecting to Elinor's remark about the uses of money.
quotations.analysis: A rhetorical question that the plot spends the next thirty chapters answering in detail. Within ten lines Marianne has priced her own competence at about two thousand a year, which is roughly the income of the man she is rejecting as too old.

quotations.text: Your competence and my wealth are very much alike, I dare say; and without them, as the world goes now, we shall both agree that every kind of external comfort must be wanting. Your ideas are only more noble than mine. Come, what is your competence?
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Turning her sister's objection about money into a question with a number in it.
quotations.analysis: The trick is to let Marianne keep the nobler word and then ask her to define it. Austen's characters argue about income the way other novels' characters argue about virtue, and the scene ends with a figure rather than a principle.

quotations.text: We have been engaged these four years.
quotations.speaker: Lucy Steele
quotations.context: Telling Elinor about her engagement to Edward Ferrars, in a conversation Lucy has carefully arranged.
quotations.analysis: Six words, placed after a long approach designed to make Elinor ask for them. The disclosure is an act of aggression disguised as intimacy: once Elinor holds the secret as a confidence, she is the one person in England who cannot use it.

quotations.text: to be as solemnly engaged to him, as if the strictest legal covenant had bound us to each other.
quotations.speaker: Lucy Steele
quotations.context: Marianne, quoting her own understanding of her position with Willoughby after his letter arrives.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a legal instrument, which is exactly what she does not have. A private understanding, however sincere, leaves no document and no claim; Lucy Steele's four-year engagement is equally unwritten and she treats it as property, which is why she wins.

quotations.text: For four months, Marianne, I have had all this hanging on my mind, without being at liberty to speak of it to a single creature; knowing that it would make you and my mother most unhappy whenever it were explained to you
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Telling Marianne, for the first time, how long she has known about Lucy's engagement.
quotations.analysis: The unit is time, not feeling: four months, without liberty to speak, while being told repeatedly that she does not feel enough. The sentence also explains the novel's structure — the reader has been kept inside Elinor's silence too, and only now learns what it weighed.

quotations.text: I acknowledge that her situation and her character ought to have been respected by me. I do not mean to justify myself, but at the same time cannot leave you to suppose that I have nothing to urge⁠—that because she was injured she was irreproachable, and because I was a libertine, she must be a saint.
quotations.speaker: John Willoughby
quotations.context: At Cleveland, at midnight, while Marianne lies dangerously ill upstairs.
quotations.analysis: He concedes the charge and then immediately reopens it, which is the pattern of the whole confession: an apology with a defence folded inside it. 'Because I was a libertine, she must be a saint' is a real argument about evidence, offered by a man who needs it not to be true.

quotations.text: I felt that she was infinitely dearer to me than any other woman
quotations.speaker: John Willoughby
quotations.context: Describing the effect of Marianne's note, received in London after he had decided to marry Miss Grey.
quotations.analysis: The comparative is the problem: she is dearer than other women, and he has already worked out what she is worth against an income. Austen allows the feeling to be genuine precisely so that the novel cannot be read as saying that charming men are simply insincere.

quotations.text: My illness has made me think. It has given me leisure and calmness for serious recollection. Long before I was enough recovered to talk, I was perfectly able to reflect. I considered the past: I saw in my own behaviour, since the beginning of our acquaintance with him last autumn, nothing but a series of imprudence towards myself, and want of kindness to others.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Convalescent at Barton, setting out her own conduct to Elinor.
quotations.analysis: The self-examination is conducted in the vocabulary of accounting — a series, a beginning, a survey of behaviour since last autumn — which is how her sister thinks, not how she does. Note that she blames imprudence and unkindness to others, never the strength of her feelings.

quotations.text: I compare it with what it ought to have been; I compare it with yours.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Refusing Elinor's attempt to excuse her conduct by comparing it with other people's.
quotations.analysis: Two clauses, the second shorter and harder than the first. She adopts an absolute standard and then names a person as its measure, which is the precise reversal of Chapter 4, where the same sister's behaviour was evidence of a cold heart.

quotations.text: I will be calm⁠—I will be mistress of myself.
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Watching from the window as a horseman she takes to be Edward dismounts at the gate.
quotations.analysis: She states self-command as an intention rather than a fact, which is the closest the novel comes to admitting what it has cost her. Two chapters of evidence follow: when Edward's news finally arrives she leaves the room and cries until she thinks she will never stop.

quotations.text: Marianne Dashwood was born to an extraordinary fate. She was born to discover the falsehood of her own opinions, and to counteract, by her conduct, her most favourite maxims. She was born to overcome an affection formed so late in life as at seventeen, and with no sentiment superior to strong esteem and lively friendship, voluntarily to give her hand to another!
quotations.context: The narrator summing up Marianne's marriage to Colonel Brandon.
quotations.analysis: The mock-heroic opening promises a destiny and delivers a list of maxims disproved. 'Born to discover the falsehood of her own opinions' makes the second marriage a correction rather than a reward, and readers have argued ever since about whether the joke is affectionate or a shrug.

quotations.text: among the merits and the happiness of Elinor and Marianne, let it not be ranked as the least considerable, that though sisters, and living almost within sight of each other, they could live without disagreement between themselves, or producing coolness between their husbands.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book closes not on either marriage but on the relation between the sisters, and phrases their achievement in the negative — no disagreement, no coolness. After a plot driven by what one sister could not tell the other, the last thing the novel counts as happiness is two women living within sight of each other and still speaking.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Printed for the author by C. Roworth and published by T. Egerton, Whitehall, in three volumes, 'By A Lady'.

atAGlance.label: Financial risk
atAGlance.note: Austen carried the cost herself and kept the copyright, which is why this novel, unlike Pride and Prejudice, went on earning for her.

atAGlance.label: Earlier form
atAGlance.note: Family tradition remembers an earlier version, probably in letters. No manuscript survives.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The engagement that drives the whole plot is disclosed to Elinor at the end of the first volume and to everyone else in the third.

criticalViews.position: A conduct-novel with a verdict
criticalViews.summary: One long-standing reading takes the title at face value: Marianne's sensibility is a fashionable excess, Elinor's judgement is the corrective, and the plot administers the lesson through illness and a second marriage.
criticalViews.counter: It has to ignore how much the novel charges Elinor for her self-command, and how carefully it refuses to say that Marianne's feelings were themselves the error.

criticalViews.position: A novel about property and dependence
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the opening chapters treats the will, the entail and the annuity conversation as the real engine: the book is about what happens to women whose income is decided by a half-brother's conscience.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far, it reduces both sisters to case studies and has little to say about the comedy, which is where most of Austen's precision actually lives.

criticalViews.position: A study in what may be said aloud
criticalViews.summary: A more formal reading attends to who knows what and when: the novel is organised around secrets, confidences and disclosures, and the reader is held inside Elinor's silence as a technical device rather than a moral example.
criticalViews.counter: This can make the ending feel arbitrary, since the secret is dissolved not by anyone's virtue but by Lucy Steele changing brothers.

essayQuestions.question: Does Sense and Sensibility side with Elinor?
essayQuestions.focus: The title as a contest, and the novel's refusal to hold one
plan: Set out the Chapter 1 contrast precisely: strength of understanding and coolness of judgment against sensible, clever and everything but prudent.
Show what Elinor's method costs in Chapter 37 — four months of silence, and the accusation of feeling nothing from her own sister.
Show what Marianne's method costs at Cleveland, and note that the illness has a physical cause, not a poetic one.
Read Chapter 46 closely: Marianne adopts her sister's standard, and Elinor in Chapter 48 has to announce self-command as an intention rather than possess it.
Conclude on the last sentence, which measures success by the sisters' relation to each other rather than by either temperament winning.

essayQuestions.question: How does Austen use money in the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Wills, annuities, competence and settlements
plan: Begin with Chapter 2 as a set piece: a promise reduced by stages, with every step argued in reasonable language.
Trace the sums that follow — five hundred pounds, a hundred a year, two thousand a year at Delaford — and note that Austen always gives the figure.
Use the competence exchange in Chapter 17 to show the sisters arguing about income in the vocabulary of virtue.
Show money deciding the plot rather than decorating it: Willoughby's debts, Mrs Ferrars's disinheritance, and Brandon's gift of a living.
Weigh whether the ending criticises this economy or simply provides two escapes from it.

essayQuestions.question: Examine the presentation of Willoughby.
essayQuestions.focus: Charm, sincerity and the midnight confession
plan: Establish how his charm works: shared taste in poetry and music, treated by Marianne as proof of shared character.
Set the letter of Chapter 29 beside the man, and note that it was dictated by another woman — his cruelty is partly delegated.
Bring in Brandon's history of the two Elizas, which converts a disappointing suitor into a demonstrable danger.
Read the Chapter 44 confession carefully: the apologies and the self-defences are interleaved, and the feeling is genuine.
Decide what the novel gains by refusing to make him simply insincere, and what it loses.

essayQuestions.question: 'The novel is driven by what cannot be said.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Secrecy, confidence and disclosure
plan: List the withheld information: Lucy's engagement, Brandon's history, Willoughby's debts, Elinor's own attachment.
Show that Lucy's disclosure in Chapter 22 works as a weapon precisely because it is framed as a confidence.
Contrast Marianne, who conceals nothing and is ruined by having no written proof of anything.
Use Mrs Dashwood's refusal to ask a direct question about an engagement as the novel's sharpest criticism of delicacy.
Close on how the secret is finally dissolved — not by honesty, but by Lucy transferring herself to the richer brother.

discussionQuestions: Elinor keeps Lucy's secret for four months because she was told it in confidence. Was she right to?
Marianne marries a man she once mocked for wearing flannel. Is the ending a reward, a compromise or a joke?
Fanny Dashwood is never punished and never in doubt. Why does Austen put her argument at the very front of the book?
Willoughby's remorse is real. Does that make him better or worse?
Mrs Jennings is vulgar and kind; Mr John Dashwood is polite and cold. What is the novel saying about manners?

timeline.label: Jane Austen born at Steventon
timeline.detail: In the Hampshire rectory where she wrote the first versions of three of her six novels.

timeline.label: Elinor and Marianne
timeline.detail: Family tradition places an early version of this story in the mid-1790s, probably told in letters. No manuscript survives.

timeline.label: First Impressions offered to a publisher and refused
timeline.detail: The novel that became Pride and Prejudice was declined unseen, and Austen published nothing for another fourteen years.

timeline.label: The Austens settle at Chawton
timeline.detail: The move to a settled house in Hampshire begins the period in which every one of Austen's novels was revised or written.

timeline.label: Sense and Sensibility published
timeline.detail: Printed for the author by C. Roworth, published by T. Egerton in three volumes, and advertised at fifteen shillings in boards.

timeline.label: The first edition sells out; a second follows
timeline.detail: In the same year Pride and Prejudice appeared as 'by the author of Sense and Sensibility', turning an anonymous debut into a commercial identity.

timeline.label: Mansfield Park published
timeline.detail: The first novel Austen wrote knowing that she had readers.

timeline.label: Austen dies at Winchester
timeline.detail: Aged forty-one, with none of her novels published under her own name.

timeline.label: Bentley's Standard Novels reprint
timeline.detail: Sense and Sensibility re-enters the market in a cheap uniform edition, and Austen's novels stop going out of print.

timeline.label: First BBC television adaptation
timeline.detail: The beginning of a long serial tradition that gives the social network around the sisters more room than a feature film can.

timeline.label: Ang Lee's film, from Emma Thompson's screenplay
timeline.detail: Thompson as Elinor, Kate Winslet as Marianne, Alan Rickman as Brandon; it won the Academy Award for Adapted Screenplay and the Golden Bear at Berlin.

timeline.label: Kandukondain Kandukondain
timeline.detail: Rajiv Menon's Tamil-language film relocates the sisters, the prospects and the delayed recognition to an Indian setting.

timeline.label: BBC serial adapted by Andrew Davies
timeline.detail: A three-part version directed by John Alexander, which restores the seduction plot to its place near the front of the story.

places.name: Sussex
places.note: Norland Park, where the Dashwoods had been settled for generations and lived for a single year as guests of the heir.

places.name: Devonshire
places.note: Barton Cottage and Barton Park: a house taken on very easy terms from a relation, which is a polite name for charity.

places.name: London
places.note: Berkeley Street and the drawing rooms where Marianne waits for a reply, and is cut in public when it comes.

places.name: Somersetshire
