places.note: Combe Magna, Willoughby's own small estate, and Cleveland, where Marianne walks in wet grass until she is dangerously ill.

places.name: Dorsetshire
places.note: Delaford, Colonel Brandon's property, with the living he gives away and the mulberry tree Mrs Jennings cannot stop describing.

places.name: Plymouth
places.note: Where the Steele sisters have their connections, and the town whose name is enough to place them socially the moment it is mentioned.

related.why: Written from the same drafts and the same decade, with the comedy pitched higher and the money kept just as visible.
Another dependent young woman with no property and a prior claim standing between her and the man she wants.
Marianne's question about what feeling is owed to convention, asked again eighty years later and answered far more bleakly.
Sensibility taken to the point where it stops being a temperament and becomes a force that wrecks two households.
Fanny Dashwood's arithmetic turned into farce, with incomes and connections interrogated out loud.

books.title: The Merchant of Venice
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Venice — the Rialto, a private house, a court of justice — and Belmont, a country estate a day's journey away
books.lengthNote: Around 2,600 lines, of which the trial takes nearly four hundred
books.openingLine: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
books.summary: A merchant borrows money he does not need, on terms he thinks are a joke, so that a friend can go courting. The comedy that follows has a courtroom at its centre, and the clever rescue there is also a confiscation: Shylock loses his money, his profession and his religion in the space of forty lines, and the play then moves to a moonlit garden and refuses to mention him again.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Merchant of Venice
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts the prose scenes continuously. Modern editions vary.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A sad merchant, a locked test, and a bond made in jest
structure.summary: Antonio cannot say why he is unhappy. Bassanio needs money to court an heiress whose father has left her unable to choose her own husband, and Shylock lends it on a forfeit of a pound of flesh — proposed, and accepted, as a piece of friendly humour by men who have just insulted each other.

scenes.title: The Rialto
scenes.summary: Antonio's friends try to explain his melancholy; Bassanio asks for a further loan to go to Belmont.

scenes.title: The will of a dead father
scenes.summary: Portia reviews her suitors with Nerissa and complains of a lottery she cannot refuse.

scenes.title: The merry bond
scenes.summary: Shylock recalls years of public abuse, then lends interest-free against a pound of Antonio's flesh.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Two wrong caskets and a daughter gone
structure.summary: Morocco and Arragon choose gold and silver and are beaten by their own assumptions about worth. In Venice, Jessica leaves her father's house dressed as a boy, taking money and jewels with her, and the Christian gentlemen of the Rialto turn Shylock's public grief into a street entertainment.

scenes.title: Morocco arrives
scenes.summary: He asks not to be judged by his complexion and is told the terms of the lottery.

scenes.title: Launcelot changes master
scenes.summary: The clown argues with his own conscience and leaves Shylock for Bassanio.

scenes.title: Jessica's plan
scenes.summary: She calls her father's house hell and asks Launcelot to carry a letter to Lorenzo.

scenes.title: The masque
scenes.summary: Lorenzo learns what gold and jewels she will bring with her.

scenes.title: Locking up
scenes.summary: Shylock, going out to supper against his judgement, tells Jessica to shut the windows.

scenes.title: The elopement
scenes.summary: Jessica throws down a casket and escapes in boy's clothes, ashamed of the disguise.

scenes.title: Gold
scenes.summary: Morocco opens the golden casket and finds a skull and a rhyme about glittering.

scenes.title: Reported grief
scenes.summary: Salanio performs Shylock's cries about his daughter and his ducats for laughs.

scenes.title: Silver
scenes.summary: Arragon takes what he deserves and is handed the portrait of a blinking idiot.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Lead won, ships lost, and a speech about eyes
structure.summary: Bassanio rejects ornament, chooses lead and wins Portia within the hour. In the same act Shylock, taunted in the street about his daughter, answers with the play's most famous demand for common humanity and ends it by promising revenge. News arrives that Antonio's ships are gone.

scenes.title: On the Rialto
scenes.summary: Salarino and Salanio bait Shylock; Tubal brings news of Jessica's spending and of a wrecked argosy.

scenes.title: Lead
scenes.summary: Bassanio chooses correctly; the rings are given; a letter from Antonio interrupts the betrothal.

scenes.title: No more speaking
scenes.summary: Shylock refuses to hear Antonio and repeats that he will have his bond.

scenes.title: Padua
scenes.summary: Portia sends for legal papers from Doctor Bellario and tells Nerissa they will go disguised.

scenes.title: Salvation and bacon
scenes.summary: Launcelot jokes that converting Jews will raise the price of pork; Jessica changes the subject.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The court, and what mercy turns out to mean
structure.summary: The longest scene in the play. Shylock refuses three times the money, Portia arrives disguised as a lawyer from Padua and preaches mercy, and then wins by reading the bond more strictly than its holder. Within forty lines Shylock has lost his estate, his livelihood and his religion.

scenes.title: The trial
scenes.summary: Mercy is argued, the bond is enforced to the letter, and an alien statute is produced against the plaintiff.

scenes.title: The rings
scenes.summary: Portia and Nerissa, still disguised, collect the rings their husbands swore never to part with.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Music at Belmont, and one man missing
structure.summary: Lorenzo and Jessica trade stories of lovers who came to bad ends, the wives expose the business of the rings, and Antonio learns that three of his ships are safe after all. Shylock is not mentioned. The comedy closes with everybody paired except the merchant it is named after.

scenes.title: Moonlight
scenes.summary: Music, the ring quarrel, the revelation of the disguise, and news that Antonio's argosies have come home.

characters.name: Shylock
characters.summary: He appears in five scenes and dominates the play. Shakespeare gives him the abuse he has taken in detail — the spitting, the name-calling, the kicks — and then has him turn that history into a legal instrument. The play neither excuses what he does nor lets his enemies off the account he reads them.
characters.clue: He keeps a ledger of insults as exactly as one of debts, asks whether a dog has money, and leaves the stage saying he is not well.

characters.name: Portia
characters.summary: Rich, quick and confined: her father's will means she may neither choose nor refuse. She takes the only freedom available by leaving Belmont in a man's gown, and the same intelligence that saves Antonio is later used to trap her own husband over a ring.
characters.clue: She may neither choose a husband nor refuse one, so she borrows a lawyer's gown from Padua and wins the biggest case in Venice.
traits: less merciful than her own speech

relationships.label: rescuer of, and rival for Bassanio
prosecutes in the guise of defending

characters.name: Antonio
characters.summary: The title character speaks the first line of the play and almost nothing in the last scene. His sadness is never explained; his willingness to die for Bassanio is stated plainly, and so is his intention to go on spitting on Shylock. He is the only major figure who ends the play unpaired.
characters.clue: He opens the play saying he does not know why he is sad, offers his own body as security for a friend's courtship, and ends it the only one without a partner.

characters.name: Bassanio
characters.summary: He has run through his money and proposes to repair it by marrying a fortune, which he explains to Antonio without embarrassment. His casket speech rejects outward show in terms that apply uncomfortably well to his own courtship, financed by a borrowed appearance of wealth.
characters.clue: He argues that the world is deceived by ornament while wearing clothes bought with a friend's borrowed money.

characters.name: Jessica
characters.summary: She robs her father, sells her mother's ring for a monkey, and converts. Shakespeare gives her the discomfort as well as the escape: she is ashamed of her boy's clothes, and in the last act she and Lorenzo exchange a string of stories about lovers whose nights ended badly.
characters.clue: She leaves her father's house in a boy's coat with his ducats in a casket, and spends the last act naming lovers who came to grief.

characters.name: Lorenzo
characters.role: A friend of Bassanio and Antonio
characters.summary: He plans the elopement as a raid, is pleased about the gold, and then speaks the play's most beautiful verse about music and the harmony of the spheres. The distance between those two facts is one of the things the last act is for.
characters.clue: He organises a theft and an elopement in the same breath, and later explains that a man with no music in him is fit for treasons.

characters.name: Nerissa
characters.summary: She doubles Portia at every level: she gives the sceptical answer in 1.2, marries the friend rather than the principal, disguises herself as a clerk, and runs the same trick with the same ring. The play works by these pairings, and she is the clearest of them.
characters.clue: She dresses as a lawyer's clerk, marries the friend rather than the hero, and plays the ring trick a second time.

characters.name: Gratiano
characters.summary: Bassanio says he speaks an infinite deal of nothing, and for three acts that is a joke about a harmless talker. In the courtroom he becomes the voice that cheers each reversal and asks for Shylock to be hanged, which is where the comic licence stops being comic.
characters.clue: A friend says he speaks an infinite deal of nothing; in court he applauds every turn of the verdict and offers the defeated man a free halter.

themes.name: Bonds and binding
themes.summary: The word runs through every plot in the play: a bond is a loan agreement, a tie of friendship, a marriage, a ring, and finally a piece of writing that can take a man's life. Venice runs on written obligation, and the tragedy is that Shylock is the only character who treats the writing as meaning exactly what it says.
themes.development: A bond is sealed in 1.3, tested in 4.1 and replaced in 5.1 by a ring — which is another bond, and also broken.

themes.name: Mercy and justice
themes.summary: Portia's argument is that mercy cannot be compelled, which is true, and she then compels Shylock into receiving it. The court offers him his life on condition that he give up his religion, and calls that leniency. The play stages the gap between the doctrine and the settlement enacted in its name.
themes.development: Mercy is preached at 4.1.191, refused by Shylock at 4.1.213, and delivered at 4.1.396 as a set of conditions including forced conversion.

themes.name: Antisemitism and the outsider
themes.summary: The Christians of Venice call Shylock dog, devil and cur to his face and in his absence, and Antonio says plainly that he will do it again. The play lets Shylock answer, at length and in prose, and then ends with his enemies in a garden and his name unmentioned.
themes.development: The abuse is itemised by its victim in 1.3, answered in 3.1, and given legal form in 4.1, where an alien is found to have no standing against a citizen.

themes.name: Worth, ornament and risk
themes.summary: Three caskets ask what a thing is worth; three suitors answer with what they think they deserve. The same question runs through the merchant plot, where ships are venture capital and a pound of flesh is valued, out loud, against mutton and beef.
themes.development: Morocco buys the outside, Arragon buys his own merit, Bassanio buys the risk — and the man who has hazarded everything has borrowed the stake.

themes.name: Friendship, marriage and rivalry
themes.summary: Antonio's feeling for Bassanio is the strongest attachment in the play and has no name available to it. Portia understands the competition exactly, which is why the ring she gives her husband is the one thing she makes him swear never to surrender, and why she has it taken from him in a courtroom.
themes.development: Antonio offers his body for Bassanio in Act I, is outbid in Act IV when Bassanio says he would give up his wife to save him, and is given a ring to return in Act V.

themes.name: Disguise and the law
themes.summary: Nothing in the trial scene is what it appears: the lawyer is a woman, the clerk is her maid, the mercy is a threat and the rescue is a confiscation. Belmont's women enter the Venetian court by the only door available to them and leave it having beaten the men at their own document.
themes.development: Jessica's boy's clothes in Act II rehearse the device; Portia's gown in Act IV makes it the machinery of the plot.

techniques.name: The legal quibble
techniques.definition: A judgment that turns on the exact words of a document rather than its evident intention.
techniques.inThisBook: Portia defeats the bond by noting that it grants flesh and says nothing of blood — a stricter reading than Shylock's own, delivered by someone who has just argued that strictness damns us all.

techniques.name: Parallel plotting
techniques.definition: Two or more actions built on the same shape, so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: The caskets, the bond and the rings are all tests in which a man must choose what to give up, and all three are set by someone with more control than he realises.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: The shift between unmetered speech and blank verse as a marker of register, class or feeling.
techniques.inThisBook: Shylock's great answer to Salarino is in prose, which is what gives it the sound of a man speaking rather than performing; Portia's mercy speech is verse, and sounds like a set piece because it is one.

techniques.name: Accumulated rhetorical questions
techniques.definition: A run of questions whose answers are obvious, used to make denial impossible.
techniques.inThisBook: Eyes, hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions: the questions pile up until the last one changes direction and asks about revenge instead of about bleeding.

techniques.name: Flesh and blood
techniques.definition: A physical image repeated until it binds unrelated scenes together.
techniques.inThisBook: The bond's pound of flesh is only the plainest instance; Shylock calls Jessica his own flesh and blood, and the court eventually divides his property along the same line between body and estate.

techniques.name: Scriptural argument
techniques.definition: Quoting or contesting scripture as a way of settling a dispute.
techniques.inThisBook: Shylock and Antonio argue over Jacob's sheep in 1.3, each claiming the Old Testament, and Portia's mercy speech borrows the language of the Lord's Prayer to address a man who does not say it.

quotations.text: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: The opening line of the play, to Salarino and Salanio on the Rialto.
quotations.analysis: A comedy begins with a man announcing an unexplained depression, and the play never supplies the explanation — his friends propose his ships and then love, and he denies both. The refusal to account for it leaves a hole at the centre of the title role that every production has to fill with something.

quotations.text: so is the will of a living daughter curbed by the will of a dead father
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: In prose to Nerissa, listing the suitors she cannot refuse.
quotations.analysis: The sentence turns on one word used twice: 'will' as desire and 'will' as legal document. Portia's problem is stated as a pun, which is a warning about the kind of play this is — the trial in Act IV will also be won by a word that carries two meanings at once.

quotations.text: Still have I borne it with a patient shrug, For sufferance is the badge of all our tribe.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Answering Antonio's request for a loan by recalling how Antonio has treated him.
quotations.analysis: A badge in Venice was not a metaphor: Jews were required to wear identifying marks, and Shylock takes that fact and makes endurance itself the uniform. The shrug is the detail that does the work — a small physical gesture, repeated over years, standing in for everything he has swallowed.

quotations.text: 'Hath a dog money? is it possible A cur can lend three thousand ducats?'
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Quoting back to Antonio the names Antonio has called him.
quotations.analysis: He performs the insult rather than complaining of it, putting Antonio's own vocabulary into a speech Antonio has to stand and listen to. Quotation marks are a weapon here: the abuse is returned intact, with the arithmetic of the loan sitting inside it.

quotations.text: I am as like to call thee so again, To spit on thee again, to spurn thee too.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: His reply, immediately before asking for the loan anyway.
quotations.analysis: He does not deny a word of the account; he promises to repeat it. The couplet is the reason the bond is not simply a piece of villainy — the borrower has just told the lender to his face that nothing will change, and then asks to be lent the money as to an enemy.

quotations.text: Give him direction for this merry bond,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Sending Antonio to the notary to seal the agreement.
quotations.analysis: 'Merry' is doing a great deal of work, and nobody in the scene challenges it. The forfeit is framed as a joke between men who have just exchanged threats, which is exactly what allows Antonio to sign it: a penalty that cannot be meant does not need to be feared.

quotations.text: Hie thee, gentle Jew. The Hebrew will turn Christian: he grows kind.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: As Shylock leaves to fetch the ducats.
quotations.analysis: 'Gentle' and 'gentile' were near-homophones, so the compliment is also a joke about conversion — and the joke turns out to be a prophecy the court will enforce at knife-point in Act IV. Antonio can praise the man only by imagining him becoming someone else.

quotations.text: Our house is hell, and thou, a merry devil, Didst rob it of some taste of tediousness.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Saying goodbye to Launcelot, who is leaving her father's service.
quotations.analysis: Her complaint is not cruelty but dullness — the house is hell because it is tedious, and the clown made it bearable. It is the only account the play gives of what living with Shylock was like, and it comes from someone about to rob him.

quotations.text: All that glitters is not gold; Often have you heard that told: Many a man his life hath sold But my outside to behold:
quotations.speaker: Morocco
quotations.context: Reading the scroll found inside the golden casket, beside a skull.
quotations.analysis: The verse is in short rhyming lines, a nursery metre for a lesson everybody claims to know already, and the casket answers in the first person as though the gold were speaking. Morocco has just argued himself into gold by reasoning about what the world values — the scroll's point is that he was reasoning at all.

quotations.text: 'My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter! Fled with a Christian! O my Christian ducats!
quotations.speaker: Salanio
quotations.context: Salanio and Salarino imitating Shylock's behaviour in the street after Jessica's flight.
quotations.analysis: The audience never sees Shylock discover the loss; it is reported as an impersonation by a man doing the voice for a laugh. Whether the alternation of daughter and ducats is grief or greed depends entirely on how far you trust the reporter, and the play deliberately gives you no other witness.

quotations.text: I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer, as a Christian is?
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: In the street, to Salarino, who has just asked what a pound of flesh is good for.
quotations.analysis: The argument is built entirely on the body, not on doctrine, and the repetitions of 'the same' make the shared ground impossible to refuse. It is in prose, which is why it sounds like a man talking rather than a set speech, and its logic is deliberately unfinished — everything so far has been about suffering, and the next sentence will apply the same equality to revenge.

quotations.text: The villany you teach me, I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, after the questions about bleeding and laughing.
quotations.analysis: He claims to be a pupil, which puts the responsibility on the teachers and leaves him doing the thing anyway. 'Better the instruction' is the sentence's cold centre: he intends not merely to match Christian revenge but to improve on it, and the play holds him to that promise in the courtroom.

quotations.text: So may the outward shows be least themselves: The world is still deceived with ornament.
quotations.speaker: Bassanio
quotations.context: Deliberating in front of the three caskets at Belmont.
quotations.analysis: He wins by distrusting appearances, having arrived in Belmont on borrowed money precisely in order to look the part. 'Still' means always, and the line indicts a world Bassanio has been working rather successfully; the play lets him say the true thing without noticing that it applies to him.

quotations.text: Which is the merchant here, and which the Jew?
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Her first words on entering the court in the gown of a doctor of laws.
quotations.analysis: The question establishes her impartiality and is also unanswerable by sight, which is the play's point about what Venice thinks it can see. She already knows which is which, so the line is a performance of neutrality by the one person in the room who has come to win.

quotations.text: The quality of mercy is not strain'd, It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven Upon the place beneath: it is twice blest; It blesseth him that gives and him that takes:
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Answering Shylock's question: on what compulsion must he be merciful?
quotations.analysis: The whole speech depends on mercy being uncompelled, which is a direct answer to the word 'compulsion' in Shylock's question. What follows in the scene contradicts it: the court will compel mercy out of Shylock at the price of his religion, and the word for what he receives will still be mercy.

quotations.text: My deeds upon my head! I crave the law,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Refusing Portia's appeal and asking for judgment on the bond.
quotations.analysis: He takes the consequences onto himself in the words of a formula that Shakespeare's audience would have heard as an echo of the Gospel account of Christ's condemnation, and which was used for centuries to justify persecution. Giving Shylock that sentence is the harshest thing the play does to him, and he says it in the act of asking only for what he is owed.

quotations.text: Tarry a little; there is something else. This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood; The words expressly are 'a pound of flesh:'
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Stopping Shylock as he prepares to cut.
quotations.analysis: She has let the case run to the point of the knife before producing the objection, which means the trap was set several hundred lines earlier. Her method is not mercy but a stricter literalism than Shylock's own: he asked for what the words say, and she gives him exactly that and no more.

quotations.text: Nay, take my life and all; pardon not that: You take my house when you do take the prop That doth sustain my house; you take my life When you do take the means whereby I live.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: After the court has divided his estate and offered to commute the fine.
quotations.analysis: The repetition of 'take' four times in four lines turns the verdict into an inventory. He refuses the distinction the court is congratulating itself on — between killing a man and removing his livelihood — and the play gives him the argument without letting him win it.

quotations.text: Two things provided more, that, for this favour, He presently become a Christian;
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Stating his terms for giving up his half of Shylock's goods.
quotations.analysis: It is called a favour, and it is attached as a condition to a pardon Shylock cannot refuse. 'Presently' means at once: the man who has just been prevented from taking a pound of flesh is required to change religion on the spot, and the scene treats this as the merciful outcome.

quotations.text: I am content.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Asked by Portia whether he accepts the court's terms.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and then four more lines asking to be allowed to leave because he is not well. Antonio had used the same phrase twelve lines earlier while dictating the terms, so the play puts the identical sentence in two mouths in one scene and lets the difference between them stand without comment.

quotations.text: How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank! Here will we sit and let the sounds of music Creep in our ears:
quotations.speaker: Lorenzo
quotations.context: In the garden at Belmont with Jessica, waiting for Portia's return.
quotations.analysis: The last act opens by changing the weather completely: after four hundred lines of courtroom prose the play produces its most lyrical verse, and does it in the mouth of the man who organised the elopement and the theft. Shakespeare buys the comedy its ending with music, and the person who says she is never merry when she hears it is sitting next to him.

quotations.text: I am never merry when I hear sweet music.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Her reply to Lorenzo's account of music's power over wild animals.
quotations.analysis: It is the last thing she says in the play. Lorenzo talks her out of it immediately, explaining that attentiveness only looks like sadness, and she does not answer — a silence that productions can play as agreement, exhaustion or something colder.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Topical references and the style of the verse place composition in the later 1590s.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The First Quarto, which remains the basis of most modern editions.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: The bond, the trial and the disguised lady-lawyer come from a tale in Ser Giovanni Fiorentino's Italian collection.

atAGlance.label: At court
atAGlance.note: The first recorded performance was on 10 February 1605, and the play was repeated before the court two days later.

criticalViews.position: A romantic comedy with an obstacle
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the play's business is three marriages and a rescue, Shylock is the blocking figure whom comedy must remove, and Act V is the proper ending rather than an evasion.
criticalViews.counter: It requires the audience to accept a forced conversion as a happy outcome, and it cannot explain why Shakespeare gave the obstacle the best prose in the play.

criticalViews.position: A play whose antisemitism is its subject rather than its accident
criticalViews.summary: Much modern criticism argues that the Christians are shown behaving exactly as Shylock describes them — spitting, mocking, confiscating — so that the comedy is built to expose the society it flatters.
criticalViews.counter: The play still ends in that society's garden, with its victim offstage, and the text nowhere condemns what the court does.

criticalViews.position: A study of contract and obligation
criticalViews.summary: Bonds, wills, caskets and rings are all binding documents, and the play tests what happens when a written promise meets the intention behind it. The trial is then less about race than about how far a society will honour its own paperwork.
criticalViews.counter: The verdict turns on a statute about aliens, which makes Shylock's standing under Venetian law inseparable from his religion.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present Shylock?
essayQuestions.focus: Sympathy, hostility and the limits of both
plan: Note first that he appears in only five scenes and never speaks after 4.1.412.
Use 1.3 to show him giving an itemised account of the abuse, and Antonio confirming every word of it.
Read 3.1 carefully: the questions establish common humanity, and the same logic then licenses revenge.
Set the reported grief of 2.8 against the direct speech of 4.1.388 and ask which the audience is allowed to trust.
Close on his exit line and on the fact that Act V does not mention him.

essayQuestions.question: 'Mercy in this play is something the powerful do to the powerless.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Justice, law and the trial scene
plan: Begin with Shylock's question at 4.1.190 — on what compulsion? — and show that Portia's speech is a direct answer to it.
Trace the reversal: mercy preached, refused, then imposed as a set of conditions at 4.1.394-404.
Examine the alien statute and what it says about who counts as a citizen of Venice.
Weigh Antonio's terms, including the conversion, against his conduct in 1.3.
Decide whether the play endorses the verdict, exposes it, or simply stages it and moves on.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Belmont?
essayQuestions.focus: Place, wealth and the structure of the play
plan: Set out the alternation: Venice for business and law, Belmont for music, riddles and marriage.
Show that Belmont is also governed by a document — a dead man's will — and so is less free than it looks.
Use the casket scenes to argue that the two worlds share one question: how do you value what you cannot see?
Note that Portia's money resolves nothing in Venice; it is her legal reading that wins.
Judge whether Act V restores Belmont or merely relocates the play's unfinished business.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of women in The Merchant of Venice.
essayQuestions.focus: Portia, Nerissa, Jessica and the uses of disguise
plan: Start from the constraint: Portia cannot choose, Jessica is locked in, Nerissa marries where her mistress does.
Show disguise as the only available instrument — a boy's coat for one, a doctor's gown for another.
Read the trial as Portia acquiring, temporarily, a competence the play otherwise reserves for men.
Use the ring plot to argue that she brings the courtroom's methods home with her.
Ask what happens to that competence in Act V, when the gowns come off.

discussionQuestions: Antonio never explains his sadness. Should a production decide what it is?
Shylock's greatest speech ends by promising revenge. Does that ending change what the speech is worth?
Portia argues that mercy cannot be compelled, and then compels it. Is she a hypocrite, or is the court?
Jessica's last line is that she is never merry when she hears sweet music. What should she do for the rest of the scene?
The play is classed as a comedy. What would have to change for it to be a tragedy?

timeline.label: Il Pecorone reaches print
timeline.detail: Ser Giovanni Fiorentino's fourteenth-century collection contains the bond, the trial and the lady disguised as a lawyer.

timeline.label: Roderigo Lopez is executed in London
timeline.detail: The queen's Portuguese physician, of Jewish descent, was convicted of conspiracy; the trial fed a wave of public feeling in the years just before the play.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: Registered to James Roberts as the Merchant of Venice, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: The earliest printed text, and the basis of most modern editions.

timeline.label: Performed at court
timeline.detail: The first recorded performance, on 10 February, with a repeat before the court two days later.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, following the quarto text closely.

timeline.label: Charles Macklin plays Shylock at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: He abandoned the comic red wig of the Restoration stage and played the part seriously, which changed the play's reputation.

timeline.label: Edmund Kean's London debut as Shylock
timeline.detail: A performance that made the moneylender a figure of tragic force rather than a stage villain.

timeline.label: Henry Irving's Shylock at the Lyceum
timeline.detail: Irving's dignified, sympathetic reading dominated the late Victorian stage and shaped expectations for decades.

timeline.label: Michael Radford's film
timeline.detail: A screen version set in a carefully reconstructed Venice, with Al Pacino as Shylock and an opening sequence about the ghetto.

places.name: Venice
places.note: The city of the bond, the street insults and the court of justice.

places.name: The Rialto
places.note: The commercial exchange where news of ships travels and where Antonio has abused Shylock in public.

places.name: Genoa
places.note: Where Tubal reports Jessica spending her father's ducats and trading her mother's ring.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Home of Doctor Bellario, whose legal opinion and borrowed credentials get Portia into the courtroom.

places.name: Tripoli
places.note: One of the ports named for Antonio's argosies, and the destination of the ship reported lost.

related.why: The other Venetian play, and the other outsider whom the city uses and then discards.
A comedy that also stops for a long argument about mercy and the letter of the law, and also ends in silence.
Another heroine who puts on a man's clothes, with the same interest in what a disguise makes possible.
The other great breeches role of these years, and a comic world built on the same device pushed in the opposite direction.
A comedy of the same period that turns for a whole act into something close to tragedy before recovering.

books.title: The Tempest
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: A ship in a storm, then an unnamed island, across a single afternoon
books.lengthNote: Around 2,000 lines — one of the shortest plays in the Folio
books.summary: A magician who was once Duke of Milan raises a storm to bring his enemies ashore on the island where he has lived in exile for twelve years. He has the whole afternoon planned before the play begins, and the interest lies in watching a man with absolute power discover what he actually wants to do with it. Almost alone among Shakespeare's plays it keeps to a single place and a few hours, so that the action and the performance take roughly the same time.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Tempest
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering; modern editions differ by a line or two. Ariel's songs are printed inside another speaker's text in some settings, and are attributed here to Ariel.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A storm, and the twelve years behind it
structure.summary: The shipwreck is staged first and explained second. Prospero then tells Miranda the history she has never been told, wakes and dispatches Ariel, insults Caliban, and steers Ferdinand into meeting his daughter — four interviews in one scene, each conducted by a man who already knows how it ends.

scenes.title: The ship
scenes.summary: Courtiers get in the way of the crew; the Boatswain tells them rank means nothing to the weather.

scenes.title: The island
scenes.summary: Prospero recounts the usurpation to Miranda, sets Ariel back to work, curses Caliban and arranges Ferdinand's arrival.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Two conspiracies, one serious and one drunk
structure.summary: On one part of the island Gonzalo imagines a commonwealth with no trade, law or labour and is mocked for it; within fifty lines Antonio has talked Sebastian into murdering his brother. On another, Caliban meets a butler with a bottle and decides that a new master is the same thing as freedom.

scenes.title: The courtiers
scenes.summary: Gonzalo's utopia is laughed down; Antonio persuades Sebastian to kill the sleeping Alonso, and Ariel wakes them.

scenes.title: The bottle
scenes.summary: Trinculo shelters under Caliban's cloak, Stephano arrives with wine, and Caliban swears allegiance to a drunkard.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A betrothal, a plot and a banquet that vanishes
structure.summary: Miranda proposes marriage to Ferdinand while her father watches unseen. Caliban lays out a workable murder — take the books first — and is repeatedly interrupted by Ariel's mimicry. The act ends with the courtiers accused of their old crime by a spirit dressed as a harpy.

scenes.title: The log-pile
scenes.summary: Ferdinand carries wood; Miranda offers herself as wife, and Prospero approves from a distance.

scenes.title: The conspiracy
scenes.summary: Caliban explains how to kill Prospero; Ariel sows confusion by throwing his voice.

scenes.title: The harpy
scenes.summary: A banquet appears and disappears; Ariel indicts Alonso, Antonio and Sebastian to their faces.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A masque, broken off
structure.summary: Prospero gives the young couple a wedding entertainment performed by spirits, and then stops it mid-dance because he has remembered Caliban. The interruption is the hinge of the play: the most beautiful thing he makes is abandoned because of the one creature he cannot govern by art.

scenes.title: The masque and the line of clothes
scenes.summary: Iris, Ceres and Juno bless the betrothal; Prospero breaks off the show, then traps the conspirators with a rack of glittering clothes.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Forgiveness, and the end of the magic
structure.summary: Ariel describes the suffering of the charmed courtiers and Prospero chooses mercy — before he has heard a word of apology from any of them. He abjures his art, restores Ferdinand to his father, claims Caliban as his own, frees Ariel, and steps forward to ask the audience for release.

scenes.title: The circle, and the epilogue
scenes.summary: Prospero breaks his staff, forgives his brother, discovers the lovers at chess, frees Ariel and asks for applause as absolution.

characters.name: Prospero
characters.role: The exiled Duke of Milan, and the island's magician
characters.summary: He lost a dukedom by preferring his library to government and has spent twelve years acquiring a power no government could match. Almost every event in the play is something he has arranged, which makes the one decision he has not rehearsed — to forgive rather than punish — the only genuine action in it.
characters.clue: A scholar who lost a dukedom to his own reading, and who runs an island the way a director runs a rehearsal room, down to the storm.

characters.name: Miranda
characters.summary: She has met three people in her life and remembers none of her own history until her father decides she should. Her instincts are consistently better than his: she pities the shipwrecked before she knows who they are, and she proposes marriage herself rather than waiting to be arranged into it.
characters.clue: She has seen three human faces in her life, weeps for strangers drowning, and asks a log-carrier to marry her before he can ask her.

characters.name: Ariel
characters.role: A spirit of the air, bound to Prospero's service
characters.summary: Everything the audience calls Prospero's magic is in fact Ariel's labour: the storm, the songs, the harpy, the masque, the invisible mischief. The relationship runs on a promise of freedom that is repeatedly deferred, and the play's most surprising moment is Ariel telling a human what pity would look like.
characters.clue: Invisible, tireless and unpaid: the one who actually raises the storm, sings the drowned father's song and asks, again, when the promise will be kept.

characters.name: Caliban
characters.role: Son of the witch Sycorax; the island's earlier inhabitant
characters.summary: He welcomed Prospero, showed him the fresh water and the fertile ground, and was enslaved for it after attempting to rape Miranda. The play gives him the case against his master and the best verse about the island, and then refuses to let either cancel the other out.
characters.clue: He showed the newcomer where the fresh springs were and has been carrying his firewood ever since; he speaks the loveliest lines about the island he says is his.

characters.name: Ferdinand
characters.summary: He is separated from the ship, told his father has drowned, and set to carrying logs — a trial that has no purpose except to make Miranda seem hard-won. He accepts the labour without complaint, which is the only test Prospero can devise and the only one he passes.

characters.name: Alonso
characters.summary: He put Antonio into Prospero's dukedom and spends the play believing he has lost his son as a consequence. Grief, not argument, is what breaks him: by Act V he is the only one of the three guilty men who says anything resembling an apology.

characters.name: Antonio
characters.role: Prospero's brother, the usurping Duke of Milan
characters.summary: He took a dukedom once and, within an hour of washing ashore, is arranging a second murder for someone else's benefit. He is forgiven in the last scene and does not reply, a silence that most productions have to make a decision about.
characters.clue: He took his brother's title while the man was reading, and washes ashore only to start talking another younger brother into the same crime.

characters.name: Sebastian
characters.summary: A mocker of other men's speeches who turns out to need only one conversation to be talked into killing his sleeping brother. He is the proof that Antonio's crime was not a single aberration but a piece of ordinary political reasoning.

characters.name: Gonzalo
characters.summary: He is the reason Prospero survived: he stocked the leaking boat with food, water and the books. His imagined commonwealth without money or magistrates is mocked on stage as nonsense, and it is also the only vision in the play of an island run by nobody.

characters.name: Stephano
characters.role: Alonso's butler, washed ashore with a butt of wine
characters.summary: Given a bottle and a worshipper, he declares himself king of the island within a scene. His plot against Prospero is the same plot as Antonio's, played by a drunk, and the parallel is the play's sharpest joke about how little ambition requires.

themes.name: Rule and service
themes.summary: Every relationship on the island is a version of master and servant: Prospero and Ariel, Prospero and Caliban, Prospero and Ferdinand at the log-pile, Stephano and his new subject. The play sets them side by side so that the differences between labour, slavery, apprenticeship and worship become visible.
themes.development: The first act establishes three servants with three grievances; the last frees one, claims another and says nothing at all about the third.

themes.name: Whose island is it
themes.summary: Caliban's claim is stated plainly in the first act and never refuted, only overruled. Shakespeare gives the dispossessed party the historical facts and the finest description of the place, and gives the occupier the power, which is why the play has been unignorable in the century of decolonisation.
themes.development: 'This island's mine' in 1.2 sets the terms; Gonzalo's commonwealth in 2.1 imagines an island belonging to nobody; the play ends without saying who is left on it.

themes.name: Magic as theatre
themes.summary: Prospero's art is indistinguishable from stagecraft: costumes, music, entrances, illusions, an interrupted masque. When he describes his own show dissolving he uses the words 'the great globe itself', spoken in a theatre of that name, and the metaphor stops being a metaphor.
themes.development: The storm is staged in 1.1, exposed as a production in 1.2, perfected in the masque of 4.1, renounced in 5.1, and handed to the audience in the epilogue.

themes.name: Freedom and what is mistaken for it
themes.summary: Three characters want to be free and each means something different by it: Ariel wants release from service, Caliban wants his island back, and Stephano's crew want a bottle and a crown. The play is careful to make the drunkards' freedom song ridiculous without making Caliban's demand ridiculous.
themes.development: Ariel asks in 1.2 and is refused; Caliban sings of a new master in 2.2; Ariel is released in the last twenty lines, and Prospero then asks to be freed himself.

themes.name: Revenge given up
themes.summary: Prospero has the power to do anything he likes to the men who ruined him, and the decisive scene is the one in which he decides not to. What makes it strange is the timing: he chooses mercy after a spirit has described their suffering to him, and before any of them has asked for it.
themes.development: Twelve years of grievance are recited in 1.2; the harpy indicts the guilty in 3.3; 5.1 turns on Ariel's remark that he would feel pity if he were human.

themes.name: Nature and nurture
themes.summary: Prospero insists that Caliban is a devil on whom nurture will never stick, having spent years teaching him. Miranda, raised on the same island by the same man with the same books, is his counter-example, and the play leaves the argument standing unresolved between them.
themes.development: Caliban is taught language in 1.2 and uses it to curse; Prospero's verdict comes in 4.1; the masque of Ceres and Juno makes fertility itself a thing to be blessed and supervised.

techniques.name: Retrospective exposition
techniques.definition: Putting the backstory into a single long scene of telling rather than showing.
techniques.inThisBook: Act I Scene 2 is nearly a third of the play and consists largely of Prospero explaining the past to people who interrupt him. Because he controls what is told and when, the exposition is also a demonstration of his character.

techniques.name: The court masque
techniques.definition: A courtly entertainment of gods, song, dance and blessing, staged for an occasion rather than a plot.
techniques.inThisBook: The betrothal masque of 4.1 imports an entire Jacobean art form into the play and then breaks it off in the middle, which no masque at court would ever have done.

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: A play drawing attention to the fact that it is a play.
techniques.inThisBook: Prospero's actors are spirits, his revels end, the great globe dissolves, and the last speech asks the audience to release him with their hands. The illusion is dismantled in front of the people it was made for.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: Sung lyric used to carry information a speech cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: Ariel's songs lead Ferdinand ashore, tell him his father is dead in language too beautiful to be grief, and wake Gonzalo in time to prevent a murder. The music does the work the plot would otherwise need scenes for.

techniques.name: Parody subplot
techniques.definition: A low plot that repeats the main plot's action in a debased form.
techniques.inThisBook: Stephano, Trinculo and Caliban plan exactly the crime Antonio and Sebastian plan, one scene apart, with a bottle in place of a sword — and are treated as a farce while the courtiers are treated as a threat.

techniques.name: The classical unities
techniques.definition: Keeping a play to one place, one day and one action.
techniques.inThisBook: Alone among the late plays, this one observes them: the characters repeatedly state the time, and the three hours of the story run at roughly the speed of the performance.

quotations.text: What cares these roarers for the name of king? To cabin: silence! trouble us not.
quotations.speaker: Boatswain
quotations.context: In the storm, ordering the king and his councillors below deck.
quotations.analysis: The play's first political statement is made by a working sailor to a monarch, and it is about the limits of titles. Within a hundred lines the audience learns that the storm was manufactured, so the one moment when rank genuinely counts for nothing turns out to have been arranged by a duke.

quotations.text: If by your art, my dearest father, you have Put the wild waters in this roar, allay them.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Her first words in the play, watching the wreck from the shore.
quotations.analysis: She knows at once that the storm is her father's doing, which tells the audience more about the household than any description could. The conditional 'if' is politeness rather than doubt, and the sentence ends in an imperative: the only person on the island who gives Prospero orders is fifteen.

quotations.text: What seest thou else In the dark backward and abysm of time?
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Testing how much Miranda remembers of her life before the island.
quotations.analysis: 'Backward' is used as a noun, which is not ordinary English then or now; the phrase makes the past a place you could fall into. He is checking the extent of her ignorance before deciding how much of it to repair, and the grandeur of the image conceals a piece of information management.

quotations.text: Hell is empty And all the devils are here.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Reporting how Ferdinand leapt from the burning ship.
quotations.analysis: Ariel is quoting a terrified boy, so the most famous line in the first act belongs to a character who never says it again. The joke underneath it is theological: the devils on this island are a spirit doing as it is told and a man who was once a duke.

quotations.text: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, Let me remember thee what thou hast promised, Which is not yet perform'd me.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: After performing the storm, before being sent out again.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is contractual rather than emotional: work has been done, a promise was made, the promise is outstanding. Prospero's answer is to recite the rescue from the cloven pine, which is the standard reply of an employer who would rather discuss gratitude than terms.

quotations.text: This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, Which thou takest from me.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Answering Prospero's summons, before the quarrel about his attempt on Miranda.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of inheritance law — by his mother, therefore his — which is exactly how Prospero would argue for Milan. Nobody on stage disputes the facts; they change the subject to his conduct, and the play never returns to settle the question of title.

quotations.text: You taught me language; and my profit on't Is, I know how to curse. The red plague rid you For learning me your language!
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: The end of his argument with Prospero and Miranda about his education.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is delivered in fluent blank verse, which quietly contradicts it: he has plainly got more from the lessons than curses. 'Profit' is a merchant's word, and 'learning' here means teaching — the exchange is being audited, and the pupil finds it a bad bargain.

quotations.text: Full fathom five thy father lies; Of his bones are coral made; Those are pearls that were his eyes: Nothing of him that doth fade But doth suffer a sea-change Into something rich and strange.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Sung invisibly to Ferdinand, who believes his father has drowned.
quotations.analysis: The song tells a lie — Alonso is alive — in the gentlest possible form, turning a corpse into jewellery so that grief arrives already consoled. 'Sea-change' enters English here, and the whole lyric is an argument that loss can be transformation, which is the claim the last act will have to make good.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, 1.2.461-466; sung by Ariel within Ferdinand's scene

quotations.text: I' the commonwealth I would by contraries Execute all things; for no kind of traffic Would I admit; no name of magistrate;
quotations.speaker: Gonzalo
quotations.context: Imagining what he would do if he were king of the island.
quotations.analysis: The speech follows Florio's translation of Montaigne closely enough that the borrowing is visible, and Shakespeare stages it as a joke: Antonio and Sebastian point out that a commonwealth with no sovereignty has just been proposed by a man who began by saying he would be king of it. The mockery does not dispose of the idea, and the contradiction is the play's own.

quotations.text: And by that destiny to perform an act Whereof what's past is prologue, what to come In yours and my discharge.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Persuading Sebastian to murder the sleeping Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The line is now quoted as though it were wisdom about history; in the play it is a murderer's argument that the past is merely the warm-up and the killing is the real performance. 'Prologue' and 'act' are theatre words, put into the mouth of the man whose plot competes with Prospero's for control of the island's plot.

quotations.text: Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Reassuring Stephano and Trinculo, who have heard Ariel playing on an invisible pipe.
quotations.analysis: The drunkards are frightened and the so-called monster is the one who knows the island is safe. Shakespeare gives the play's most delicate verse to the character everyone on stage calls a beast, three minutes after he has explained how to drive a nail into a man's skull.

quotations.text: Remember First to possess his books; for without them He's but a sot, as I am, nor hath not One spirit to command
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Instructing Stephano on how the murder of Prospero must be done.
quotations.analysis: It is the most accurate piece of political analysis in the play, and it comes from the servant: the power is not in the man, it is in the library. Prospero lost Milan to his books and now holds the island by them, and the only character who understands the mechanism is the one with no share in it.

quotations.text: I am your wife, if you will marry me; If not, I'll die your maid: to be your fellow You may deny me; but I'll be your servant, Whether you will or no.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Proposing to Ferdinand at the log-pile, with Prospero watching unseen.
quotations.analysis: She proposes, sets out the alternatives and closes off the last of them: the grammar moves from a condition to a refusal to accept one. Having been given no information about her own life for twelve years, she takes the single decision available to her without consulting the man who arranged the meeting.

quotations.text: Our revels now are ended. These our actors, As I foretold you, were all spirits and Are melted into air, into thin air:
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Breaking off the wedding masque on remembering Caliban's conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: He is apologising to his son-in-law for a cancelled entertainment, and the apology grows into the play's largest statement about existence within eight lines. Note that he says 'as I foretold you': the consolation is that the disappearance was always in the design, which is true of a masque and is what he needs to believe about a dukedom.

quotations.text: We are such stuff As dreams are made on, and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The close of the same speech, before he admits his mind is troubled.
quotations.analysis: 'Made on' means made of, so human beings are built out of the same material as the vanished spirits — not that life resembles a dream but that it is cut from it. 'Rounded' can mean surrounded or finished off, and the line declines to choose, which is why it can be read as consolation or as the bleakest sentence in the play.

quotations.text: A devil, a born devil, on whose nature Nurture can never stick; on whom my pains, Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost;
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after breaking off the masque.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered by a man who has just spent years teaching the creature he says cannot be taught, and the repetitions — 'all, all lost, quite lost' — are those of someone arguing with himself. It is also the play's clearest statement of the position Miranda's existence contradicts.

quotations.text: Though with their high wrongs I am struck to the quick, Yet with my nobler reason 'gaitist my fury Do I take part: the rarer action is In virtue than in vengeance
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Immediately after Ariel says that he would pity the charmed courtiers if he were human.
quotations.analysis: The decision that ends twelve years of planning is made in four lines and prompted by a spirit. 'Rarer' means both more unusual and finer, which concedes that mercy is the less natural response; and the reason he gives is not that they deserve it but that it is the better piece of work.

quotations.text: But this rough magic I here abjure, and, when I have required Some heavenly music, which even now I do, To work mine end upon their senses that This airy charm is for, I'll break my staff, Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, And deeper than did ever plummet sound I'll drown my book.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Ending the long invocation of the elves of hills, brooks and groves.
quotations.analysis: He renounces the art in the middle of using it: the sentence that abjures magic also orders up the heavenly music that will disarm his enemies. The staff is broken, but the book is drowned deeper than any sounding line can reach, which is a peculiar precaution against an object he says he no longer wants.

quotations.text: How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world, That has such people in't!
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: On seeing the assembled courtiers for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The people she is admiring include the two men who set her adrift to die and a third who tried to murder his brother two days ago. Prospero's reply — three words, 'Tis new to thee — is the most economical piece of irony in Shakespeare, and it is the last thing he says to his daughter in the play.

quotations.text: Two of these fellows you Must know and own; this thing of darkness! Acknowledge mine.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Presenting the three conspirators to Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to balance: two servants belong to the king, one belongs to me. 'Acknowledge' is doing a great deal of work — it can mean simply claiming a possession, or admitting a kinship, and the entire modern performance history of the play turns on which of those an actor decides to play.

quotations.text: As you from crimes would pardon'd be, Let your indulgence set me free.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The last two lines of the epilogue, spoken alone to the audience.
quotations.analysis: The man who has spent the play releasing or refusing to release other people ends by asking to be released himself, and the currency is applause. 'Indulgence' was also the word for a remission of punishment granted by the Church, so the audience is being asked to perform an absolution that the play's own theology could not quite supply.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After reports of the 1609 Sea Venture wreck reached London, and before the recorded court performance of November 1611.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto exists. The First Folio prints it first in the volume, at the head of the comedies.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Shipwreck pamphlets, Florio's Montaigne, Ovid and the court masque, combined rather than adapted.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I Scene 2 alone runs to about a third of the play.

criticalViews.position: The play as Shakespeare's farewell
criticalViews.summary: The oldest popular reading takes Prospero's renunciation of magic as the dramatist laying down his own art, and the epilogue as a retirement speech.
criticalViews.counter: It sits badly with the facts of the career: Shakespeare went on to collaborate on at least two more plays, and the epilogue is a conventional appeal for applause of a kind other plays also make.

criticalViews.position: The play as a colonial document
criticalViews.summary: Read beside the Bermuda pamphlets and the Virginia venture, the island becomes a place with an inhabitant, a claim and an occupation, and Caliban's case is the one the drama cannot dispose of.
criticalViews.counter: The Mediterranean geography is insistent — Milan, Naples, Tunis, Algiers — and a reading built entirely on the Atlantic has to work around it.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of service
criticalViews.summary: A third approach puts Ariel rather than Caliban at the centre and reads the island as a workplace: promised wages, deferred release, labour that is invisible because it is magical.
criticalViews.counter: It risks flattening the difference between a spirit who is freed in the last scene and a man whose future the play never mentions.

essayQuestions.question: How far does The Tempest endorse Prospero's rule of the island?
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, service and the limits of art
plan: Begin with the fact that the audience is shown the storm before it is told who made it, so the first experience of his power is as a catastrophe.
Set Ariel's petition in 1.2 beside Caliban's claim in the same scene: two servants, two grievances, two completely different answers from the same master.
Use the breaking of the masque in 4.1 to show that his control is dependent on his attention, and collapses the moment he remembers a threat.
Weigh the decision in 5.1: mercy chosen freely, but only after a spirit has had to describe what pity is.
Close on the epilogue, where a man who has ruled everything asks an audience for the power to leave.

essayQuestions.question: 'The most eloquent character in the play is its slave.' Discuss Caliban.
essayQuestions.focus: Language, dispossession and sympathy
plan: Establish what Caliban actually claims in 1.2 and note that nobody on stage denies the history, only changes the subject.
Examine the verse of 'the isle is full of noises' and ask why Shakespeare gives this speech to this character at this point in a conspiracy scene.
Balance the sympathy against 1.2 and the attempt on Miranda, which the play states plainly and does not excuse.
Compare his understanding of Prospero's power — take the books first — with the courtiers' failure to understand anything.
Finish with 'this thing of darkness', and with the play's silence about what becomes of him.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of staging the masque in Act IV and then interrupting it?
essayQuestions.focus: Spectacle, form and control
plan: Describe what a Jacobean masque was for: blessing, order, flattery of the ruler who paid for it.
Show how the Ceres and Juno masque fits that description exactly, down to the banishing of Venus and Cupid from the betrothal.
Identify the interruption as the only point where Prospero's plan is affected by something outside it.
Read the 'revels' speech as an attempt to convert a failure of stage management into a philosophy.
Consider the staging consequences: how a production makes the spirits vanish determines how seriously it takes the speech.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of The Tempest a reconciliation?
essayQuestions.focus: Forgiveness, silence and what is left unresolved
plan: List what is settled in 5.1: the dukedom restored, the marriage arranged, Ariel freed, the ship repaired.
Set against it what is not: Antonio says nothing, Sebastian jokes, Caliban's future is never mentioned.
Look closely at Miranda's 'brave new world' and Prospero's reply as a test of how much the audience is being asked to believe.
Use Gonzalo's summary at 5.1.235-241 — all of us found ourselves when no man was his own — and ask whether the play has earned it.
Decide what the epilogue changes: a character stepping out of the fiction to ask for pardon from people who have not been wronged.

discussionQuestions: Prospero forgives his enemies before any of them apologises. Does that make the forgiveness stronger or emptier?
Ariel and Caliban are both unfree. Why does the play release one and say nothing about the other?
Miranda has been told nothing about her own history until the day the play begins. What does her father gain from that?
The conspiracy of the drunkards repeats the conspiracy of the courtiers almost exactly. Why is one funny?
If a production cuts the epilogue, what is lost?

timeline.label: Florio's translation of Montaigne published
timeline.detail: The English 'Of the Cannibals' behind Gonzalo's commonwealth speech becomes available.

timeline.label: The Sea Venture wrecked on Bermuda
timeline.detail: Bound for Virginia, the ship broke up on the reefs; the survivors reached Jamestown the following year.

timeline.label: Jourdain's A Discovery of the Barmudas printed
timeline.detail: One of the pamphlets that turned the wreck into a London story of storm, survival and abundant islands.

timeline.label: Performed before James I at Whitehall on 1 November
timeline.detail: The Revels record is the earliest firm evidence that the play existed and was being acted.

timeline.label: Played at court during the festivities for Princess Elizabeth's marriage
timeline.detail: One of a group of plays given by the King's Men that winter for the betrothal and wedding celebrations.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, and the volume opens with it — unusually well printed, with full stage directions and a cast list.

timeline.label: Dryden and Davenant's The Enchanted Island
timeline.detail: A Restoration rewriting that gave Miranda a sister and Caliban a mate, and held the stage for well over a century.

timeline.label: Peter Brook directs John Gielgud as Prospero
timeline.detail: At the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre; remembered for a Prospero of severity rather than serenity.

timeline.label: Jonathan Miller's colonial production
timeline.detail: Casting made the island's politics explicit, and helped establish a reading British theatre has not since put down.

timeline.label: Peter Greenaway's Prospero's Books
timeline.detail: A film that takes the library rather than the island as the centre of the play.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor's film, with Helen Mirren as Prospera
timeline.detail: Changing the magician's sex reorganises the play's questions about parenthood, exile and authority.

places.name: Milan
places.note: The dukedom Prospero lost to his brother while he studied.

places.name: Naples
places.note: Alonso's kingdom, and the wedding party the shipwrecked court was returning from.

places.name: Tunis
places.note: Where Claribel was married, and the voyage home from which the storm interrupts.

places.name: Algiers
places.note: Argier in the text: the city from which Sycorax was banished to the island.

places.name: Bermuda
places.note: The still-vex'd Bermoothes of Ariel's speech, and the site of the 1609 wreck behind the play's storm.

places.name: Whitehall Palace, London
places.note: Where the first recorded performance was given before James I on 1 November 1611.

related.why: The other late play in which a ruler's damage is repaired after years, though there the miracle is a statue rather than a storm.
Written at about the same time, and equally willing to let romance conventions do work that tragedy would refuse.
Shipwreck, a lost daughter and reunion at sea: the pattern The Tempest compresses into one afternoon.
More's island commonwealth stands behind the tradition Gonzalo is drawing on, and being mocked for.
The earlier play of spirits, spells and interrupted entertainments, with the magic used for comedy rather than government.
